declared chart and records the one fact that the presentation's own momentum
charts satisfy it. It asserts no existence of canonical coordinates beyond
the model's charts, no global statement on multiply connected phase domains,
no dynamics and no measured value. A chart that is merely a diffeomorphism
need not be canonical; the determinant test
$|\det D\theta|=1$ is necessary but, in dimension $2m\ge4$, not sufficient
for canonicity (the scope remark of this page records the witness).

Adopt the force model with potential presentation $(U,d)$ and mechanical
Lagrangian $L=K-U$ of [[def-cm07-action-and-mechanical-lagrangian]] with the
data and conventions of [[def-cm12-cotangent-momentum]]: masses
$m_{1},\dots,m_{N}>0$ and open configuration domain $Q\subseteq\mathbb R^{3N}$
([[def-cm01-configuration]]), time window $I_{0}$, mass operator $\mathsf M$,
a $C^{2}$ potential $U:I_{0}\times Q\to\mathbb R$ of dimension
$\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-2}$ and residual forces $d$ of the standing regularity
([[def-cm03-potential-and-mechanical-energy]],
[[post-cm02-force-superposition]]). Dimensions are read by
[[def-cm01-units]], the Euclidean product on $\mathbb R^{3N}$ is
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]], and differentiability classes are those of
[[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]. Write $n:=3N\ge1$. The
Cartesian momentum phase chart of the presentation is
$I_{0}\times Q\times\mathbb R^{3N}$ with the momentum $p=\mathsf Mv$ of
[[def-cm12-cotangent-momentum]], and the momentum phase chart of a
generalized-coordinate map $X:\Omega\to Q$ with $r$ coordinates is
$I_{0}\times\Omega\times\mathbb R^{r}$ with the generalized momentum
$P=G(q)v$, $G(q)=DX(q)^{\mathsf T}\mathsf M\,DX(q)$
([[def-cm07-generalized-coordinates-and-forces]],
[[def-cm12-hyperregularity]]).

**(a) Cartesian chart.** The **Cartesian phase domain of the presentation** is
the nonempty open set

$$W:=Q\times\mathbb R^{3N}\subseteq\mathbb R^{2n},\qquad z=(x,p),$$

a phase domain in the sense of [[def-cm-phase-domain-and-standard-symplectic-two-form]]
(openness is clause (a) of [[def-cm01-configuration]]). On $W$ the
**canonical one-form of the presentation in the Cartesian chart** is the smooth
one-form

$$\lambda_{(x,p)}(\delta x,\delta p):=p\cdot\delta x\qquad\bigl((x,p)\in W,\ (\delta x,\delta p)\in\mathbb R^{3N}\times\mathbb R^{3N}\bigr),$$

where $p\cdot\delta x$ is the Euclidean pairing of the momentum covector with
the displacement, and the **two-form of the presentation in the Cartesian
chart** is

$$\omega:=-d\lambda$$

([[def-smooth-differential-k-form]]). In coordinates, reading
$x=(x^{1},\dots,x^{3N})$ and $p=(p_{1},\dots,p_{3N})$ as the standard
coordinates of $W$,

$$\lambda=\sum_{a=1}^{3N}p_{a}\,dx^{a},\qquad \omega=\sum_{a=1}^{3N}dx^{a}\wedge dp_{a},\qquad \omega_{(x,p)}\bigl((\delta x,\delta p),(\delta x',\delta p')\bigr)=\delta x\cdot\delta p'-\delta p\cdot\delta x',$$

the last identity using the Euclidean product. The dimension of both forms is
that of action, $\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-1}$: the pairing of a momentum
($\mu\ell\tau^{-1}$) with a displacement ($\ell$). The forms have no
explicit time dependence; for each $t\in I_{0}$ the slice $\{t\}\times W$
carries the same two-form. The momentum phase chart with time,
$I_{0}\times W$ with coordinates $(t,x,p)$, is the domain of the Hamiltonians
and fields of this page. The **sign convention** fixed by
[[def-hamiltonian-vector-field-and-hamiltonian-function]] and used
throughout is $\iota_{X}\omega=dH$; $H$ denotes a phase function as in that
item.

**(b) Generalized-coordinate chart.** Let $X:\Omega\to Q$ be a
generalized-coordinate map with substituted Lagrangian $\widetilde L$ and
kinetic metric $G$, and let $r$ be its number of coordinates
([[def-cm07-generalized-coordinates-and-forces]]). The **chart map of the
presentation in the coordinates $X$** is

$$\Phi_{X}:\Omega\times\mathbb R^{r}\longrightarrow Q\times\mathbb R^{3N},\qquad \Phi_{X}(q,P):=\Bigl(X(q),\ \mathsf M\,DX(q)\,G(q)^{-1}P\Bigr).$$

Here $DX(q)$ is the $(3N)\times r$ Jacobian of $X$ at $q$
([[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]), $G(q)=DX(q)^{\mathsf T}\mathsf M\,DX(q)$
is symmetric positive definite ([[def-transpose-of-a-matrix]],
[[def-invertible-matrix-and-general-linear-group]]), and $P$ is a
generalized momentum. The image of $\Phi_{X}$ is

$$\Phi_{X}(\Omega\times\mathbb R^{r})=\bigl\{\,(X(q),\mathsf M\,DX(q)v)\ :\ q\in\Omega,\ v\in\mathbb R^{r}\,\bigr\},$$

the momentum chart of the presentation in the coordinates $X$; indeed
$P\mapsto v=G(q)^{-1}P$ is a linear bijection of $\mathbb R^{r}$. The map
$\Phi_{X}$ is $C^{1}$ by the displayed algebra, and it is a $C^{1}$ immersion:
its derivative is injective at every point, because $DX(q)$ is injective
([[def-cm07-generalized-coordinates-and-forces]],
[[def-euclidean-submersions-and-immersions]]) and $P\mapsto G(q)^{-1}P$ is a
linear bijection; when $r=3N$ its derivative is invertible and it is a local
diffeomorphism onto $W$
(equivalently $\mathsf M\,DX(q)G(q)^{-1}=DX(q)^{-\mathsf T}$: see the
recorded identity below). The **forms of the presentation in the
coordinates $X$** are the pullbacks

$$\lambda_{X}:=\Phi_{X}^{*}\lambda,\qquad \omega_{X}:=\Phi_{X}^{*}\omega$$

([[def-pullback-of-a-differential-form]]). In the coordinates $(q,P)$ on
$\Omega\times\mathbb R^{r}$ the following identities hold, and are proved in
clause 2 of the symplectic-structure theorem of this page:

$$\lambda_{X}=\sum_{a=1}^{r}P_{a}\,dq^{a},\qquad \omega_{X}=\sum_{a=1}^{r}dq^{a}\wedge dP_{a};$$

moreover, when $r=3N$ and $DX(q)$ is invertible,
$\mathsf M\,DX(q)G(q)^{-1}=DX(q)^{-\mathsf T}$, so that on an open
generalized-coordinate chart the chart map reads
$\Phi_{X}(q,P)=\bigl(X(q),DX(q)^{-\mathsf T}P\bigr)$ and the chart
transition between the two descriptions of the same momentum datum is a
$C^{1}$ local diffeomorphism.

**(c) Status.** The item defines the two-form datum of the declared
presentation on its declared charts, together with the sign convention for
fields. It asserts no closedness, no nondegeneracy, no equation of motion, no
conservation law and no measured value; those are the subject of the other
items of this page. The forms depend on the declared chart and its coordinate
dimensions, but not on the residual forces $d$ nor on the normalization
$U\mapsto U+c(t)$ of the potential representative. All objects are model
objects of the idealization declared by the force branch.

Lagrangian $L=K-U$ of [[def-cm07-action-and-mechanical-lagrangian]] with the
data, charts and forms of [[def-cm13-two-form]]: masses $m_{1},\dots,m_{N}>0$,
open configuration domain $Q\subseteq\mathbb R^{3N}$ and mass operator
$\mathsf M$ ([[def-cm01-configuration]]), time window $I_{0}$, $C^{2}$
potential $U$ and residual forces $d$ of the standing regularity
([[def-cm03-potential-and-mechanical-energy]],
[[post-cm02-force-superposition]], [[def-cm01-units]]), the Cartesian phase
domain $W=Q\times\mathbb R^{3N}$ with $n=3N$, its canonical one-form
$\lambda$ and two-form $\omega=-d\lambda$, and for each generalized-coordinate
map $X:\Omega\to Q$ with $r$ coordinates and kinetic metric $G$ the chart map
$\Phi_{X}(q,P)=(X(q),\mathsf M\,DX(q)G(q)^{-1}P)$ with pullbacks
$\lambda_{X}=\Phi_{X}^{*}\lambda$ and $\omega_{X}=\Phi_{X}^{*}\omega$
([[def-cm07-generalized-coordinates-and-forces]],

2. **(generalized-coordinate chart)** On $\Omega\times\mathbb R^{r}$,

The statement is a conditional deduction from the adopted force branch, the
declared presentation and the cited mathematics. It asserts no equation of
motion, no conservation law, no completeness of any flow and no empirical
content.

Let $(I,\theta)$ be period-one action-angle coordinates with
$\omega=\sum_{i=1}^n d\theta_i\wedge dI_i$ as supplied by
[[thm-cm-liouville-arnold-action-angle-repaired]] and
[[def-action-and-angle-coordinates]]. Define the rescaled coordinates

$$\theta_i^{\mathrm{rad}}:=2\pi\,\theta_i,\qquad I_i^{\mathrm{rad}}:=\frac{I_i}{2\pi}\qquad(i=1,\dots,n).$$

Then $(\theta^{\mathrm{rad}},I^{\mathrm{rad}})$ are $C^\infty$ coordinates on the same chart,

$$\omega=\sum_{i=1}^n d\theta_i^{\mathrm{rad}}\wedge dI_i^{\mathrm{rad}},$$

the angles $\theta^{\mathrm{rad}}$ are $2\pi$-periodic (radian-valued), and if a Hamiltonian is
$H=h(I)$ with $h$ of class $C^2$ in the period-one coordinates then in the radian coordinates it is
$H=\tilde h(I^{\mathrm{rad}})$ with $\tilde h(I^{\mathrm{rad}})=h(2\pi I^{\mathrm{rad}})$ and
$\dot\theta^{\mathrm{rad}}_i=\partial\tilde h/\partial I^{\mathrm{rad}}_i$.

Adopt the force model with potential presentation $(U,d)$ and mechanical
Lagrangian $L=K-U$ of [[def-cm07-action-and-mechanical-lagrangian]] with the
data, charts and Hamiltonian field of [[def-cm13-two-form]],
[[def-cm13-hamiltonian-field]]: masses $m_{1},\dots,m_{N}>0$ and open
configuration domain $Q\subseteq\mathbb R^{3N}$ with mass operator
$\mathsf M$ ([[def-cm01-configuration]]), time window $I_{0}$, $C^{2}$
potential $U$ and residual forces $d$ of the standing regularity
([[def-cm03-potential-and-mechanical-energy]],
[[post-cm02-force-superposition]], [[def-cm01-units]]), the Cartesian
Hamiltonian $H(t,x,p)=\tfrac12p\cdot\mathsf M^{-1}p+U(t,x)$ and, for a
generalized-coordinate map $X:\Omega\to Q$ with kinetic metric
$G=DX^{\mathsf T}\mathsf M\,DX$, the chart Hamiltonian
$\widetilde H(t,q,P)=\tfrac12P\cdot G(q)^{-1}P+\widetilde U(t,q)$
([[def-cm12-hamiltonian]], [[pthm-cm12-mechanical-hyperregularity]],
[[def-cm07-generalized-coordinates-and-forces]],
[[def-cm12-cotangent-momentum]]). Let $J\subseteq I_{0}$ be a nonempty open
interval. Then:

1. **(potential branch, Cartesian chart)** Assume $d\equiv0$ on the state
   domain. For a $C^{2}$ curve $x:J\to Q$ with $p(t):=\mathsf Mx'(t)$ the
   following are equivalent: (a) $x$ is a motion of the model
   ([[def-cm02-newtonian-flow]]); (b) $\dot x(t)=H_{p}(t,x(t),p(t))$ and
   $\dot p(t)=-H_{x}(t,x(t),p(t))$ for every $t\in J$; (c) the curve
   $t\mapsto(x(t),p(t))$ is an integral curve of the time-dependent field
   $t\mapsto X_{H_{t}}$, i.e. satisfies
   $\dot z(t)=X_{H_{t}}(z(t))$ with $z=(x,p)$
   ([[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]]).
2. **(generalized-coordinate chart)** Let $X:\Omega\to Q$ be a
   generalized-coordinate map and let $q:J\to\Omega$ be a $C^{2}$ curve with
   $x:=X\circ q$ and $P(t):=G(q(t))q'(t)$. Then the declared Lagrange
   equations with residual generalized force,
   $\Lambda(\widetilde L)(q)(t)=Q^{\mathrm{res}}(t,q(t),q'(t))$, are
   equivalent to
   $q'(t)=\widetilde H_{P}(t,q(t),P(t))$ and
   $P'(t)=-\widetilde H_{q}(t,q(t),P(t))+Q^{\mathrm{res}}(t,q(t),q'(t))$;
   in particular, when $d\equiv0$, they are equivalent to
   $(q,P)$ being an integral curve of $X_{\widetilde H_{t}}$.
3. **(residual forces, Cartesian chart)** For a $C^{2}$ curve $x:J\to Q$
   with $p=\mathsf Mx'$, the model's forced equation
   $\mathsf Mx''=-\nabla_{x}U(t,x)+d(t,x,x')$ holds on $J$ if and only if
   $\dot x=H_{p}$ and $\dot p=-H_{x}+d(t,x,\mathsf M^{-1}p)$ on $J$.
4. **(when is the forced field Hamiltonian?)** The forced field
   $(x,p)\mapsto\bigl(\mathsf M^{-1}p,-\nabla_{x}U(t,x)+d(t,x,\mathsf M^{-1}p)\bigr)$
   is the Hamiltonian field of a $C^{2}$ phase function on its domain if and
   only if there is a $C^{2}$ function $V:I_{0}\times Q\to\mathbb R$ with
   $d(t,x,v)=-\nabla_{x}V(t,x)$ for every $(t,x,v)$ of the state domain; in
   that case the phase function is $H+V$ up to an independently chosen
   additive $C^2$ function of $t$ on each connected component of $Q$, and the model's forced motions are the motions of the potential
   presentation $(U+V,0)$.

The statement is conditional on the adopted force branch, the declared
presentation and the declared chart; it asserts no existence or uniqueness of
solutions, no completeness, no conservation law and no empirical content.

Adopt the force model with potential presentation $(U,d)$ and mechanical
Lagrangian $L=K-U$ of [[def-cm07-action-and-mechanical-lagrangian]] with the
data and conventions of [[def-cm12-cotangent-momentum]]: masses
$m_{1},\dots,m_{N}>0$, open configuration domain $Q\subseteq\mathbb R^{3N}$,
time window $I_{0}$, mass operator $\mathsf M$
([[def-cm01-configuration]]), $C^{2}$ potential
$U:I_{0}\times Q\to\mathbb R$ and residual forces $d$ of the standing
regularity ([[def-cm03-potential-and-mechanical-energy]],
[[post-cm02-force-superposition]]). Let $H$ be the Cartesian Hamiltonian of
[[def-cm12-hamiltonian]], let $X:\Omega\to Q$ be a generalized-coordinate map
with substituted Lagrangian $\widetilde L$, kinetic metric
$G(q)=DX(q)^{\mathsf T}\mathsf M\,DX(q)$, substituted potential
$\widetilde U(t,q)=U(t,X(q))$ and residual generalized force
$Q^{\mathrm{res}}(t,q,v)=DX(q)^{\mathsf T}d(t,X(q),DX(q)v)$, and let
$\widetilde H$ be the Hamiltonian in the coordinates $X$
([[def-cm07-generalized-coordinates-and-forces]],
[[def-cm12-hamiltonian]]). Let $J\subseteq I_{0}$ be a nonempty open interval
and let $x:J\to Q$ be a $C^{2}$ curve, with $p(t):=\mathsf Mx'(t)$
([[def-cm12-cotangent-momentum]]). Then:

1. **(potential branch)** Assume $d\equiv0$ on the state domain. The following
   are equivalent:
   (a) $x$ is a motion of the model on $J$
   ([[def-cm02-newtonian-flow]]);
   (b) $(x,p)$ satisfies $x'(t)=H_{p}\bigl(t,x(t),p(t)\bigr)$ and
   $p'(t)=-H_{x}\bigl(t,x(t),p(t)\bigr)$ for every $t\in J$;
   (c) for all reals $a<b$ with $[a,b]\subseteq J$ the restriction
   $x|_{[a,b]}$ is stationary for the action $S$ of $L$ on $[a,b]$
   ([[def-cm-time-dependent-lagrangian-and-action]],
   [[pthm-cm07-euler-lagrange-equations]]).

2. **(residual forces)** For a $C^{2}$ curve $x:J\to Q$ with
   $p(t)=\mathsf Mx'(t)$ the following are equivalent:
   (a) $\mathsf Mx''(t)=-\nabla_{x}U\bigl(t,x(t)\bigr)+d\bigl(t,x(t),x'(t)\bigr)$
   for every $t\in J$;
   (b) $x'(t)=H_{p}\bigl(t,x(t),p(t)\bigr)$ and
   $p'(t)=-H_{x}\bigl(t,x(t),p(t)\bigr)+d\bigl(t,x(t),\mathsf M^{-1}p(t)\bigr)$
   for every $t\in J$.

3. **(coordinate form)** Let $q:J\to\Omega$ be a $C^{2}$ curve and put

   [[def-cm07-generalized-coordinates-and-forces]] clause (e) are equivalent

$$\Lambda(\widetilde L)(q)(t)=Q^{\mathrm{res}}\bigl(t,q(t),q'(t)\bigr)\ \Longleftrightarrow\ q'(t)=\widetilde H_{p}\bigl(t,q(t),p(t)\bigr),\quad p'(t)=-\widetilde H_{q}\bigl(t,q(t),p(t)\bigr)+Q^{\mathrm{res}}\bigl(t,q(t),q'(t)\bigr);$$

   in particular, when $d\equiv0$ the vanishing of the Lagrange operator is
   equivalent to $q'=\widetilde H_{p}$ and $p'=-\widetilde H_{q}$.

4. **(constraint elimination)** Assume in addition that $d\equiv0$ and that

   locus in the sense of [[def-cm07-generalized-coordinates-and-forces]]
   clause (d), with the ideal-reaction law of
   [[post-cm06-ideal-reaction-law]]. Then the equivalent conditions of
   clause 3 with $Q^{\mathrm{res}}\equiv0$ hold for $q$ if and only if
   $x=X\circ q$ is a constrained motion of the model with an ideal reaction
   ([[pthm-cm07-lagrangian-reduction-of-ideal-constraints]]).

The statement is conditional on the adopted force branch, the declared
presentation, the declared chart and, in clause 4, the constraint datum and
ideal-reaction law; it asserts no existence or uniqueness of solutions, no
conservation law and no empirical content.

Let a force model of [[post-cm02-force-superposition]] be given: time window
$I_{0}\subseteq\mathbb R$ nondegenerate and open, configuration domain
$Q\subseteq\mathbb R^{3N}$ open ([[def-cm01-configuration]] clause (a)),
fixed masses $m_{1},\dots,m_{N}>0$ ([[post-cm01-worldlines]] clause (v)), and a
force map $F$ with the standing continuity and state-local-Lipschitz
hypotheses of clause (iii) of that postulate.

**(a) State domain and inverse-mass operator.** The **state domain** of the
model is

$$D:=I_{0}\times Q\times(\mathbb R^{3})^{N}\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^{3N}\times\mathbb R^{3N},$$

an open subset of $\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^{6N}$; a point $(t,x,v)\in D$ is a
time together with the **state** $z=(x,v)$ of positions $x\in Q$ and coordinate
velocities $v\in(\mathbb R^{3})^{N}$ of the labels ([[def-cm01-velocity-acceleration]],
[[def-cm01-units]]). The **inverse-mass operator** is the linear map

$$\mathsf M^{-1}:\mathbb R^{3N}\to\mathbb R^{3N},\qquad \mathsf M^{-1}(u_{1},\dots,u_{N}):=\Bigl(\frac{u_{1}}{m_{1}},\dots,\frac{u_{N}}{m_{N}}\Bigr),$$

the inverse of the mass operator $\mathsf M$ of clause (d) of
[[def-cm01-configuration]].

**(b) Associated first-order system.** The **associated first-order field** of
the model is

$$\mathcal F:D\longrightarrow\mathbb R^{3N}\times\mathbb R^{3N},\qquad \mathcal F(t,x,v):=\Bigl(v,\ \mathsf M^{-1}F(t,x,v)\Bigr),$$

and the **associated first-order system** is $z'=\mathcal F(t,z)$ on the open
domain $D$, in the sense of
[[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]]; here
$z=(x,v)\in\mathbb R^{6N}$. The map $\mathcal F$ satisfies the
Picard–Lindelöf hypotheses of
[[thm-picard-lindelof-local-existence-and-uniqueness]]: it is continuous on
$D$, and it is locally Lipschitz in the state variable $z$ locally uniformly
in time, because its first component $z\mapsto v$ is linear and its second is
the composition of the force map $F$ — which is locally Lipschitz in $(x,v)$
locally uniformly in time by [[post-cm02-force-superposition]] clause (iii) —
with the linear map $\mathsf M^{-1}$.

**(c) Motions.** Let $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval with nonempty
interior, endpoints read with one-sided derivatives as in
[[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]]. A **motion** of
the model on $J$ is a curve $x:J\to Q$ of class $C^{2}$ such that
$t\in I_{0}$ for every $t\in J$ and

$$m_{i}\,\ddot x_{i}(t)=F_{i}\bigl(t,x(t),\dot x(t)\bigr)\qquad(i=1,\dots,N,\ t\in J).$$

Equivalently: the state curve $z=(x,\dot x):J\to D$ is a solution of the
associated first-order system on $J$. Indeed, if $x$ is a motion then
$z=(x,x')$ is $C^{1}$ with
$z'=(x',x'')=(x',\mathsf M^{-1}F(t,x,x'))=\mathcal F(t,z)$ and $z(t)\in D$;
conversely, if $z=(x,v)$ is a solution with $z(t)\in D$ for all $t$, then
$x'=v$ and $v'=\mathsf M^{-1}F(t,x,v)$, so $v$ is $C^{1}$, $x$ is $C^{2}$, and
multiplying the second equation by the masses returns the displayed
second-order equation. Motions of the labels of the model are exactly these
curves by [[post-cm02-force-superposition]] clause (iv).

**(d) Initial data and maximal motion.** An **initial datum** of the model is
a triple $(t_{0},x_{0},v_{0})$ with $t_{0}\in I_{0}$, $x_{0}\in Q$ and
$v_{0}\in(\mathbb R^{3})^{N}$; write $z_{0}:=(x_{0},v_{0})$. A **maximal
motion** with this datum is a motion $x:J_{\max}\to Q$ with $x(t_{0})=x_{0}$
and $\dot x(t_{0})=v_{0}$ that has no extension to a motion of the model on a
strictly larger interval. By the Picard–Lindelöf hypotheses verified in (b)
and the maximal-solution theorem
[[thm-existence-and-uniqueness-of-a-maximal-ode-solution]] (with
[[def-maximal-ode-solution]]): every initial datum has exactly one maximal
motion, its **maximal interval** $J_{\max}$ is an open interval containing
$t_{0}$ and contained in $I_{0}$, and every motion with the same datum is the
restriction of the maximal one. The restriction statement transfers from the
associated first-order system to motions through the equivalence in (c).

**(e) Newtonian flow.** The **Newtonian flow** of the model is the map

$$\Phi:\Omega\longrightarrow Q\times\mathbb R^{3N},\qquad \Omega:=\bigl\{(t,t_{0},z_{0}):t_{0}\in I_{0},\ z_{0}\in Q\times\mathbb R^{3N},\ t\in J_{\max}(t_{0},z_{0})\bigr\},$$

defined by $\Phi(t;t_{0},z_{0}):=z(t)$, where $t\mapsto z(t)=(x(t),\dot x(t))$
is the state curve of the maximal motion with datum $(t_{0},z_{0})$. By (d) the
assignment is well defined: the maximal motion is unique, so $\Phi$ is a
function on $\Omega$ and not merely a relation. For fixed $t_{0}$ and $z_{0}$
the curve $t\mapsto\Phi(t;t_{0},z_{0})$ is defined exactly on the maximal
interval $J_{\max}(t_{0},z_{0})$.

Adopt the force model with potential presentation $(U,d)$ and mechanical
Lagrangian $L=K-U$ of [[def-cm07-action-and-mechanical-lagrangian]], in the
fixed inertial frame with adapted coordinates $(t,x)$ used there: $N\ge1$
labels with masses $m_{1},\dots,m_{N}>0$, open configuration domain
$Q\subseteq\mathbb R^{3N}$, time window $I_{0}$, mass operator $\mathsf M$
([[def-cm01-configuration]]), $C^{2}$ potential $U:I_{0}\times Q\to\mathbb R$
of dimension $\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-2}$ and residual forces $d$ of the standing
regularity ([[def-cm03-potential-and-mechanical-energy]],
[[post-cm02-force-superposition]]). Dimensions are read by [[def-cm01-units]],
the Euclidean inner product of $\mathbb R^{3N}$ is [[def-euclidean-inner-product]],
and gradients and Jacobians are those of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]
and [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]].

**(a) Cartesian momentum.** For a state $(t,x,v)\in I_{0}\times Q\times\mathbb R^{3N}$
define the **momentum of the labels** by

$$p(t,x,v):=\mathsf M v\;=\;(m_{1}v_{1},\dots,m_{N}v_{N}),$$

whose label components are $p_{i}=m_{i}v_{i}$ ([[def-cm01-configuration]]
clause (d)); its dimension is $\mu\ell\tau^{-1}$ (read in
$\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm m\,\mathrm s^{-1}$). The space $\mathbb R^{3N}$ is
identified with its dual by the Euclidean inner product, so that $p$ is a
**covector** acting on a velocity $w$ by the dot product $p\cdot w$. The pair
$(x,p)$ is the **cotangent datum** of the state, and $I_{0}\times Q\times\mathbb R^{3N}$
with coordinates $(t,x,p)$ is the **momentum phase chart** of the
presentation.

**(b) Fibre derivative.** The **fibre derivative** (the velocity Legendre
coordinate) of the presentation is $p:=\mathcal L_{v}(t,x,v)$, the Legendre
map of the fibre-full chart $(O,L)$ of clause (c) of
[[def-cm07-action-and-mechanical-lagrangian]], in the sense of
[[def-cm-legendre-map-in-a-time-dependent-chart]] (the chart data are those of
[[def-cm-time-dependent-lagrangian-and-action]]). Because $L=K-U$ with
$K'(v)=\mathsf Mv$ and $U$ independent of the velocity slot (clause (a) of
[[def-cm07-action-and-mechanical-lagrangian]]), one has
$\mathcal L_{v}(t,x,v)=\mathsf Mv$: the fibre derivative and the momentum of
clause (a) are the same covector, and the Legendre map of the presentation is
$(t,x,v)\mapsto(t,x,\mathsf Mv)$.

**(c) Generalized momenta.** Let $X:\Omega\to Q$ be a generalized-coordinate
map of the model, with substituted Lagrangian $\widetilde L$, substituted
potential $\widetilde U$ and kinetic metric $G(q)=DX(q)^{\mathsf T}\mathsf M\,DX(q)$
([[def-cm07-generalized-coordinates-and-forces]] clauses (a)-(b),
[[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]], [[def-transpose-of-a-matrix]]).
The **generalized momentum** of the presentation in the coordinates $X$ is
the covector

$$p(t,q,v):=\widetilde L_{v}(t,q,v)=G(q)v,$$

whose components $p_{a}=\partial\widetilde L/\partial v_{a}$ have dimension
$\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-1}\gamma_{a}^{-1}$ (action divided by the dimension
$\gamma_{a}$ of the coordinate $q_{a}$), while the **pairing**
$p\cdot v=\sum_{a}p_{a}v^{a}$ has dimension $\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-2}$. For the
Cartesian chart, $X=\mathrm{id}$, $\Omega=Q$, $G=\mathsf M$, and clause (c)
reduces to clause (a).

**(d) Status and warnings.** The item defines the momentum datum of a declared
presentation as a model object. It introduces no force law, no equation of
motion and no measured value; it depends on the declared chart and on the
declared coordinate dimensions $\gamma_{a}$, and it is independent of the
residual forces $d$ and of the normalization $U\mapsto U+c(t)$ of the
potential representative ([[def-cm03-potential-and-mechanical-energy]]
clause (c)). The momentum is not in general mass times coordinate velocity: in
the coordinates $X$ it is $G(q)v$, and the identity $p_{i}=m_{i}v_{i}$ is
specific to Cartesian data. The evaluation of the velocity Hessian, the
invertibility of the fiberwise momentum map, the Hamiltonian of an inverse
branch and the evolution equations are the subject of the other items of this
page, not of this definition. All differentiability classes are those of
[[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]].

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: Clauses 1 and 3: by [F1] the hypotheses of [F2] are in force, so after shrinking the base ball and the neighbourhood there is a $C^{\infty}$ diffeomorphism $(I,\theta):U\to B'\times T^{n}$ onto its image with $\omega=\sum_{i}d\theta_{i}\wedge dI_{i}$ and every $C^{\infty}$ function constant on the fibres of $\pi$ (in particular each $F_{i}$, and $H=F_{1}$) a function of $I$ alone; write $F_{i}=f_{i}(I)$ and $H=h(I)=f_{1}(I)$.

Clause 2: by [F4] the two-form has action dimension; in the coordinates $(I,\theta)$ the form is $\sum_{i}d\theta_{i}\wedge dI_{i}$ with the angles period-one and dimensionless by [F2] and [[def-action-and-angle-coordinates]], so comparing dimensions term by term gives $[I_{i}]=\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-1}$.

Clause 4: in the canonical chart $(\theta,I)$ of the presentation the field of the $C^{\infty}$ function $h(I)$ has, by [F3] applied with $q=\theta$, $p=I$, the components $X_{h}=(\partial h/\partial I,0)$; hence its integral curves satisfy $\dot I=0$ and $\dot\theta=\partial h/\partial I(I)$, and integrating on $\mathbb R^{n}/\mathbb Z^{n}$ gives the displayed linear formula. By [F6] these integral curves are exactly the momentum-phase curves of the model's motions on $U$ (on the potential branch).

Clause 5: [F5] applied to the coordinates of step 1.1 gives the invariance of the two-form under the rescaling, the transformed Hamiltonian $\tilde h$ and the rescaled evolution equation; the relation $\dot\theta^{\mathrm{rad}}=2\pi\dot\theta$ identifies the cyclic frequencies $\partial h/\partial I_{i}$ of clause 4 with the angular rates $2\pi\partial h/\partial I_{i}$ in the radian chart.
Collection: clause 1 is step 1.1 (form), clause 2 is step 1.2, clause 3 is step 1.1 (fibrewise constants), clause 4 is step 2.1 and clause 5 is step 3.1; this proves the statement.

boundaries.evidence: The base ball and the saturated neighbourhood are nonempty and the fibre is nonempty by the regular-value hypothesis (statement, step 1.1).
The angle zero is a point of the torus and the linear formula is read modulo $\mathbb Z^{n}$; a vanishing frequency is allowed and gives a constant angle (statement, step 2.1).
$n=1$ is included and is realized by the oscillator example on the companion page (statement, step 1.1).
Critical (nonregular) fibres are excluded by the regularity and compactness hypotheses; the shrinking of the base ball keeps the fibres regular (statement, step 1.1).

boundaries.reason: The tori have no boundary and the linear formula is stated modulo $\mathbb Z^{n}$ (statement).

boundaries.evidence: $\mathrm{AC}_{\omega}$ is assumed in the statement and consumed through the cited repaired action-angle theorem in step 1.1.

boundaries.reason: The statement collects existence, dimension, fibre-function and motion conclusions; no equivalence is asserted.
No reverse implication is asserted by the statement.

citations.quote:
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_{\omega}$
([[def-countable-choice]]). Adopt the force model with potential
presentation $(U,d)$ and mechanical Lagrangian $L=K-U$ of
[[def-cm07-action-and-mechanical-lagrangian]], with the momentum charts,
forms and canonical coordinates of [[def-cm13-two-form]],
[[pthm-cm13-two-form-is-symplectic]] and [[def-cm13-canonical-form]], the
Hamiltonian fields of [[def-cm13-hamiltonian-field]], the bracket of
[[def-cm13-poisson]] and the branch Hamiltonian $H$ of
[[def-cm12-hamiltonian]]. Let $W_{0}$ be a nonempty open phase domain of a
momentum chart, of dimension $2n$, and let $F=(F_{1}=H|_{W_{0}},\dots,F_{n})$
be a completely integrable datum of the presentation on $W_{0}$
([[def-cm14-complete-integrability]]). Let $b_{0}$ be a regular value with
nonempty compact connected regular fibre $N=F^{-1}(b_{0})$, and assume
that there are a saturated open neighbourhood $U\subseteq W_{0}$ of $N$
and a ball $B\subseteq\mathbb R^{n}$ of regular values with $F(U)=B$ such
that $\pi=F|_{U}:U\to B$ is a proper submersion with connected fibres.
Then, after shrinking $B$ to a smaller ball $B'$ and $U$ to
$\pi^{-1}(B')$ (and writing $U$ for the shrunk neighbourhood again), there
are action-angle coordinates

$$(I,\theta):U\longrightarrow B'\times T^{n},\qquad T^{n}=\mathbb R^{n}/\mathbb Z^{n},$$

of class $C^{\infty}$, diffeomorphic onto their image, such that:

1. **(form)** the angles are period-one and the presentation's two-form
   takes the canonical action-angle form
   $$\omega=\sum_{i=1}^{n}d\theta_{i}\wedge dI_{i}$$
   on $U$, in the sense of [[def-action-and-angle-coordinates]];
2. **(dimension)** each action coordinate $I_{i}$ has dimension
   $\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-1}$ (action) and each angle $\theta_{i}$ is
   dimensionless, consistently with the action dimension of the
   presentation's two-form in its original canonical charts
   ([[def-cm01-units]]);
3. **(fibrewise constants)** every $C^{\infty}$ function on $U$ that is
   constant on the fibres of $\pi$ is a function of $I$ alone; in
   particular $F_{i}=f_{i}(I)$ for $C^{\infty}$ functions $f_{i}$ and the
   branch Hamiltonian is $H=h(I)$ with $h=f_{1}$;
4. **(linear motion)** the solutions of the Hamiltonian system of $h$ in
   the chart $(I,\theta)$ are exactly the momentum-phase curves of the
   model's motions on $U$ (which is the presentation reading of clause 1
   of [[pthm-cm13-hamiltonian-field-integrates-the-model-equations]]),
   and they satisfy
$$\dot I=0,\qquad \dot\theta=\frac{\partial h}{\partial I}(I),\qquad\theta(t)=\theta(0)+t\,\frac{\partial h}{\partial I}\bigl(I(0)\bigr)\pmod{\mathbb Z^{n}},$$
   so that each motion on a torus is periodic or dense according to its
   frequency vector;
5. **(radian rescaling)** with the rescaled coordinates
   $\theta^{\mathrm{rad}}:=2\pi\theta$ and
   $I^{\mathrm{rad}}:=I/(2\pi)$ one has
   $\omega=\sum_{i}d\theta^{\mathrm{rad}}_{i}\wedge dI^{\mathrm{rad}}_{i}$,
   the angles $\theta^{\mathrm{rad}}$ are $2\pi$-periodic, and
   $H=\tilde h(I^{\mathrm{rad}})$ with
   $\tilde h(I^{\mathrm{rad}})=h(2\pi I^{\mathrm{rad}})$ and
   $\dot\theta^{\mathrm{rad}}=\partial\tilde h/\partial I^{\mathrm{rad}}$;
   the components $\partial h/\partial I_{i}$ are **cyclic frequencies**
   (cycles per unit time), not angular rates, the angular rates being
   $2\pi\,\partial h/\partial I_{i}$.

The statement is conditional on the adopted force branch, the declared
presentation, the smooth completely integrable datum, the fibre
hypotheses and $\mathrm{AC}_{\omega}$; it asserts no global
action-angle coordinates on $W_{0}$, no statement about critical or
noncompact fibres and no empirical content.

Adopt the force model with potential presentation $(U,d)$ and mechanical
Lagrangian $L=K-U$ of [[def-cm07-action-and-mechanical-lagrangian]] with the
momentum charts, the phase domains and the two-form datum of
[[def-cm13-two-form]]: the Cartesian phase domain $W=Q\times\mathbb R^{3N}$
with $n=3N$, its two-form $\omega$, and for each generalized-coordinate map
$X:\Omega\to Q$ with $r$ coordinates the chart map $\Phi_{X}$ and the form
$\omega_{X}$ ([[def-cm07-generalized-coordinates-and-forces]],
[[def-cm12-cotangent-momentum]], [[def-cm01-configuration]]). All
differentiability classes are those of
[[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]].

**(a) Canonical coordinates.** Let $W_{0}\subseteq W$ (or
$W_{0}\subseteq\Omega\times\mathbb R^{r}$) be nonempty open, and let

$$\theta=(\theta^{1},\dots,\theta^{2m}):W_{0}\longrightarrow V\subseteq\mathbb R^{2m}$$

be a $C^{1}$ chart of $W_{0}$ onto an open set $V$ ([[def-metric-topology]]),
with $m$ the half-dimension of $W_{0}$. The coordinates $\theta$ are
**canonical coordinates for the presentation's two-form** on $W_{0}$ when the
two-form takes the **canonical form**

$$\omega=\sum_{a=1}^{m}d\theta^{a}\wedge d\theta^{m+a}$$

on $W_{0}$ ([[def-smooth-differential-k-form]]); equivalently, when the
pullback identity $\theta^{*}\omega_{V}^{\mathrm{st}}=\omega|_{W_{0}}$ holds
for the standard two-form $\omega_{V}^{\mathrm{st}}$ of $V$
([[def-cm-phase-domain-and-standard-symplectic-two-form]],
[[def-pullback-of-a-differential-form]]), equivalently when
$D\theta(z)^{\mathsf T}J\,D\theta(z)=J$ for the standard symplectic matrix
$J$ at every $z\in W_{0}$
([[prop-cm-canonical-map-tests-and-hamiltonian-transport]]). A **canonical
chart of the presentation** is a chart whose coordinates are canonical in
this sense; the equivalence with the canonical maps defined later on this
page is recorded with those definitions.

**(b) The model's own charts are canonical.** The Cartesian coordinates
$(x,p)$ on $W$ are canonical coordinates: by clause 1 of
[[pthm-cm13-two-form-is-symplectic]] the two-form is
$\omega=\sum_{a}dx^{a}\wedge dp_{a}$. For a generalized-coordinate map, the
coordinates $(q,P)$ on $\Omega\times\mathbb R^{r}$ are canonical coordinates
for the pulled-back form $\omega_{X}$: by clause 2 of
[[pthm-cm13-two-form-is-symplectic]] one has
$\omega_{X}=\sum_{a}dq^{a}\wedge dP_{a}$, and when the map is a genuine chart
($r=3N$) the chart transition is a change of canonical coordinates on
overlaps.

**(c) Canonical one-form up to gauge.** The canonical one-form $\lambda$ of
[[def-cm13-two-form]] is said to be **in canonical form up to gauge** in the
canonical coordinates $\theta$ when the difference
$\lambda-\sum_{a}\theta^{m+a}d\theta^{a}$ is a closed one-form on $W_{0}$;
exactness of that difference is not required. For the presentation's own
charts the difference of the two canonical one-forms is closed by clause 3 of
[[pthm-cm13-two-form-is-symplectic]].

**(d) Status and warnings.** The item defines a coordinate condition on a
declared chart and records the one fact that the presentation's own momentum
charts satisfy it. It asserts no existence of canonical coordinates beyond
the model's charts, no global statement on multiply connected phase domains,
no dynamics and no measured value. A chart that is merely a diffeomorphism
need not be canonical; the determinant test
$|\det D\theta|=1$ is necessary but, in dimension $2m\ge4$, not sufficient
for canonicity (the scope remark of this page records the witness).

Let $\varepsilon>0$, let $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ and $S\subseteq\mathbb R$ be intervals with nonempty interiors ([[def-interval]]), and let $h:J\times S\to\mathbb R$ and $k:J\times\mathbb R\times S\to\mathbb R$ be of class $C^2$ ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]), with $k$ $2\pi$-periodic in its second variable:

$$k(I,\theta+2\pi,s)=k(I,\theta,s)\qquad\text{for all }(I,\theta,s)\in J\times\mathbb R\times S .$$

The **transformed Hamiltonian** of the datum is

$$K(I,\theta,s):=h(I,s)+\varepsilon\,k(I,\theta,s),$$

its **frequency function** is

$$\omega(I,s):=\partial_Ih(I,s),$$

its **angle average** is $\langle k\rangle(I,s):=\frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}k(I,\theta,s)\,d\theta$, and, on the set where $\omega\ne0$, its **drift generator** is

$$g(I,\theta,s):=\frac{k(I,\theta,s)-\langle k\rangle(I,s)}{\omega(I,s)} .$$

The **branch vector field** of the datum is the map $\Phi:J\times\mathbb R\times S\to\mathbb R^3$,

$$\Phi(I,\theta,s):=\Bigl(-\varepsilon\,\partial_\theta k(I,\theta,s),\ \ \partial_Ih(I,\theta,s)+\varepsilon\,\partial_Ik(I,\theta,s),\ \ \varepsilon\Bigr),$$

and a **branch solution** on an interval $T\subseteq\mathbb R$ with nonempty interior is a differentiable $(I,\theta,s):T\to J\times\mathbb R\times S$ solving the first-order system $(I,\theta,s)'=\Phi(I,\theta,s)$ on $T$ in the sense of [[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]] ([[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]). Partial derivatives are those of the ambient Euclidean coordinates.

Let $\varepsilon>0$, $A>0$, $\omega_0>0$, let $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ and $S\subseteq\mathbb R$ be intervals with nonempty interiors, and let $h:J\times S\to\mathbb R$ and $k:J\times\mathbb R\times S\to\mathbb R$ be of class $C^2$ with $k$ $2\pi$-periodic in its second variable ([[def-cm-parameter-dependent-action-angle-branch]], [[def-interval]]). Let $K\subseteq J$ and $S_0\subseteq S$ be compact intervals, let $s_0\in S_0$, and suppose

$$|\partial_Ih(I,s)|\ge\omega_0\qquad\bigl((I,s)\in K\times S_0\bigr).$$

Let $(I,\theta,s):[0,A/\varepsilon]\to J\times\mathbb R\times S$ be a branch solution of the branch vector field of the datum ([[def-cm-parameter-dependent-action-angle-branch]]) with $s(0)=s_0$, and suppose that for every $t\in[0,A/\varepsilon]$ one has $I(t)\in K$ and $s(t)\in S_0$. Then for every $t\in[0,A/\varepsilon]$,

$$|I(t)-I(0)|\le\varepsilon\Bigl[2\sup_{K\times[0,2\pi]\times S_0}|g|+A\sup_{K\times[0,2\pi]\times S_0}\bigl|\partial_Ig\,\partial_\theta k-\partial_\theta g\,\partial_Ik-\partial_sg\bigr|\Bigr],$$

where $g=(k-\langle k\rangle)/\partial_Ih$ is the drift generator of the datum.

Adopt the force model with potential presentation $(U,d)$ and mechanical
Lagrangian $L=K-U$ of [[def-cm07-action-and-mechanical-lagrangian]] with the
data, charts and Hamiltonian field of [[def-cm13-two-form]],
[[def-cm13-hamiltonian-field]]: masses $m_{1},\dots,m_{N}>0$ and open
configuration domain $Q\subseteq\mathbb R^{3N}$ with mass operator
$\mathsf M$ ([[def-cm01-configuration]]), time window $I_{0}$, $C^{2}$
potential $U$ and residual forces $d$ of the standing regularity
([[def-cm03-potential-and-mechanical-energy]],
[[post-cm02-force-superposition]], [[def-cm01-units]]), the Cartesian
Hamiltonian $H(t,x,p)=\tfrac12p\cdot\mathsf M^{-1}p+U(t,x)$ and, for a
generalized-coordinate map $X:\Omega\to Q$ with kinetic metric
$G=DX^{\mathsf T}\mathsf M\,DX$, the chart Hamiltonian
$\widetilde H(t,q,P)=\tfrac12P\cdot G(q)^{-1}P+\widetilde U(t,q)$
([[def-cm12-hamiltonian]], [[pthm-cm12-mechanical-hyperregularity]],
[[def-cm07-generalized-coordinates-and-forces]],
[[def-cm12-cotangent-momentum]]). Let $J\subseteq I_{0}$ be a nonempty open
interval. Then:

1. **(potential branch, Cartesian chart)** Assume $d\equiv0$ on the state
   domain. For a $C^{2}$ curve $x:J\to Q$ with $p(t):=\mathsf Mx'(t)$ the
   following are equivalent: (a) $x$ is a motion of the model
   ([[def-cm02-newtonian-flow]]); (b) $\dot x(t)=H_{p}(t,x(t),p(t))$ and
   $\dot p(t)=-H_{x}(t,x(t),p(t))$ for every $t\in J$; (c) the curve
   $t\mapsto(x(t),p(t))$ is an integral curve of the time-dependent field
   $t\mapsto X_{H_{t}}$, i.e. satisfies
   $\dot z(t)=X_{H_{t}}(z(t))$ with $z=(x,p)$
   ([[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]]).
2. **(generalized-coordinate chart)** Let $X:\Omega\to Q$ be a
   generalized-coordinate map and let $q:J\to\Omega$ be a $C^{2}$ curve with
   $x:=X\circ q$ and $P(t):=G(q(t))q'(t)$. Then the declared Lagrange
   equations with residual generalized force,
   $\Lambda(\widetilde L)(q)(t)=Q^{\mathrm{res}}(t,q(t),q'(t))$, are
   equivalent to
   $q'(t)=\widetilde H_{P}(t,q(t),P(t))$ and
   $P'(t)=-\widetilde H_{q}(t,q(t),P(t))+Q^{\mathrm{res}}(t,q(t),q'(t))$;
   in particular, when $d\equiv0$, they are equivalent to
   $(q,P)$ being an integral curve of $X_{\widetilde H_{t}}$.
3. **(residual forces, Cartesian chart)** For a $C^{2}$ curve $x:J\to Q$
   with $p=\mathsf Mx'$, the model's forced equation
   $\mathsf Mx''=-\nabla_{x}U(t,x)+d(t,x,x')$ holds on $J$ if and only if
   $\dot x=H_{p}$ and $\dot p=-H_{x}+d(t,x,\mathsf M^{-1}p)$ on $J$.
4. **(when is the forced field Hamiltonian?)** The forced field
   $(x,p)\mapsto\bigl(\mathsf M^{-1}p,-\nabla_{x}U(t,x)+d(t,x,\mathsf M^{-1}p)\bigr)$
   is the Hamiltonian field of a $C^{2}$ phase function on its domain if and
   only if there is a $C^{2}$ function $V:I_{0}\times Q\to\mathbb R$ with
   $d(t,x,v)=-\nabla_{x}V(t,x)$ for every $(t,x,v)$ of the state domain; in
   that case the phase function is $H+V$ up to an independently chosen
   additive $C^2$ function of $t$ on each connected component of $Q$, and the model's forced motions are the motions of the potential
   presentation $(U+V,0)$.

The statement is conditional on the adopted force branch, the declared
presentation and the declared chart; it asserts no existence or uniqueness of
solutions, no completeness, no conservation law and no empirical content.

Adopt the force model with potential presentation $(U,d)$ and mechanical
Lagrangian $L=K-U$ of [[def-cm07-action-and-mechanical-lagrangian]] with the
data and conventions of [[def-cm12-cotangent-momentum]]: masses
$m_{1},\dots,m_{N}>0$, open configuration domain $Q\subseteq\mathbb R^{3N}$,
time window $I_{0}$, mass operator $\mathsf M$
([[def-cm01-configuration]]), $C^{2}$ potential
$U:I_{0}\times Q\to\mathbb R$ and residual forces $d$ of the standing
regularity ([[def-cm03-potential-and-mechanical-energy]],
[[post-cm02-force-superposition]]). Let $H$ be the Cartesian Hamiltonian of
[[def-cm12-hamiltonian]], let $X:\Omega\to Q$ be a generalized-coordinate map
with substituted Lagrangian $\widetilde L$, kinetic metric
$G(q)=DX(q)^{\mathsf T}\mathsf M\,DX(q)$, substituted potential
$\widetilde U(t,q)=U(t,X(q))$ and residual generalized force
$Q^{\mathrm{res}}(t,q,v)=DX(q)^{\mathsf T}d(t,X(q),DX(q)v)$, and let
$\widetilde H$ be the Hamiltonian in the coordinates $X$
([[def-cm07-generalized-coordinates-and-forces]],
[[def-cm12-hamiltonian]]). Let $J\subseteq I_{0}$ be a nonempty open interval
and let $x:J\to Q$ be a $C^{2}$ curve, with $p(t):=\mathsf Mx'(t)$
([[def-cm12-cotangent-momentum]]). Then:

1. **(potential branch)** Assume $d\equiv0$ on the state domain. The following
   are equivalent:
   (a) $x$ is a motion of the model on $J$
   ([[def-cm02-newtonian-flow]]);
   (b) $(x,p)$ satisfies $x'(t)=H_{p}\bigl(t,x(t),p(t)\bigr)$ and
   $p'(t)=-H_{x}\bigl(t,x(t),p(t)\bigr)$ for every $t\in J$;
   (c) for all reals $a<b$ with $[a,b]\subseteq J$ the restriction
   $x|_{[a,b]}$ is stationary for the action $S$ of $L$ on $[a,b]$
   ([[def-cm-time-dependent-lagrangian-and-action]],
   [[pthm-cm07-euler-lagrange-equations]]).

2. **(residual forces)** For a $C^{2}$ curve $x:J\to Q$ with
   $p(t)=\mathsf Mx'(t)$ the following are equivalent:
   (a) $\mathsf Mx''(t)=-\nabla_{x}U\bigl(t,x(t)\bigr)+d\bigl(t,x(t),x'(t)\bigr)$
   for every $t\in J$;
   (b) $x'(t)=H_{p}\bigl(t,x(t),p(t)\bigr)$ and
   $p'(t)=-H_{x}\bigl(t,x(t),p(t)\bigr)+d\bigl(t,x(t),\mathsf M^{-1}p(t)\bigr)$
   for every $t\in J$.

3. **(coordinate form)** Let $q:J\to\Omega$ be a $C^{2}$ curve and put
   $p(t):=G(q(t))q'(t)$. Then the declared Lagrange equations of
   [[def-cm07-generalized-coordinates-and-forces]] clause (e) are equivalent
   to the Hamilton system of $\widetilde H$: for every $t\in J$,

$$\Lambda(\widetilde L)(q)(t)=Q^{\mathrm{res}}\bigl(t,q(t),q'(t)\bigr)\ \Longleftrightarrow\ q'(t)=\widetilde H_{p}\bigl(t,q(t),p(t)\bigr),\quad p'(t)=-\widetilde H_{q}\bigl(t,q(t),p(t)\bigr)+Q^{\mathrm{res}}\bigl(t,q(t),q'(t)\bigr);$$

   in particular, when $d\equiv0$ the vanishing of the Lagrange operator is
   equivalent to $q'=\widetilde H_{p}$ and $p'=-\widetilde H_{q}$.

4. **(constraint elimination)** Assume in addition that $d\equiv0$ and that
   $X$ is a parametrization of a scleronomic regular holonomic-constraint
   locus in the sense of [[def-cm07-generalized-coordinates-and-forces]]
   clause (d), with the ideal-reaction law of
   [[post-cm06-ideal-reaction-law]]. Then the equivalent conditions of
   clause 3 with $Q^{\mathrm{res}}\equiv0$ hold for $q$ if and only if
   $x=X\circ q$ is a constrained motion of the model with an ideal reaction
   ([[pthm-cm07-lagrangian-reduction-of-ideal-constraints]]).

The statement is conditional on the adopted force branch, the declared
presentation, the declared chart and, in clause 4, the constraint datum and
ideal-reaction law; it asserts no existence or uniqueness of solutions, no
conservation law and no empirical content.

Let a force model of [[post-cm02-force-superposition]] be given: time window
$I_{0}\subseteq\mathbb R$ nondegenerate and open, configuration domain
$Q\subseteq\mathbb R^{3N}$ open ([[def-cm01-configuration]] clause (a)),
fixed masses $m_{1},\dots,m_{N}>0$ ([[post-cm01-worldlines]] clause (v)), and a
force map $F$ with the standing continuity and state-local-Lipschitz
hypotheses of clause (iii) of that postulate.

**(a) State domain and inverse-mass operator.** The **state domain** of the
model is

$$D:=I_{0}\times Q\times(\mathbb R^{3})^{N}\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^{3N}\times\mathbb R^{3N},$$

an open subset of $\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^{6N}$; a point $(t,x,v)\in D$ is a
time together with the **state** $z=(x,v)$ of positions $x\in Q$ and coordinate
velocities $v\in(\mathbb R^{3})^{N}$ of the labels ([[def-cm01-velocity-acceleration]],
[[def-cm01-units]]). The **inverse-mass operator** is the linear map

$$\mathsf M^{-1}:\mathbb R^{3N}\to\mathbb R^{3N},\qquad \mathsf M^{-1}(u_{1},\dots,u_{N}):=\Bigl(\frac{u_{1}}{m_{1}},\dots,\frac{u_{N}}{m_{N}}\Bigr),$$

the inverse of the mass operator $\mathsf M$ of clause (d) of
[[def-cm01-configuration]].

**(b) Associated first-order system.** The **associated first-order field** of
the model is

$$\mathcal F:D\longrightarrow\mathbb R^{3N}\times\mathbb R^{3N},\qquad \mathcal F(t,x,v):=\Bigl(v,\ \mathsf M^{-1}F(t,x,v)\Bigr),$$

and the **associated first-order system** is $z'=\mathcal F(t,z)$ on the open
domain $D$, in the sense of
[[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]]; here
$z=(x,v)\in\mathbb R^{6N}$. The map $\mathcal F$ satisfies the
Picard–Lindelöf hypotheses of
[[thm-picard-lindelof-local-existence-and-uniqueness]]: it is continuous on
$D$, and it is locally Lipschitz in the state variable $z$ locally uniformly
in time, because its first component $z\mapsto v$ is linear and its second is
the composition of the force map $F$ — which is locally Lipschitz in $(x,v)$
locally uniformly in time by [[post-cm02-force-superposition]] clause (iii) —
with the linear map $\mathsf M^{-1}$.

**(c) Motions.** Let $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval with nonempty
interior, endpoints read with one-sided derivatives as in
[[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]]. A **motion** of
the model on $J$ is a curve $x:J\to Q$ of class $C^{2}$ such that
$t\in I_{0}$ for every $t\in J$ and

$$m_{i}\,\ddot x_{i}(t)=F_{i}\bigl(t,x(t),\dot x(t)\bigr)\qquad(i=1,\dots,N,\ t\in J).$$

Equivalently: the state curve $z=(x,\dot x):J\to D$ is a solution of the
associated first-order system on $J$. Indeed, if $x$ is a motion then
$z=(x,x')$ is $C^{1}$ with
$z'=(x',x'')=(x',\mathsf M^{-1}F(t,x,x'))=\mathcal F(t,z)$ and $z(t)\in D$;
conversely, if $z=(x,v)$ is a solution with $z(t)\in D$ for all $t$, then
$x'=v$ and $v'=\mathsf M^{-1}F(t,x,v)$, so $v$ is $C^{1}$, $x$ is $C^{2}$, and
multiplying the second equation by the masses returns the displayed
second-order equation. Motions of the labels of the model are exactly these
curves by [[post-cm02-force-superposition]] clause (iv).

**(d) Initial data and maximal motion.** An **initial datum** of the model is
a triple $(t_{0},x_{0},v_{0})$ with $t_{0}\in I_{0}$, $x_{0}\in Q$ and
$v_{0}\in(\mathbb R^{3})^{N}$; write $z_{0}:=(x_{0},v_{0})$. A **maximal
motion** with this datum is a motion $x:J_{\max}\to Q$ with $x(t_{0})=x_{0}$
and $\dot x(t_{0})=v_{0}$ that has no extension to a motion of the model on a
strictly larger interval. By the Picard–Lindelöf hypotheses verified in (b)
and the maximal-solution theorem
[[thm-existence-and-uniqueness-of-a-maximal-ode-solution]] (with
[[def-maximal-ode-solution]]): every initial datum has exactly one maximal
motion, its **maximal interval** $J_{\max}$ is an open interval containing
$t_{0}$ and contained in $I_{0}$, and every motion with the same datum is the
restriction of the maximal one. The restriction statement transfers from the
associated first-order system to motions through the equivalence in (c).

**(e) Newtonian flow.** The **Newtonian flow** of the model is the map

$$\Phi:\Omega\longrightarrow Q\times\mathbb R^{3N},\qquad \Omega:=\bigl\{(t,t_{0},z_{0}):t_{0}\in I_{0},\ z_{0}\in Q\times\mathbb R^{3N},\ t\in J_{\max}(t_{0},z_{0})\bigr\},$$

defined by $\Phi(t;t_{0},z_{0}):=z(t)$, where $t\mapsto z(t)=(x(t),\dot x(t))$
is the state curve of the maximal motion with datum $(t_{0},z_{0})$. By (d) the
assignment is well defined: the maximal motion is unique, so $\Phi$ is a
function on $\Omega$ and not merely a relation. For fixed $t_{0}$ and $z_{0}$
the curve $t\mapsto\Phi(t;t_{0},z_{0})$ is defined exactly on the maximal
interval $J_{\max}(t_{0},z_{0})$.

derivations.claim: By [F1] and [F4], the chart expression $(I(t),\theta(t))$ of the model's motion satisfies $\dot I=-\partial_{\theta}K_{s(t)}$ and $\dot\theta=\partial_{I}K_{s(t)}$ for the branch Hamiltonian of hypothesis 1; substituting $K=h+\varepsilon k$ gives $\dot I=-\varepsilon\,\partial_{\theta}k(I,\theta,s(t))$ and $\dot\theta=\partial_{I}h(I,s(t))+\varepsilon\,\partial_{I}k(I,\theta,s(t))$. With the parameter path $s(t)=s_{0}+\varepsilon t$ from hypothesis 3, the triple $(I,\theta,s)$ therefore solves the branch system of [F2] on $[0,A/\varepsilon]$.

The compact trapping of hypothesis 3 gives $I(t)\in K$ and $s(t)\in S_{0}$ for every $t\in[0,A/\varepsilon]$, and hypothesis 2 gives $|\partial_{I}h|\ge\omega_{0}$ on $K\times S_{0}$; hence all hypotheses of [F3] are met for the branch solution of step 1.1.

Applying [F3] to the branch solution of step 1.1 yields the displayed estimate for every $t\in[0,A/\varepsilon]$, with the drift generator $g=(k-\langle k\rangle)/\partial_{I}h$ of the datum; the hypotheses of [F3] were checked in step 2.1.
The estimate of step 3.1 is the conclusion; collecting, the model's action coordinate drifts by at most order $\varepsilon$ on the $O(1/\varepsilon)$ horizon under the stated hypotheses.

boundaries.evidence: The compact sets $K$ and $S_{0}$ are assumed nonempty and the branch solution is assumed trapped in them (statement, step 2.1).
$\varepsilon>0$ and $\omega_{0}>0$; no zero-$\varepsilon$ limiting statement is made and exact zero drift is not claimed (statement, step 2.1).
The datum is one-frequency by definition of the cited branch datum (statement, step 1.1).
The degenerate case of vanishing frequency is excluded by $|\partial_{I}h|\ge\omega_{0}>0$; separatrix and chart crossings are outside the statement (statement).
The estimate is asserted on the closed horizon $[0,A/\varepsilon]$, endpoints included, and step 2.1 integrates over the whole closed interval.

boundaries.reason: No selection principle is used; the cited drift theorem and the identification are choice-free (step 1.1).
The theorem is one-directional: hypotheses (1)-(3) yield the order-epsilon drift bound, and no 'if' side of any biconditional is at issue at the boundary values of J, S0 or epsilon.
A small action drift is not claimed to force the slow-datum decomposition or the frequency bound; no reverse implication forms part of the statement.

citations.quote:
**(i) Setting.** Work in the one-dimensional model class of
[[def-cm04-one-dimensional-models-and-equilibria]] with time window
$I_{0}=\mathbb R$, configuration domain $Q=\mathbb R$, a fixed mass $m>0$
and a **spring constant** $k>0$ of dimension $\mu\tau^{-2}$, read in newtons
per metre ([[def-cm01-units]]). The **harmonic model** is the model whose
force law is the **linear restoring force**
$$F(x,v):=-k\,x .$$
Its equation of motion is $m\,x''=-k\,x$, equivalently $m\,x''+k\,x=0$; the
model is autonomous and velocity-independent, and its potential is
$$U(x):=\tfrac12 k\,x^{2},$$
of dimension $\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-2}$ (joules), which presents the force law in
the sense of clause (d) of [[def-cm04-one-dimensional-models-and-equilibria]]:
$U$ is of class $C^{2}$ and $-U'(x)=-k\,x=F(x)$ ([[lem-derivative-of-a-power]],
[[def-derivative]]). The harmonic model is therefore a **conservative**
model of the class, with the potential representative $U$ declared above and
no residual force.

**(ii) Regularity and framework status.** The force law is affine in the
state; it is continuous, and $\lvert F(x)-F(x')\rvert=k\lvert x-x'\rvert\le
k\,\lVert(x,v)-(x',v')\rVert_{2}$, so it is locally Lipschitz in the state
variable with the global constant $k$, uniformly in time
([[def-locally-lipschitz-in-the-state-variable]]). The harmonic model is
thus an admissible model of the class of clause (a) of
[[def-cm04-one-dimensional-models-and-equilibria]], and the existence,
uniqueness and conservation statements of this page apply to it. It is
adopted as a restricted model class of the framework, at the same primitive
level as the force maps of [[post-cm02-force-superposition]]: the force law
is model input.

**(iii) Physical reading and regime.** The model idealizes a **restoring
force linear in the displacement**: an ideal spring, or the quadratic
approximation of a potential $U$ near a strict local minimum $x_{*}$ with $U''(x_*)>0$, where
the Taylor expansion of the effective potential begins with the quadratic
term $\tfrac12 U''(x_{*})(x-x_{*})^{2}$ and the linearized equation carries
the **effective spring constant** $U''(x_{*})$ (the sources' linearization
procedure). The model is adopted for a stated regime — displacements so
small that the neglected remainder of the potential is adequate for the
purpose at hand — and it is **not** claimed to describe large-amplitude
oscillations, nonlinear springs, plasticity, or any given real system. The
coefficient $k$ is a model parameter, not a constant of the framework; when
its value is taken from a calibration experiment, that value is an empirical
premise carrying the apparatus conditions and the measurement uncertainty,
and the framework asserts none of it here. The linear form is the simplest
restoring law satisfying the standing regularity; that is a modelling
convenience, not a derivation.

**(iv) Status.** Adopted assumption of the framework when a model invokes
it; it selects no law of nature on its own. Every consequence below is a
conditional statement about the declared equation of motion.

Adopt the harmonic model of [[post-cm04-harmonic-model]]: the
one-dimensional model of [[def-cm04-one-dimensional-models-and-equilibria]]
with $m>0$, $k>0$, force law $F(x)=-kx$ and potential $U(x)=\tfrac12kx^{2}$.
Write
$$\omega:=\sqrt{\frac{k}{m}}>0$$
for its **undamped frequency** in the sense of
[[def-cm-oscillator-model-and-phase-system]]. Then:

1. **Motions.** Let $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval with nonempty
   interior and let $t_{0}\in J$. A curve $x:J\to\mathbb R$ is a motion of the
   model on $J$ if and only if there are reals $A,B$ with
   $$x(t)=A\cos\bigl(\omega(t-t_{0})\bigr)+B\sin\bigl(\omega(t-t_{0})\bigr) \qquad(t\in J).$$
   For every datum $(t_{0},x_{0},v_{0})$ there is exactly one maximal motion,
   it is defined on all of $\mathbb R$, and its coefficients are
   $A=x_{0}$, $B=v_{0}/\omega$; every motion with that datum is its
   restriction.
All claims involving every real time, periods or the whole phase ellipse below refer to the unique maximal extension of clause 1; on a local motion interval the same formulas hold by restriction.

2. **Amplitude and phase.** With $A,B$ as in clause 1 put
   $R:=\sqrt{A^{2}+B^{2}}$. Then $\lvert x(t)\rvert\le R$ for every $t$; if
   $R>0$ there is a real $\varphi$ with $\cos\varphi=A/R$ and
   $\sin\varphi=B/R$, and then
   $$x(t)=R\cos\bigl(\omega(t-t_{0})-\varphi\bigr)\qquad(t\in\mathbb R).$$
   If $R=0$ the motion is the rest motion $x\equiv0$.
3. **Period and frequency.** For every motion $x(t+T)=x(t)$ holds for all
   $t$ whenever $\omega T\in2\pi\mathbb Z$. If $R>0$, conversely every
   period $T>0$ of $x$ satisfies $\omega T\in2\pi\mathbb Z$, so the **least
   positive period** of the motion is $T_{\mathrm{per}}=2\pi/\omega$, and the
   **frequency** in cycles per second is $f=1/T_{\mathrm{per}}=\omega/(2\pi)$.
   If $R=0$ every $T$ is a period.
4. **Energy and phase curves.** Along every motion with coefficients $A,B$
   the mechanical energy is
   $$E\bigl(x(t),x'(t)\bigr)=\tfrac12k\bigl(A^{2}+B^{2}\bigr)=\tfrac12kR^{2}$$
   for every $t$, the phase curve is contained in the ellipse
   $$\Sigma_{R}:=\Bigl\{(x,v)\in\mathbb R^{2}:\frac{x^{2}}{R^{2}}+\frac{v^{2}}{\omega^{2}R^{2}}=1\Bigr\}$$
   when $R>0$, and it is exactly that ellipse: every point of $\Sigma_{R}$
   lies on the phase curve of the motion and is attained at exactly the times
   $t=t_{0}+\bigl(\theta_{1}+\varphi+2\pi n\bigr)/\omega$, $n\in\mathbb Z$,
   for the appropriate $\theta_{1}$. For $R=0$ the phase curve is the single
   point $(0,0)$, which is also the level set of energy $0$.
5. **Rest point.** The origin $(0,0)$ is the only rest point of the model,
   and it is Lyapunov stable, by
   [[pthm-cm04-equilibrium-stability-at-a-strict-minimum]]; no asymptotic
   stability is asserted.

The statement uses the declared data $m,k$ only through $\omega$ and the
energy; no value of $m$ or $k$ is asserted, and no real oscillator is claimed
to obey the model.

Adopt the force model with potential presentation $(U,d)$ and mechanical
Lagrangian $L=K-U$ of [[def-cm07-action-and-mechanical-lagrangian]] with the
data and conventions of [[def-cm12-cotangent-momentum]]: masses
$m_{1},\dots,m_{N}>0$, open configuration domain $Q\subseteq\mathbb R^{3N}$,
time window $I_{0}$, mass operator $\mathsf M$
([[def-cm01-configuration]]), $C^{2}$ potential
$U:I_{0}\times Q\to\mathbb R$ and residual forces $d$ of the standing
regularity ([[def-cm03-potential-and-mechanical-energy]],
[[post-cm02-force-superposition]]). Let $X:\Omega\to Q$ be a
generalized-coordinate map with substituted Lagrangian $\widetilde L$,
kinetic metric $G(q)=DX(q)^{\mathsf T}\mathsf M\,DX(q)$ and substituted
potential $\widetilde U(t,q)=U(t,X(q))$
([[def-cm07-generalized-coordinates-and-forces]]), and let $H$ and
$\widetilde H$ be the Hamiltonians of [[def-cm12-hamiltonian]]. Then:

1. **(Cartesian chart)** The fibre momentum map
   $\mathbb F_{t,x}(v)=\mathsf Mv$ is a bijection of $\mathbb R^{3N}$ onto
   $\mathbb R^{3N}$ for every $(t,x)\in I_{0}\times Q$, and the inverse
   Legendre branch is the $C^{2}$ map
   $v(t,x,p)=\mathsf M^{-1}p$ on the whole phase chart
   $I_{0}\times Q\times\mathbb R^{3N}$. Hence the presentation is
   hyperregular on the Cartesian chart in the sense of
   [[def-cm12-hyperregularity]], and the Hamiltonian of the branch is

$$H(t,x,p)=\tfrac12\,p\cdot\mathsf M^{-1}p+U(t,x),$$

with the dot product of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]],

   a $C^{2}$ function of dimension $\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-2}$.

2. **(generalized-coordinate chart)** The fibre map
   $v\mapsto G(q)v$ is a bijection of $\mathbb R^{r}$ onto $\mathbb R^{r}$
   for every $(t,q)\in I_{0}\times\Omega$, and the inverse Legendre branch is
   the $C^{2}$ map $v(t,q,p)=G(q)^{-1}p$ on
   $I_{0}\times\Omega\times\mathbb R^{r}$. Hence the presentation is
   hyperregular on the chart of $X$, and the Hamiltonian in the coordinates
   $X$ is

$$\widetilde H(t,q,p)=\tfrac12\,p\cdot G(q)^{-1}p+\widetilde U(t,q),$$

   a $C^{2}$ function of dimension $\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-2}$.

The statement is conditional on the adopted force branch and the declared
presentation; it asserts no equation of motion, no conservation law and no
empirical content.

Adopt the force model with potential presentation $(U,d)$ and mechanical
Lagrangian $L=K-U$ of [[def-cm07-action-and-mechanical-lagrangian]] with the
data and conventions of [[def-cm12-cotangent-momentum]]: masses
$m_{1},\dots,m_{N}>0$, open configuration domain $Q\subseteq\mathbb R^{3N}$,
time window $I_{0}$, mass operator $\mathsf M$
([[def-cm01-configuration]]), $C^{2}$ potential $U$ and residual forces $d$ of
the standing regularity ([[def-cm03-potential-and-mechanical-energy]],
[[post-cm02-force-superposition]]); dimensions are read by
[[def-cm01-units]] and the Euclidean pairing is
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]].

**(a) Cartesian Hamiltonian.** Assume the presentation is hyperregular on the
Cartesian chart, with inverse Legendre branch
$v:I_{0}\times Q\times\mathbb R^{3N}\to\mathbb R^{3N}$
([[def-cm12-hyperregularity]], [[def-cm-legendre-map-in-a-time-dependent-chart]]).
The **Hamiltonian of the presentation on the Cartesian chart** is the function

$$H:I_{0}\times Q\times\mathbb R^{3N}\longrightarrow\mathbb R,\qquad H(t,x,p):=p\cdot v(t,x,p)-L\bigl(t,x,v(t,x,p)\bigr),$$

where $p\cdot v(t,x,p)$ is the Euclidean pairing of the momentum covector
with the inverse-branch velocity ([[def-cm12-cotangent-momentum]],
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]]). The momentum phase chart
$I_{0}\times Q\times\mathbb R^{3N}$ with coordinates $(t,x,p)$ is the
**Hamiltonian phase chart** of the presentation on the Cartesian chart.

**(b) Generalized-coordinate Hamiltonian.** Let $X:\Omega\to Q$ be a
generalized-coordinate map with substituted Lagrangian $\widetilde L$, kinetic
metric $G$ and inverse Legendre branch $v$ on
$I_{0}\times\Omega\times\mathbb R^{r}$ ([[def-cm07-generalized-coordinates-and-forces]],
[[def-cm12-hyperregularity]]). The **Hamiltonian of the presentation in the
coordinates $X$** is

$$\widetilde H:I_{0}\times\Omega\times\mathbb R^{r}\longrightarrow\mathbb R,\qquad \widetilde H(t,q,p):=p\cdot v(t,q,p)-\widetilde L\bigl(t,q,v(t,q,p)\bigr).$$

For the Cartesian chart, $X=\mathrm{id}$ and $\widetilde H=H$; the general
definition is the same formula applied to the substituted fibre-full chart.

**(c) Dimensions and conventions.** Each term of the defining difference has
dimension $\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-2}$ (energy): the pairing $p\cdot v$ multiplies
$\mu\ell\tau^{-1}$ by $\ell\tau^{-1}$ in Cartesian data
([[def-cm12-cotangent-momentum]]), and $L$ has energy dimension
([[def-cm07-action-and-mechanical-lagrangian]]). In the coordinates $X$ the
pairing is dimensionally consistent for every declared coordinate dimension
$\gamma_{a}$ and the dimension is unchanged. The Hamiltonian is $C^{1}$ on
its domain, being a sum of products of $C^{1}$ maps
([[thm-ck-euclidean-maps-closed-under-algebra-and-composition]],
[[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]). The pairing is the coordinate
Euclidean product; no metric on momentum space and no symplectic form is
introduced by this definition.

**(d) Dependence and status.** The Hamiltonian depends on the declared chart,
on the declared inverse Legendre branch (when more than one branch exists it
is part of the data, as in [[def-cm12-hyperregularity]]) and on the potential
representative: replacing $U$ by $U+c(t)$ leaves the branch unchanged and
replaces $L$ by $L-c(t)$, hence replaces $H$ by $H+c(t)$
([[def-cm03-potential-and-mechanical-energy]] clause (c),
[[def-cm07-action-and-mechanical-lagrangian]] clause (b)). It asserts no
equation of motion, no conservation property and no measured value; the
explicit kinetic-plus-potential form of $H$ for the mechanical branch, the
equivalence of its equations with the model's equation of motion and its
relation to the mechanical energy are the theorems of this page. Matrix
identities used by those theorems are read through
[[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]].

Let a force model of [[post-cm02-force-superposition]] be given: time window
$I_{0}\subseteq\mathbb R$ nondegenerate and open, configuration domain
$Q\subseteq\mathbb R^{3N}$ open ([[def-cm01-configuration]] clause (a)),
fixed masses $m_{1},\dots,m_{N}>0$ ([[post-cm01-worldlines]] clause (v)), and a
force map $F$ with the standing continuity and state-local-Lipschitz
hypotheses of clause (iii) of that postulate.

**(a) State domain and inverse-mass operator.** The **state domain** of the
model is

$$D:=I_{0}\times Q\times(\mathbb R^{3})^{N}\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^{3N}\times\mathbb R^{3N},$$

an open subset of $\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^{6N}$; a point $(t,x,v)\in D$ is a
time together with the **state** $z=(x,v)$ of positions $x\in Q$ and coordinate
velocities $v\in(\mathbb R^{3})^{N}$ of the labels ([[def-cm01-velocity-acceleration]],
[[def-cm01-units]]). The **inverse-mass operator** is the linear map

$$\mathsf M^{-1}:\mathbb R^{3N}\to\mathbb R^{3N},\qquad \mathsf M^{-1}(u_{1},\dots,u_{N}):=\Bigl(\frac{u_{1}}{m_{1}},\dots,\frac{u_{N}}{m_{N}}\Bigr),$$

the inverse of the mass operator $\mathsf M$ of clause (d) of
[[def-cm01-configuration]].

**(b) Associated first-order system.** The **associated first-order field** of
the model is

$$\mathcal F:D\longrightarrow\mathbb R^{3N}\times\mathbb R^{3N},\qquad \mathcal F(t,x,v):=\Bigl(v,\ \mathsf M^{-1}F(t,x,v)\Bigr),$$

and the **associated first-order system** is $z'=\mathcal F(t,z)$ on the open
domain $D$, in the sense of
[[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]]; here
$z=(x,v)\in\mathbb R^{6N}$. The map $\mathcal F$ satisfies the
Picard–Lindelöf hypotheses of
[[thm-picard-lindelof-local-existence-and-uniqueness]]: it is continuous on
$D$, and it is locally Lipschitz in the state variable $z$ locally uniformly
in time, because its first component $z\mapsto v$ is linear and its second is
the composition of the force map $F$ — which is locally Lipschitz in $(x,v)$
locally uniformly in time by [[post-cm02-force-superposition]] clause (iii) —
with the linear map $\mathsf M^{-1}$.

**(c) Motions.** Let $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval with nonempty
interior, endpoints read with one-sided derivatives as in
[[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]]. A **motion** of
the model on $J$ is a curve $x:J\to Q$ of class $C^{2}$ such that
$t\in I_{0}$ for every $t\in J$ and

$$m_{i}\,\ddot x_{i}(t)=F_{i}\bigl(t,x(t),\dot x(t)\bigr)\qquad(i=1,\dots,N,\ t\in J).$$

Equivalently: the state curve $z=(x,\dot x):J\to D$ is a solution of the
associated first-order system on $J$. Indeed, if $x$ is a motion then
$z=(x,x')$ is $C^{1}$ with
$z'=(x',x'')=(x',\mathsf M^{-1}F(t,x,x'))=\mathcal F(t,z)$ and $z(t)\in D$;
conversely, if $z=(x,v)$ is a solution with $z(t)\in D$ for all $t$, then
$x'=v$ and $v'=\mathsf M^{-1}F(t,x,v)$, so $v$ is $C^{1}$, $x$ is $C^{2}$, and
multiplying the second equation by the masses returns the displayed
second-order equation. Motions of the labels of the model are exactly these
curves by [[post-cm02-force-superposition]] clause (iv).

**(d) Initial data and maximal motion.** An **initial datum** of the model is
a triple $(t_{0},x_{0},v_{0})$ with $t_{0}\in I_{0}$, $x_{0}\in Q$ and
$v_{0}\in(\mathbb R^{3})^{N}$; write $z_{0}:=(x_{0},v_{0})$. A **maximal
motion** with this datum is a motion $x:J_{\max}\to Q$ with $x(t_{0})=x_{0}$
and $\dot x(t_{0})=v_{0}$ that has no extension to a motion of the model on a
strictly larger interval. By the Picard–Lindelöf hypotheses verified in (b)
and the maximal-solution theorem
[[thm-existence-and-uniqueness-of-a-maximal-ode-solution]] (with
[[def-maximal-ode-solution]]): every initial datum has exactly one maximal
motion, its **maximal interval** $J_{\max}$ is an open interval containing
$t_{0}$ and contained in $I_{0}$, and every motion with the same datum is the
restriction of the maximal one. The restriction statement transfers from the
associated first-order system to motions through the equivalence in (c).

**(e) Newtonian flow.** The **Newtonian flow** of the model is the map

$$\Phi:\Omega\longrightarrow Q\times\mathbb R^{3N},\qquad \Omega:=\bigl\{(t,t_{0},z_{0}):t_{0}\in I_{0},\ z_{0}\in Q\times\mathbb R^{3N},\ t\in J_{\max}(t_{0},z_{0})\bigr\},$$

defined by $\Phi(t;t_{0},z_{0}):=z(t)$, where $t\mapsto z(t)=(x(t),\dot x(t))$
is the state curve of the maximal motion with datum $(t_{0},z_{0})$. By (d) the
assignment is well defined: the maximal motion is unique, so $\Phi$ is a
function on $\Omega$ and not merely a relation. For fixed $t_{0}$ and $z_{0}$
the curve $t\mapsto\Phi(t;t_{0},z_{0})$ is defined exactly on the maximal
interval $J_{\max}(t_{0},z_{0})$.

Let $k\in\mathbb N$, let $m,q\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$. A map $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$ is of class $C^k$ when each component is of class $C^k$. Each scalar component uses the word-derivative convention of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]], whose source dimension is positive. The map is **smooth**, or $C^\infty$, when it is $C^k$ for every $k\in\mathbb N$.

Let $n\ge1$ and let $U,V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open. A bijection $f:U\to V$ is a **$C^k$ diffeomorphism** when both $f$ and $f^{-1}$ are $C^k$. For $k\ge1$, a **local $C^k$ diffeomorphism at $a\in U$** is a restriction $f|_P:P\to Q$ between open neighbourhoods of $a$ and $f(a)$ that is a $C^k$ diffeomorphism. At $k=1$ this agrees with [[def-c-one-map-and-local-inverse]]: continuous first partial derivatives give the required total derivative by [[thm-continuous-partial-derivatives-imply-total-differentiability]], while continuity of the total derivative gives continuity of its matrix entries and hence of the first partial derivatives.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, $a\in U$, $v\in\mathbb R^m$, and $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$. If the line map $t\mapsto f(a+tv)$ is defined near $0$, its derivative at $0$ is the **directional derivative**

$$D_vf(a):=\lim_{t\to0}\frac{f(a+tv)-f(a)}{t}.$$

For a standard basis vector $e_j$ ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]), $D_{e_j}f(a)$ is the **$j$th partial derivative**, written $\partial_jf(a)$. These are ordinary vector-valued one-variable derivatives in the sense of [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]].

If every partial derivative $\partial_jf_i(a)$ of $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ exists, the **Jacobian matrix** is $Jf(a)=(\partial_jf_i(a))_{i<n,j<m}$. For scalar-valued $f$, its **gradient** is

$$\nabla f(a):=(\partial_0f(a),\ldots,\partial_{m-1}f(a))\in\mathbb R^m,$$

with coordinates understood in the standard basis ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]). The partial derivatives are those of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]].

The functions $\sin$ and $\cos$ are differentiable on $\mathbb R$, with
$$(\sin x)'=\cos x,\qquad(\cos x)'=-\sin x.$$
Also $\sin0=0$ and $\cos0=1$.

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) at which $g$ is differentiable
([[def-derivative]]), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

For every real $x$,
$$\sin(2x)=2\sin x\cos x,\quad \cos(2x)=\cos^2x-\sin^2x=2\cos^2x-1=1-2\sin^2x,$$
and
$$\sin^2x=(1-\cos2x)/2,\qquad \cos^2x=(1+\cos2x)/2.$$
When defined, $\tan(2x)=2\tan x/(1-\tan^2x)$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[thm-sine-and-cosine-addition-formulas]], [[cor-trigonometric-parity-and-pythagorean-identity]], [[def-tangent-cotangent-secant-cosecant]].

For every real $x$,
$$\sin x=0\Longleftrightarrow x=m\pi\text{ for some }m\in\mathbb Z,\qquad \cos x=0\Longleftrightarrow x=(m+1/2)\pi\text{ for some }m\in\mathbb Z.$$
Both sine and cosine have period $2\pi$, and no smaller positive number is a common period.

For every real $x$,
$$\sin(-x)=-\sin x,\qquad\cos(-x)=\cos x,\qquad\sin^2x+\cos^2x=1.$$
Consequently $|\sin x|\le1$ and $|\cos x|\le1$.

Let $m \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge 1$ and let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$.

1. **Fundamental theorem, second part, in $\mathbb{R}^{m}$.** Let
   $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ be differentiable at every point of $[a,b]$ as
   a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]), and
   suppose $f' : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ is integrable. Then
   $$\int_a^b f' \;=\; f(b) - f(a).$$
2. **A bounded derivative gives a Lipschitz function.** Let
   $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable at
   every point of $(a,b)$, and let $M \ge 0$ satisfy
   $\lVert f'(t)\rVert_2 \le M$ for every $t \in (a,b)$. Then
   $$\lVert f(t) - f(s)\rVert_2 \;\le\; M\,|t-s| \qquad \text{for all } s,t \in [a,b],$$
   that is, $f$ is Lipschitz with constant $M$ as a map
   $([a,b], d_{\mathbb{R}}) \to (\mathbb{R}^{m}, d_2)$
   ([[def-lipschitz-holder-contraction]], [[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]],
   [[lem-metrics-on-rn]]).

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be bounded
([[def-bounded-set]]). Write $\mathcal{P}$ for the set of all partitions of
$[a,b]$ ([[def-partition-and-refinement]]) and put

$$\mathcal{L} \;:=\; \{\, L(f,P) \ : \ P \in \mathcal{P} \,\}, \qquad \mathcal{U} \;:=\; \{\, U(f,P) \ : \ P \in \mathcal{P} \,\}$$

for the sets of lower and of upper Darboux sums ([[def-darboux-sums]]).

### Both extrema exist

**$\mathcal{P}$ is nonempty**: the pair $(1, t)$ with $t_0 := a$ and $t_k := b$
for $k \ge 1$ is a partition of $[a,b]$, since $a < b$. So $\mathcal{L}$ and
$\mathcal{U}$ are nonempty.

**$\mathcal{L}$ is bounded above and $\mathcal{U}$ is bounded below.** Fix any
$Q \in \mathcal{P}$. By claim 2 of [[lem-refinement-inequalities]],
$L(f,P) \le U(f,Q)$ for every $P \in \mathcal{P}$, so $U(f,Q)$ is an upper bound
of $\mathcal{L}$; and $L(f,Q) \le U(f,P)$ for every $P$, so $L(f,Q)$ is a lower
bound of $\mathcal{U}$.

Hence a nonempty set bounded above has a supremum
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]) and a nonempty set bounded below has an infimum
([[thm-infimum-property]], [[def-infimum]]), each unique ([[lem-sup-unique]]).
The **lower** and **upper Darboux integrals** of $f$ over $[a,b]$ are the real
numbers

$$\underline{\int_a^b} f \;:=\; \sup \mathcal{L} \;=\; \sup_{P} L(f,P), \qquad \overline{\int_a^b} f \;:=\; \inf \mathcal{U} \;=\; \inf_{P} U(f,P) .$$

### The lower integral never exceeds the upper one

$$\underline{\int_a^b} f \;\le\; \overline{\int_a^b} f .$$

Indeed, for each fixed $Q \in \mathcal{P}$ the number $U(f,Q)$ is an upper bound
of $\mathcal{L}$, so the least upper bound satisfies
$\underline{\int_a^b} f \le U(f,Q)$. As $Q$ was arbitrary, $\underline{\int_a^b}f$
is a lower bound of $\mathcal{U}$, and the greatest lower bound satisfies
$\underline{\int_a^b} f \le \overline{\int_a^b} f$ ([[def-infimum]]).

Moreover, for **every** partition $P$,

$$L(f,P) \;\le\; \underline{\int_a^b} f \;\le\; \overline{\int_a^b} f \;\le\; U(f,P) ,$$

the outer inequalities because a member of a set is at most its supremum and at
least its infimum.

### Integrability

$f$ is **Darboux integrable on $[a,b]$**, and on this page simply
**integrable**, when

$$\underline{\int_a^b} f \;=\; \overline{\int_a^b} f ,$$

and then the common value is written

$$\int_a^b f \qquad \text{or} \qquad \int_a^b f(x)\,\mathrm{d}x ,$$

the **integral of $f$ over $[a,b]$**. It is a single well-determined real
number, being the common value of two numbers each of which is unique
([[lem-sup-unique]]). Without the displayed equality the symbol $\int_a^b f$ is
not defined and is never written.

**The inequality above is the whole difficulty.** By the previous paragraph
integrability is *never* a question of one integral exceeding the other, only of
the gap $\overline{\int_a^b} f - \underline{\int_a^b} f \ge 0$ being $0$; and by
[[thm-riemann-criterion]] that gap is $0$ exactly when a single partition can be
found making $U(f,P) - L(f,P)$ small. Whether that is possible is settled
completely, in terms of the discontinuities of $f$, by
[[thm-lebesgue-criterion]].

**"Riemann integrable" means the same thing here.** The definition above is
Darboux's. Riemann's own definition, in terms of tagged partitions of small
mesh, is [[def-tagged-partition-and-riemann-sum]], and the two define the same
class of functions with the same integral by [[thm-darboux-equals-riemann]].
Until that theorem is proved the two phrases are kept apart; after it they are
used interchangeably, as they are throughout the literature.

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-ordered-field]]) with its order
([[def-real-order]]).

A subset $I \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is **order-convex** when

$$x, y \in I \text{ and } x \le z \le y \;\Longrightarrow\; z \in I .$$

The **intervals** of $\mathbb{R}$ are the sets of the following nine forms, where
$a, b \in \mathbb{R}$:

| | bounded forms | | one-sided and full forms |
|---|---|---|---|
| $(a,b)$ | $\{x : a < x < b\}$ | $(a,\infty)$ | $\{x : a < x\}$ |
| $[a,b]$ | $\{x : a \le x \le b\}$ | $[a,\infty)$ | $\{x : a \le x\}$ |
| $[a,b)$ | $\{x : a \le x < b\}$ | $(-\infty,b)$ | $\{x : x < b\}$ |
| $(a,b]$ | $\{x : a < x \le b\}$ | $(-\infty,b]$ | $\{x : x \le b\}$ |
| | | $(-\infty,\infty)$ | $\mathbb{R}$ |

An interval is **open** when both of its written endpoints are excluded, that is
for the forms $(a,b)$, $(a,\infty)$, $(-\infty,b)$ and $(-\infty,\infty)$; it is
**closed** when both written endpoints are included, that is for $[a,b]$,
$[a,\infty)$, $(-\infty,b]$ and $(-\infty,\infty)$. The forms $[a,b)$ and
$(a,b]$ are **half-open**.

**The symbols $\pm\infty$ are notation and not elements of $\mathbb{R}$.** They
mark which side carries no endpoint condition at all; the five forms in the right
column are defined by the displayed conditions on $x$ alone, and no arithmetic is
ever performed with $\infty$. This is the same refusal to extend $\mathbb{R}$
