silently that [[rem-sup-conventions]] records for suprema.

**Every one of the nine forms is order-convex.** Each is defined by a conjunction
of at most two conditions, each of the shape $a < x$, $a \le x$, $x < b$ or
$x \le b$, and each such condition is inherited by an intermediate point: if
$a < x$ and $x \le z$ then $a < z$, and if $z \le y$ and $y < b$ then $z < b$,
by transitivity of the order ([[def-ordered-field]]). Applying this to whichever
one or two conditions define the form in question gives $z \in I$ whenever
$x, y \in I$ and $x \le z \le y$.

**Bounded intervals.** An interval is **bounded** ([[def-bounded-set]]) exactly
when it is of one of the four forms in the left column: for those, $a$ is a lower
bound and $b$ an upper bound. The other five forms are unbounded, on the side or
sides written with $\infty$; the verification is in the remarks below.

**Nondegeneracy.** An interval is **degenerate** when it has at most one element,
and **nondegenerate** when it has at least two. For the four bounded forms with
endpoints $a$ and $b$:

- $[a,b]$ is nonempty exactly when $a \le b$, and it is nondegenerate exactly
  when $a < b$. It is the singleton $\{a\}$ when $a = b$.
- $(a,b)$, $[a,b)$ and $(a,b]$ are nonempty exactly when $a < b$, and then each
  is nondegenerate.

The only assertion here that is not immediate from the defining conditions is
that $a < b$ makes $(a,b)$ nonempty with at least two points. It holds because
$a < (a+b)/2 < b$, which follows from $a < b$ by adding $a$, respectively $b$, to
both sides and halving ([[def-ordered-field]]); repeating the halving inside
$(a, (a+b)/2)$ produces a second point.

**Closed bounded intervals.** These are the sets $[a,b]$ with $a \le b$, which is
exactly the condition making them nonempty. They are the intervals the nested
interval property is stated for, and the phrase *closed bounded interval* always
carries the hypothesis $a \le b$ in this library.

**Length.** The **length** of a bounded interval presented by its endpoints
$a \le b$ is

$$\ell = b - a \;\ge\; 0 .$$

Length is attached to the presentation by endpoints and is not recovered from the
set: $(a,b)$, $[a,b)$ and $(a,b]$ are all empty when $a = b$, and so is
$(c,c)$ for any other $c$, while each of these presentations has length $0$, so
nothing inconsistent arises; but the endpoints are named explicitly at every
point where a length is used in this library, and never inferred from the set.
Unbounded intervals are assigned no length.

Adopt the force model with potential presentation $(U,d)$ and mechanical
Lagrangian $L=K-U$ of [[def-cm07-action-and-mechanical-lagrangian]] with the
data and conventions of [[def-cm12-cotangent-momentum]]: masses
$m_{1},\dots,m_{N}>0$, open configuration domain $Q\subseteq\mathbb R^{3N}$,
time window $I_{0}$, mass operator $\mathsf M$
([[def-cm01-configuration]]), $C^{2}$ potential $U$ and residual forces $d$
of the standing regularity ([[def-cm03-potential-and-mechanical-energy]],
[[post-cm02-force-superposition]]). Assume the presentation is hyperregular
on its charts, with the Hamiltonians $H$ and $\widetilde H$ and inverse
Legendre branches of [[def-cm12-hamiltonian]],
[[def-cm12-hyperregularity]],
[[pthm-cm12-mechanical-hyperregularity]]. The momentum charts, their forms
and their canonical coordinates are those of [[def-cm13-two-form]] and
[[def-cm13-canonical-form]]; dimensions are read by [[def-cm01-units]] and
differentiability classes are those of
[[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]].

**(a) The chart datum.** Fix one momentum chart of the presentation: either
the Cartesian chart with the coordinates $(t,x,p)$ on
$I_{0}\times Q\times\mathbb R^{3N}$ and the Hamiltonian $H$ of
[[def-cm12-hamiltonian]] clause (a), or the chart of a
generalized-coordinate map $X:\Omega\to Q$ with $r$ coordinates, the
coordinates $(t,q,p)$ on $I_{0}\times\Omega\times\mathbb R^{r}$ and the
Hamiltonian $\widetilde H$ of clause (b). Write $m\in\{3N,r\}$ for the
number of momentum pairs, let $V\subseteq\mathbb R^{m}$ denote the
configuration-coordinate domain of the chart ($Q$ in the Cartesian case,
$\Omega$ in the other), and write $H$ for the corresponding Hamiltonian,

$$H:I_{0}\times V\times\mathbb R^{m}\longrightarrow\mathbb R,\qquad (t,q,p)\longmapsto H(t,q,p),$$

a function of class $C^{2}$ and dimension $\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-2}$ (energy) by
[[pthm-cm12-mechanical-hyperregularity]]. Let $J'\subseteq I_{0}$,
$U'\subseteq V$ and $A'\subseteq\mathbb R^{m}$ be nonempty open sets
([[def-metric-topology]], [[def-interval]]).

**(b) Solutions of the equation.** A map

$$S:J'\times U'\times A'\longrightarrow\mathbb R,\qquad (t,q,\alpha)\longmapsto S(t,q,\alpha),$$

of class $C^{3}$ **solves the Hamilton-Jacobi equation associated with $H$
on $J'\times U'\times A'$** when

$$S_{t}(t,q,\alpha)+H\bigl(t,\,q,\,S_{q}(t,q,\alpha)\bigr)=0\qquad\bigl((t,q,\alpha)\in J'\times U'\times A'\bigr),$$
where $S_{t}$ is the partial derivative in $t$ and
$S_{q}=(S_{q^{1}},\dots,S_{q^{m}})$ is the gradient in $q$
([[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]],
[[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]); the momentum slot of $H$ is
substituted by $p=S_{q}(t,q,\alpha)$. This is exactly the mathematical
Hamilton-Jacobi equation of
[[def-cm-hamilton-jacobi-equation-and-complete-integral]] associated with
the function $H$ on the open set $J'\times U'\times\mathbb R^{m}$, read in
the chart coordinates $(t,q,p)$; the two definitions determine the same
class of functions.

**(c) Dimensions and chart consistency.** The equation forces
$[S]=\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-1}$ (action): $S_{t}$ has dimension $[S]\tau^{-1}$
and $H$ has dimension $\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-2}$, while each $S_{q^{a}}$ has
dimension $[S]/\gamma_{a}$ with $\gamma_{a}$ the declared dimension of the
coordinate $q^{a}$ in this chart; the substitution is dimensionally
consistent in every chart because the chart momenta of
[[def-cm12-cotangent-momentum]] have dimension
$\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-1}\gamma_{a}^{-1}$. In the Cartesian chart all
$\gamma_{a}=\ell$ and $[S]/\ell=\mu\ell\tau^{-1}$, the momentum dimension.

**(d) Status.** The equation is attached to the declared datum: replacing
the chart, the inverse Legendre branch or the potential representative
changes $H$ by the rules recorded in clause (d) of
[[def-cm12-hamiltonian]] and hence changes the equation, and a solution
family $S$ is a solution for that datum only. The item defines a class of
functions; whether a given datum admits solutions, and how solutions
produce curves of the model, is not asserted here. In particular no
existence theorem, no global solution, no equation of motion for the model,
no conservation law and no measured value is claimed.

Adopt the datum of [[def-cm14-hamilton-jacobi-equation]]: one momentum chart
of a hyperregular potential presentation, its $C^{2}$ Hamiltonian $H$ of
dimension $\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-2}$ on $I_{0}\times V\times\mathbb R^{m}$, open
sets $J'\subseteq I_{0}$, $U'\subseteq V$ and $A'\subseteq\mathbb R^{m}$,
and a $C^{3}$ map $S:J'\times U'\times A'\to\mathbb R$ that solves the
Hamilton-Jacobi equation associated with $H$ on $J'\times U'\times A'$.
Dimensions are read by [[def-cm01-units]] and differentiability classes are
those of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]].

**(a) Complete integral.** Let $(t_{0},q_{0},\alpha_{0})\in
J'\times U'\times A'$. The solution $S$ is a **complete integral of the
model's Hamilton-Jacobi equation at $(t_{0},q_{0},\alpha_{0})$** when the
mixed derivative

$$S_{q\alpha}(t,q,\alpha):=\Bigl(\frac{\partial^{2}S}{\partial q^{a}\partial\alpha_{j}}(t,q,\alpha)\Bigr)_{a,j=1}^{m}\in\mathbb R^{m\times m}$$
is invertible at the base point, $\det S_{q\alpha}(t_{0},q_{0},\alpha_{0})
\ne0$ ([[def-determinant-of-a-square-matrix]],
[[def-invertible-euclidean-linear-map]], mixed partials being those of
[[def-total-derivative-in-euclidean-space]]). This is exactly the
mathematical notion of a complete integral of
[[def-cm-hamilton-jacobi-equation-and-complete-integral]] applied to the
function $H$ on the chart domain $J'\times U'\times\mathbb R^{m}$.

**(b) Parameters and their dimensions.** The third variable
$\alpha=(\alpha_{1},\dots,\alpha_{m})$ is read with the declared coordinate
dimensions $\gamma_{a}$ of $q$ in the fixed chart,
$[\alpha_{j}]=\gamma_{j}$. With this reading the entries of
$S_{q\alpha}$ are dimensionless, so the nondegeneracy condition is
dimensionally meaningful and chart-consistent, and the momentum map below
carries the momentum dimension.

**(c) Momentum map and Jacobi constants.** For a complete integral $S$ the
**momentum map** and the **Jacobi constants** of $S$ are the maps

$$p(t,q,\alpha):=S_{q}(t,q,\alpha),\qquad\beta(t,q,\alpha):=S_{\alpha}(t,q,\alpha),$$
so that $p$ has the chart-momentum dimensions of
[[def-cm12-cotangent-momentum]], $[p_{a}]=\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-1}
\gamma_{a}^{-1}$, and $\beta$ has the same dimensions as $p$,
$[\beta_{j}]=\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-1}\gamma_{j}^{-1}$: the product
$\beta_{j}\,\alpha_{j}$ has the action dimension $\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-1}$ of
$S$. The pair $(\beta,\alpha)$ is the **Jacobi data** of the complete
integral at the base point.

**(d) Status.** The item defines data attached to the presentation and to
the chosen solution. It asserts neither that a complete integral exists
for a given presentation, nor that its characteristic curves are motions
of the model, nor that $\beta$ is constant along such curves; those are
the claims of the page's characteristics theorem. It also
asserts no global statement: $\det S_{q\alpha}\ne0$ is required at the
base point only, and the theorem below records its local consequences.

Adopt the force model with potential presentation $(U,d)$ and mechanical
Lagrangian $L=K-U$ of [[def-cm07-action-and-mechanical-lagrangian]] with the
data and conventions of [[def-cm12-cotangent-momentum]]: masses
$m_{1},\dots,m_{N}>0$, open configuration domain $Q\subseteq\mathbb R^{3N}$,
time window $I_{0}$, mass operator $\mathsf M$
([[def-cm01-configuration]]), $C^{2}$ potential $U$ and residual forces $d$
of the standing regularity ([[def-cm03-potential-and-mechanical-energy]],
[[post-cm02-force-superposition]]), the presentation being hyperregular on
its charts ([[pthm-cm12-mechanical-hyperregularity]],
[[def-cm12-hamiltonian]]). Fix one momentum chart of the presentation
(Cartesian coordinates $(t,x,p)$, or the chart $(t,q,p)$ of a
generalized-coordinate map $X:\Omega\to Q$
([[def-cm07-generalized-coordinates-and-forces]])), with $m$ pairs of
coordinates and Hamiltonian $H$ of class $C^{2}$ on
$J_{0}\times V\times\mathbb R^{m}$; let $S:J\times U\times A\to\mathbb R$
be a $C^{3}$ complete integral of the model's Hamilton-Jacobi equation at
$(t_{0},q_{0},\alpha_{0})\in J\times U\times A$ in the sense of
[[def-cm14-hamilton-jacobi-equation]] and [[def-cm14-complete-integral]]
($J\subseteq J_{0}$, $U\subseteq V$, $A\subseteq\mathbb R^{m}$ open), and
put

$$\beta_{0}:=S_{\alpha}(t_{0},q_{0},\alpha_{0}).$$

Then:

1. **(characteristic curves)** For every $\alpha$ sufficiently close to
   $\alpha_{0}$ there is an open interval $I_{\alpha}\ni t_{0}$ and a
   $C^{1}$ curve $q:I_{\alpha}\to U$ with $q(t_{0})=q_{0}$ solving
   $q'(t)=H_{p}\bigl(t,q(t),S_{q}(t,q(t),\alpha)\bigr)$, and with
   $p(t):=S_{q}(t,q(t),\alpha)$ the pair $(q,p)$ satisfies Hamilton's
   equations $q'=H_{p}$, $p'=-H_{q}$ on $I_{\alpha}$. If the chart is the
   Cartesian chart and $d\equiv0$ on the state domain, then $x:=q$ is a
   motion of the model on $I_{\alpha}$ and $p(t)=\mathsf Mx'(t)$
   ([[def-cm02-newtonian-flow]], [[def-cm12-cotangent-momentum]]); if the
   chart is the chart of a generalized-coordinate map and $d\equiv0$, then
   $q$ solves the declared Lagrange equations of the substituted
   Lagrangian and $p(t)=G(q(t))q'(t)$
   ([[def-cm07-generalized-coordinates-and-forces]],
   [[pthm-cm12-hamilton-equivalence]]).
2. **(Jacobi constants)** With $(q,p)$ as in clause 1,
   $\beta(t):=S_{\alpha}(t,q(t),\alpha)$ is constant on $I_{\alpha}$ and
   equal to $S_{\alpha}(t_{0},q_{0},\alpha)$.
3. **(local converse)** For $(\alpha,\beta)$ sufficiently close to
   $(\alpha_{0},\beta_{0})$ the equation $\beta=S_{\alpha}(t,q,\alpha)$
   can be solved locally for $q=Q(t,\alpha,\beta)$, and with
   $p:=S_{q}\bigl(t,Q(t,\alpha,\beta),\alpha\bigr)$ the curve
   $t\mapsto(Q,p)$ solves Hamilton's equations; in the Cartesian chart on
   the potential branch it is the momentum-phase curve of a motion of the
   model.
4. **(canonical labels)** On the domain of the local diffeomorphism
   $(q,p)\mapsto(\beta,\alpha)$ obtained by composing
   $(q,p)\mapsto(q,\alpha)$ (solving $p=S_{q}$) with
   $(q,\alpha)\mapsto(\beta,\alpha)$, one has
   $\omega=d\beta\wedge d\alpha$ at every fixed $t$, where $\omega$ is the
   two-form of the presentation in this chart
   ([[def-cm13-two-form]]); equivalently, $(\beta,\alpha)$ are canonical
   coordinates of the presentation in the sense of clause (a) of
   [[def-cm13-canonical-form]].

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_{\omega}$
([[def-countable-choice]]). Adopt the force model with potential
presentation $(U,d)$ and mechanical Lagrangian $L=K-U$ of
[[def-cm07-action-and-mechanical-lagrangian]], with the momentum charts,
forms and canonical coordinates of [[def-cm13-two-form]],
[[pthm-cm13-two-form-is-symplectic]] and [[def-cm13-canonical-form]], the
Hamiltonian fields of [[def-cm13-hamiltonian-field]], the bracket of
[[def-cm13-poisson]] and the branch Hamiltonian $H$ of
[[def-cm12-hamiltonian]]. Let $W_{0}$ be a nonempty open phase domain of a
momentum chart, of dimension $2n$, and let $F=(F_{1}=H|_{W_{0}},\dots,F_{n})$
be a completely integrable datum of the presentation on $W_{0}$
([[def-cm14-complete-integrability]]). Let $b_{0}$ be a regular value with
nonempty compact connected regular fibre $N=F^{-1}(b_{0})$, and assume
that there are a saturated open neighbourhood $U\subseteq W_{0}$ of $N$
and a ball $B\subseteq\mathbb R^{n}$ of regular values with $F(U)=B$ such
that $\pi=F|_{U}:U\to B$ is a proper submersion with connected fibres.
Then, after shrinking $B$ to a smaller ball $B'$ and $U$ to
$\pi^{-1}(B')$ (and writing $U$ for the shrunk neighbourhood again), there
are action-angle coordinates

$$(I,\theta):U\longrightarrow B'\times T^{n},\qquad T^{n}=\mathbb R^{n}/\mathbb Z^{n},$$

of class $C^{\infty}$, diffeomorphic onto their image, such that:

1. **(form)** the angles are period-one and the presentation's two-form
   takes the canonical action-angle form
   $$\omega=\sum_{i=1}^{n}d\theta_{i}\wedge dI_{i}$$
   on $U$, in the sense of [[def-action-and-angle-coordinates]];
2. **(dimension)** each action coordinate $I_{i}$ has dimension
   $\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-1}$ (action) and each angle $\theta_{i}$ is
   dimensionless, consistently with the action dimension of the
   presentation's two-form in its original canonical charts
   ([[def-cm01-units]]);
3. **(fibrewise constants)** every $C^{\infty}$ function on $U$ that is
   constant on the fibres of $\pi$ is a function of $I$ alone; in
   particular $F_{i}=f_{i}(I)$ for $C^{\infty}$ functions $f_{i}$ and the
   branch Hamiltonian is $H=h(I)$ with $h=f_{1}$;
4. **(linear motion)** the solutions of the Hamiltonian system of $h$ in
   the chart $(I,\theta)$ are exactly the momentum-phase curves of the
   model's motions on $U$ (which is the presentation reading of clause 1
   of [[pthm-cm13-hamiltonian-field-integrates-the-model-equations]]),
   and they satisfy
$$\dot I=0,\qquad \dot\theta=\frac{\partial h}{\partial I}(I),\qquad\theta(t)=\theta(0)+t\,\frac{\partial h}{\partial I}\bigl(I(0)\bigr)\pmod{\mathbb Z^{n}},$$
   so that each motion on a torus is periodic or dense according to its
   frequency vector;
5. **(radian rescaling)** with the rescaled coordinates
   $\theta^{\mathrm{rad}}:=2\pi\theta$ and
   $I^{\mathrm{rad}}:=I/(2\pi)$ one has
   $\omega=\sum_{i}d\theta^{\mathrm{rad}}_{i}\wedge dI^{\mathrm{rad}}_{i}$,
   the angles $\theta^{\mathrm{rad}}$ are $2\pi$-periodic, and
   $H=\tilde h(I^{\mathrm{rad}})$ with
   $\tilde h(I^{\mathrm{rad}})=h(2\pi I^{\mathrm{rad}})$ and
   $\dot\theta^{\mathrm{rad}}=\partial\tilde h/\partial I^{\mathrm{rad}}$;
   the components $\partial h/\partial I_{i}$ are **cyclic frequencies**
   (cycles per unit time), not angular rates, the angular rates being
   $2\pi\,\partial h/\partial I_{i}$.

The statement is conditional on the adopted force branch, the declared
presentation, the smooth completely integrable datum, the fibre
hypotheses and $\mathrm{AC}_{\omega}$; it asserts no global
action-angle coordinates on $W_{0}$, no statement about critical or
noncompact fibres and no empirical content.

Adopt the force model with potential presentation $(U,d)$ and mechanical
Lagrangian $L=K-U$ of [[def-cm07-action-and-mechanical-lagrangian]] with the
momentum charts, the phase domains and the two-form datum of
[[def-cm13-two-form]]: the Cartesian phase domain $W=Q\times\mathbb R^{3N}$
with $n=3N$, its two-form $\omega$, and for each generalized-coordinate map
$X:\Omega\to Q$ with $r$ coordinates the chart map $\Phi_{X}$ and the form
$\omega_{X}$ ([[def-cm07-generalized-coordinates-and-forces]],
[[def-cm12-cotangent-momentum]], [[def-cm01-configuration]]). All
differentiability classes are those of
[[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]].

**(a) Canonical coordinates.** Let $W_{0}\subseteq W$ (or
$W_{0}\subseteq\Omega\times\mathbb R^{r}$) be nonempty open, and let

$$\theta=(\theta^{1},\dots,\theta^{2m}):W_{0}\longrightarrow V\subseteq\mathbb R^{2m}$$

be a $C^{1}$ chart of $W_{0}$ onto an open set $V$ ([[def-metric-topology]]),
with $m$ the half-dimension of $W_{0}$. The coordinates $\theta$ are
**canonical coordinates for the presentation's two-form** on $W_{0}$ when the
two-form takes the **canonical form**

$$\omega=\sum_{a=1}^{m}d\theta^{a}\wedge d\theta^{m+a}$$

on $W_{0}$ ([[def-smooth-differential-k-form]]); equivalently, when the
pullback identity $\theta^{*}\omega_{V}^{\mathrm{st}}=\omega|_{W_{0}}$ holds
for the standard two-form $\omega_{V}^{\mathrm{st}}$ of $V$
([[def-cm-phase-domain-and-standard-symplectic-two-form]],
[[def-pullback-of-a-differential-form]]), equivalently when
$D\theta(z)^{\mathsf T}J\,D\theta(z)=J$ for the standard symplectic matrix
$J$ at every $z\in W_{0}$
([[prop-cm-canonical-map-tests-and-hamiltonian-transport]]). A **canonical
chart of the presentation** is a chart whose coordinates are canonical in
this sense; the equivalence with the canonical maps defined later on this
page is recorded with those definitions.

**(b) The model's own charts are canonical.** The Cartesian coordinates
$(x,p)$ on $W$ are canonical coordinates: by clause 1 of
[[pthm-cm13-two-form-is-symplectic]] the two-form is
$\omega=\sum_{a}dx^{a}\wedge dp_{a}$. For a generalized-coordinate map, the
coordinates $(q,P)$ on $\Omega\times\mathbb R^{r}$ are canonical coordinates
for the pulled-back form $\omega_{X}$: by clause 2 of
[[pthm-cm13-two-form-is-symplectic]] one has
$\omega_{X}=\sum_{a}dq^{a}\wedge dP_{a}$, and when the map is a genuine chart
($r=3N$) the chart transition is a change of canonical coordinates on
overlaps.

**(c) Canonical one-form up to gauge.** The canonical one-form $\lambda$ of
[[def-cm13-two-form]] is said to be **in canonical form up to gauge** in the
canonical coordinates $\theta$ when the difference
$\lambda-\sum_{a}\theta^{m+a}d\theta^{a}$ is a closed one-form on $W_{0}$;
exactness of that difference is not required. For the presentation's own
charts the difference of the two canonical one-forms is closed by clause 3 of
[[pthm-cm13-two-form-is-symplectic]].

**(d) Status and warnings.** The item defines a coordinate condition on a
declared chart and records the one fact that the presentation's own momentum
charts satisfy it. It asserts no existence of canonical coordinates beyond
the model's charts, no global statement on multiply connected phase domains,
no dynamics and no measured value. A chart that is merely a diffeomorphism
need not be canonical; the determinant test
$|\det D\theta|=1$ is necessary but, in dimension $2m\ge4$, not sufficient
for canonicity (the scope remark of this page records the witness).

**Action–angle coordinates** on a neighbourhood $U$ fibred by Lagrangian
tori are a diffeomorphism

$$ (I,\theta):U\longrightarrow B\times(\mathbb R/\mathbb Z)^n,$$

where $B\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ is open, such that the components
$I=(I_1,\ldots,I_n)$ and
$\theta=(\theta_1,\ldots,\theta_n)$ have fibres $I=\mathrm{constant}$ and

$$\omega=\sum_{i=1}^n d\theta_i\wedge dI_i.$$

This page uses period one for every angle. Replacing angles by period $2\pi$
rescales the corresponding actions and formulas. The order
$d\theta_i\wedge dI_i$ is forced by the library convention
$\iota_{X_H}\omega=dH$: it gives $\dot\theta_i=\partial H/\partial I_i$.

Let $(I,\theta)$ be period-one action-angle coordinates with
$\omega=\sum_{i=1}^n d\theta_i\wedge dI_i$ as supplied by
[[thm-cm-liouville-arnold-action-angle-repaired]] and
[[def-action-and-angle-coordinates]]. Define the rescaled coordinates

$$\theta_i^{\mathrm{rad}}:=2\pi\,\theta_i,\qquad I_i^{\mathrm{rad}}:=\frac{I_i}{2\pi}\qquad(i=1,\dots,n).$$

Then $(\theta^{\mathrm{rad}},I^{\mathrm{rad}})$ are $C^\infty$ coordinates on the same chart,

$$\omega=\sum_{i=1}^n d\theta_i^{\mathrm{rad}}\wedge dI_i^{\mathrm{rad}},$$

the angles $\theta^{\mathrm{rad}}$ are $2\pi$-periodic (radian-valued), and if a Hamiltonian is
$H=h(I)$ with $h$ of class $C^2$ in the period-one coordinates then in the radian coordinates it is
$H=\tilde h(I^{\mathrm{rad}})$ with $\tilde h(I^{\mathrm{rad}})=h(2\pi I^{\mathrm{rad}})$ and
$\dot\theta^{\mathrm{rad}}_i=\partial\tilde h/\partial I^{\mathrm{rad}}_i$.

derivations.claim: Derivatives of $S$: with $c:=\cos(\omega t)$ and $s:=\sin(\omega t)$, [L2] gives $S_{x}=m\omega\bigl(x\cot(\omega t)-\alpha\csc(\omega t)\bigr)$ and $S_{t}=\frac{m\omega^{2}}{2}\Bigl[-(x^{2}+\alpha^{2})\csc^{2}(\omega t) +2x\alpha\,\csc(\omega t)\cot(\omega t)\Bigr].$ Substituting $p=S_{x}$ into $H$, $S_{t}+H(x,S_{x})=\frac{m\omega^{2}}{2}\Bigl[-(x^{2}+\alpha^{2})\csc^{2} +2x\alpha\csc\cot+\bigl(x\cot-\alpha\csc\bigr)^{2}+x^{2}\Bigr] =\frac{m\omega^{2}}{2}x^{2}\bigl(-\csc^{2}+\cot^{2}+1\bigr)=0,$ because $\cot^{2}-\csc^{2}=-1$; and $S_{x\alpha}=-m\omega\,\csc(\omega t)\neq0$ on $V$. Hence $S$ is a $C^{\infty}$ complete integral of the model's Hamilton-Jacobi equation at every point of $V$, which is claim 1. Dimensions: $[m\omega x^{2}]=\mu\tau^{-1}\ell^{2}=[S]$.

The characteristic motion: put $x(t):=\alpha_{0}\cos(\omega t)-\beta(m\omega)^{-1}\sin(\omega t)$ and $p(t):=S_{x}(t,x(t),\alpha_{0})$. By [L2], $x'(t)=-\alpha_{0}\omega\sin(\omega t)-\beta m^{-1}\cos(\omega t)$ and $\frac{p(t)}{m}=\omega\Bigl[x(t)\frac{c}{s}-\alpha_{0}\frac{1}{s}\Bigr] =\omega\Bigl[\bigl(\alpha_{0}c-\frac{\beta}{m\omega}s\bigr)\frac{c}{s} -\frac{\alpha_{0}}{s}\Bigr] =-\omega\alpha_{0}s-\frac{\beta}{m}c=x'(t),$ using $\alpha_{0}(c^{2}-1)/s=-\alpha_{0}s$, so $p=mx'=H_{p}$, and $p'(t)=-m\omega^{2}\alpha_{0}c+\beta\omega s=-m\omega^{2}x(t)=-H_{x}$. For the constants, differentiating the displayed $S$ in $\alpha$ gives $S_{\alpha}(t,x,\alpha)=m\omega\bigl(\alpha\cot(\omega t)-x\csc(\omega t)\bigr)$, so $S_{\alpha}(t,x(t),\alpha_{0}) =m\omega\Bigl[\alpha_{0}\cot(\omega t)-\Bigl(\alpha_{0}c -\frac{\beta}{m\omega}s\Bigr)\csc(\omega t)\Bigr] =m\omega\alpha_{0}\bigl(\cot-c\,\csc\bigr)+\beta=\beta,$ since $\cot u-\cos u\,\csc u=0$. Hence the characteristic curve lies on the level set $S_{\alpha}=\beta$, it is a motion of the model with $p=mx'$ by [L1], and $\beta=S_{\alpha}$ is constant along it, which is claim 2.

The canonical chart: write $x=\sqrt{I/(\pi m\omega)}\,\sin(2\pi\theta)$ and $p=\sqrt{Im\omega/\pi}\,\cos(2\pi\theta)$; by [L2], $x_{\theta}p_{I}-x_{I}p_{\theta} =\cos^{2}(2\pi\theta)+\sin^{2}(2\pi\theta)=1,$ the computation being: $x_{\theta}=2\pi\sqrt{I/(\pi m\omega)}\cos$, $p_{I}=\tfrac12\sqrt{m\omega/\pi}\,I^{-1/2}\cos$ give $x_{\theta}p_{I}=\cos^{2}$; and $x_{I}=\tfrac12(\pi m\omega I)^{-1/2}\sin$, $p_{\theta}=-2\pi\sqrt{Im\omega/\pi}\sin$ give $x_{I}p_{\theta}=-\sin^{2}$. Hence $\{x,p\}=1$ in the chart, i.e. the coordinates are canonical for the presentation's bracket and $\omega_{\mathrm{form}}=d\theta\wedge dI$. Substituting into $H$, $H=\frac{p^{2}}{2m}+\frac{m\omega^{2}}{2}x^{2} =\frac{I\omega}{2\pi}\bigl(\cos^{2}+\sin^{2}\bigr)=\frac{I\omega}{2\pi} =\frac{I}{T}=h(I).$ By [L5], $\dot I=0$ and $\dot\theta=h'(I)=1/T$ along the motions, which is claim 3.

The period integral: parametrize the motion of step 3.1 with $I>0$, $\theta_{0}=0$ by $x(t)=A\sin(\omega t)$, $A:=\sqrt{I/(\pi m\omega)}$, so that $p(t)=mx'(t)=mA\omega\cos(\omega t)$ and the least positive period is $T$ by [L1]. Then by [L2], $\oint p\,dx=\int_{0}^{T}p(t)x'(t)\,dt=mA^{2}\omega^{2}\int_{0}^{T} \cos^{2}(\omega t)\,dt=mA^{2}\omega^{2}\cdot\frac{T}{2} =mA^{2}\omega\pi=I,$ because $\cos^{2}(\omega t)=(1+\cos 2\omega t)/2$, the integral of $\cos(2\omega t)$ over $[0,T]$ vanishes being an increment of $\sin(2\omega t)/(2\omega)$ at $\sin(2\pi k)=0$, and $mA^{2}\omega\pi=m\frac{I}{\pi m\omega}\omega\pi=I$. This is claim 4.

Radian rescaling: by [L5], $\theta^{\mathrm{rad}}=2\pi\theta$ and $I^{\mathrm{rad}}=I/(2\pi)$ keep the two-form and give $H=h(2\pi I^{\mathrm{rad}})=2\pi I^{\mathrm{rad}}/T=\omega I^{\mathrm{rad}}$ and $\dot\theta^{\mathrm{rad}}=2\pi\dot\theta=2\pi/T=\omega$; inverting the rescaling in the chart of step 3.1 gives $x=\sqrt{2I^{\mathrm{rad}}/(m\omega)}\sin\theta^{\mathrm{rad}}$ and $p=\sqrt{2I^{\mathrm{rad}}m\omega}\cos\theta^{\mathrm{rad}}$, the source's chart. This is claim 5.
Claims 1-5 are verified by steps 1.1, 2.1, 3.1, 4.1 and 4.2 respectively; the example is verified.

boundaries.reason: All data are explicit for a single label; no possibly empty family occurs (example).

boundaries.evidence: The labels $\alpha=0$ and $\beta=0$ are included in the algebra, and the rest motion $I=0$ is the excluded boundary of the chart $I>0$ (example, step 1.1).
One degree of freedom is the case of the example (example).
The excluded set $\sin(\omega t)=0$ is exactly where the chart and the complete integral degenerate; it is handled in step 1.1 and in the companion caustic example.
The period integral runs over the closed interval $[0,T]$ and the boundary values agree, giving the exact normalization check (step 4.1).

boundaries.reason: Only finite explicit computations are made (steps 1.1-4.2).
Claims 1-5 are verified for the one declared (m,k) instance by explicit computation; no biconditional between the Hamilton-Jacobi equation and the action-angle chart is asserted.
The example does not assert that every solution of the model arises from this family of S, nor that H=I/T alone forces the displayed chart to be canonical.

citations.quote:
Adopt the following gravitational model and empirical premises for the
two-body part of this page, inside the force and interaction branches of
[[post-cm02-force-superposition]] and [[post-cm02-interactions]] and the
central-force class of [[post-cm05-central-model]] clause (i).

**(i) The two-label gravitational model.** A model of the gravitational
branch is a model of class (i) of [[post-cm05-central-model]] with
$J_0=(0,\infty)$, $Q=\{x=(x_1,x_2):x_1\ne x_2\}$, masses $m_1,m_2>0$ in the
equation of motion, and the **gravitational pair potential**
$$U(x_1,x_2)=-\frac{G_{\mathrm N}\,m_1^{g}m_2^{g}}{\lvert x_1-x_2\rvert},$$
where $G_{\mathrm N}>0$ is the **Newtonian constant of gravitation**, a
constant of dimension $\ell^{3}\mu^{-1}\tau^{-2}$ read in
$\mathrm{m^3\,kg^{-1}\,s^{-2}}$, and $m_1^{g},m_2^{g}>0$ are the
**gravitational coupling parameters** of the labels, primitive model data
distinct from the inertial masses $m_1,m_2$ ([[post-cm02-interactions]]
clause (v), [[def-cm01-units]]). The corresponding central pair potential of
class (i) is $u(\rho)=-\kappa/\rho$ with
$$\kappa:=G_{\mathrm N}\,m_1^{g}m_2^{g}>0,\qquad\text{dimension } \mu\ell^{3}\tau^{-2};$$
it is of class $C^\infty$ on $(0,\infty)$, the model has no external forces,
and coincident configurations are excluded. The force is attractive, and its
inverse-square form is an **adopted law** of this branch, not a consequence
of the equation of motion.

**(ii) The empirical mass identification.** For the quantitative
applications of this page, adopt in addition the identification
$$m_i^{g}=m_i\qquad(i=1,2)$$
of the gravitational coupling parameters with the inertial masses. This is an
**empirical assumption**, not part of clause (i) and not a consequence of the
equation of motion ([[post-cm02-interactions]] clause (vi)); it is the
content of the weak equivalence principle for these labels, and it is
adopted here only where a statement explicitly says so. When it is adopted,
$\kappa=G_{\mathrm N}m_1m_2$, and every conclusion that uses it inherits its
empirical status; statements that never invoke clause (ii) remain conditional
on clause (i) alone, with $\kappa$ expressed through $m_1^{g},m_2^{g}$.

**(iii) The measured value of the constant.** When a model of this page is
used quantitatively, $G_{\mathrm N}$ may be **assigned** the CODATA 2022
recommended value
$$G_{\mathrm N}=6.674\,30(15)\times10^{-11}\ \mathrm{m^{3}\,kg^{-1}\,s^{-2}},$$
with standard uncertainty $0.000\,15\times10^{-11}$ in the same unit and
relative standard uncertainty $2.2\times10^{-5}$: a qualified empirical
premise, not a definition and not an exact value. The recommendation is a
least-squares value from 16 measurements whose mutual inconsistency led the
CODATA Task Group to expand its uncertainty by a factor of $3.9$, and the
2022 value agrees with the 2018 value because the input data were unchanged.
Any numerical conclusion that uses this assignment inherits the uncertainty
of $G_{\mathrm N}$ together with the uncertainties and conditions of the
other model data actually used; no such numerical conclusion is drawn by
this postulate itself.

**(iv) Scope and exclusions.** The model is non-relativistic and weak-field;
it treats the two labels as point particles with fixed masses, ignores
external bodies, rotation, deformation, mass loss, radiation and any
non-gravitational force, and excludes coincident configurations. It is not
asserted that any physical system is exactly of this form; in particular,
the identification of clause (ii) is not a framework-wide identification,
and the inverse-square law is not derived from the balance laws of the
framework.

**(v) Status.** Clauses (i), (ii) and (iii) are adopted assumptions of the
model and its empirical inputs; this item contains no proof and no
measurement of its own. The theorems of this page that invoke the model are
conditional on these clauses, and agreement of their predictions with
observations would test the combined model and apparatus assumptions rather
than prove them.

Adopt, as the **central-force model** for the two-body part of this page, the
following restricted model class inside the force and interaction branches of
[[post-cm02-force-superposition]] and [[post-cm02-interactions]].

**(i) The two-label central model.** A model of class (i) is a force model of
[[post-cm02-force-superposition]] with $N=2$ labels, fixed masses
$m_1,m_2>0$ ([[post-cm01-worldlines]] clause (v)), a time window $I_0$, the
collision-excluded configuration domain
$$Q:=\{\,x=(x_1,x_2)\in(\mathbb R^3)^2:\lvert x_1-x_2\rvert\in J_0\,\}$$
for an open interval $J_0\subseteq(0,\infty)$
([[def-cm01-configuration]]), and the force map presented through the
time-independent **static central pair potential**
$$U(x_1,x_2):=u(\lvert x_1-x_2\rvert),\qquad u:J_0\to\mathbb R\ \text{of class }C^2,$$
so that $F_i(t,x,v)=-\nabla_{x_i}U(x)$ on the state domain (clauses (iii)
and (iv) of [[post-cm02-interactions]]; $U$ is of class $C^2$ on the open
$Q$ by [[lem-cm05-radial-potential-gradient]]). In the external-plus-pair
presentation of clause (i) of that postulate the model has
$F_i^{\mathrm{ext}}\equiv0$: no external forces act on the labels of a model
of class (i).

**(ii) The reduced one-label problem.** For a model of class (i) put
$\mu:=m_1m_2/(m_1+m_2)>0$ of dimension $\mu$ ([[def-cm01-units]]). The
**reduced problem** of the model is the one-label problem of mass $\mu$ whose
unknown is the relative coordinate $r=x_1-x_2$ and whose equation is
$$\mu\,r''=-\frac{u'(\lvert r\rvert)}{\lvert r\rvert}\,r;$$
by [[pthm-cm05-relative-reduction]] the relative coordinate of every motion
of a model of class (i) solves this equation, and every pair of a uniform
centre-of-mass motion and a solution of the reduced equation on a common
interval reconstructs a motion of the model. Adopt the reduced problem as the
object that the central-force statements of this page describe, and the
central-force-trajectory vocabulary of
[[def-cm-central-force-trajectory]] (attached angular momentum
$j=\mu\,r\times r'$ and energy $E=\tfrac12\mu\lVert r'\rVert_2^2+u(\lvert
r\rvert)$) as the vocabulary in which those statements are phrased.

**(iii) The one-label fixed-centre idealization.** A **one-label central
model** is a force model of [[post-cm02-force-superposition]] with $N=1$,
mass $\mu>0$, time window $I_0$, a fixed **centre** $c\in\mathbb R^3$, the
configuration domain $Q_c=\{x\in\mathbb R^3:\lvert x-c\rvert\in J_0\}$, and
the external force map
$$F(t,x,v)=-\frac{u'(\lvert x-c\rvert)}{\lvert x-c\rvert}\,(x-c),$$
presented through the potential $u(\lvert x-c\rvert)$ with the same function
$u\in C^2(J_0)$. This model is the **fixed-centre idealization** of the
reduced problem: it drops the centre-of-mass degree of freedom and holds the
force centre fixed. It is a separate adopted model class, not a consequence
of class (i), and every use of it must state that the idealization is
intended.

**(iv) Reading conventions.** In the statements of this page: the **force
centre** of the reduced problem is the origin of the relative coordinate
$r$; an **orbit** is the trajectory $t\mapsto r(t)$ of the reduced problem
(equivalently, by [[pthm-cm05-relative-reduction]], the trajectory of either
label relative to the centre of mass, up to the mass ratio); "circular" and
"elliptic" name properties of that trajectory; and the words "planet",
"satellite", "central body" and "test particle" name labels of a model of
class (i) or (iii). These words carry no empirical claim about nature.

**(v) Exclusions and status.** The class excludes: velocity-dependent and
explicitly time-dependent central forces; non-central and non-potential
forces; constraints and reaction forces; colliding configurations
$x_1=x_2$ (equivalently $r=0$); external forces on the labels; and models
with more than two labels. Finite-size, rotational, deformational, dissipative
and relativistic effects are outside the class. The masses, the interval
$J_0$ and the function $u$ (including any parameters it carries) are model
data, not measured values ([[def-cm01-units]]); quantitative empirical use
requires separately stated measured inputs with their uncertainties, and no
statement of this page asserts that any physical system is exactly a model
of this class.

Adopt the force model of [[post-cm02-force-superposition]] with $N=2$
labels, masses $m_1,m_2>0$ ([[post-cm01-worldlines]] clause (v)), a time
window $I_0$, and the collision-excluded configuration domain
$$Q:=\{\,x=(x_1,x_2)\in(\mathbb R^3)^2:\lvert x_1-x_2\rvert\in J_0\,\}$$
for an open interval $J_0\subseteq(0,\infty)$
([[def-cm01-configuration]]). Suppose the model presents its force map
through the time-independent potential
$$U(x_1,x_2):=u(\lvert x_1-x_2\rvert),$$
where $u:J_0\to\mathbb R$ is of class $C^2$
([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]), so that
$F_i(t,x,v)=-\nabla_{x_i}U(x)$ on the state domain ([[post-cm02-interactions]],
clauses (iii) and (iv), [[lem-cm05-radial-potential-gradient]]). Let
$x:J\to Q$ be a **motion** of the model on an interval $J$ with nonempty
interior ([[def-cm02-newtonian-flow]]) and write
$$M:=m_1+m_2,\quad \mu:=\frac{m_1m_2}{M},\quad X:=\frac{m_1x_1+m_2x_2}{M},\quad V:=X',\quad P:=m_1x_1'+m_2x_2',\quad r:=x_1-x_2,$$
with $\lvert\cdot\rvert=\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ the Euclidean norm
([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]) and dimensions as in [[def-cm01-units]]
($[M]=[\mu]=\mu$, $[X]=[r]=\ell$, $[P]=\mu\ell\tau^{-1}$). Then:

1. **(Pair forces.)** On $J$ the evaluated forces are
   $$F_1\bigl(t,x(t),x'(t)\bigr)=-\frac{u'(\lvert r\rvert)}{\lvert r\rvert}\,r,\qquad F_2\bigl(t,x(t),x'(t)\bigr)=+\frac{u'(\lvert r\rvert)}{\lvert r\rvert}\,r;$$
   thus the model invokes the external-plus-pair presentation of
   [[post-cm02-interactions]] clause (i) with
   $F_i^{\mathrm{ext}}\equiv0$ and the single pair force
   $F_{12}=-u'(\lvert r\rvert)r/\lvert r\rvert=-F_{21}$, which is central
   and antisymmetric in the sense of clause (ii).
2. **(Centre of mass.)** $P$ is constant on $J$ and $X$ is affine: for all
   $t,t_0\in J$, $X(t)=X(t_0)+(t-t_0)V$ with the constant
   $V=X'=M^{-1}P$.
3. **(Relative motion.)** $r$ is of class $C^2$ on $J$, satisfies
   $$\mu\,r''(t)=-\frac{u'(\lvert r(t)\rvert)}{\lvert r(t)\rvert}\,r(t)\qquad(t\in J),$$
   and is therefore a **central-force trajectory for $(\mu,u)$** in the
   sense of [[def-cm-central-force-trajectory]]; its angular momentum vector
   $j=\mu\,r\times r'$ and energy $E=\tfrac12\mu\lVert r'\rVert_2^2+
   u(\lvert r\rvert)$ are the attached objects of that definition.
4. **(Reconstruction and bijection.)** The identities
   $x_1=X+\frac{m_2}{M}r$ and $x_2=X-\frac{m_1}{M}r$ hold on $J$.
   Conversely, if $X^{\circ}:J\to\mathbb R^3$ is affine with
   $(X^{\circ})''=0$ and $r^{\circ}:J\to\mathbb R^3$ is a $C^2$ curve with
   $\lvert r^{\circ}(t)\rvert\in J_0$ and
   $\mu(r^{\circ})''=-u'(\lvert r^{\circ}\rvert)r^{\circ}/\lvert r^{\circ}\rvert$
   on $J$, then
   $$x_1^{\circ}:=X^{\circ}+\frac{m_2}{M}r^{\circ},\qquad x_2^{\circ}:=X^{\circ}-\frac{m_1}{M}r^{\circ}$$
   define a motion $x^{\circ}:J\to Q$ of the model whose centre of mass is
   $X^{\circ}$ and whose relative coordinate is $r^{\circ}$. Consequently
   the assignment $x\mapsto(X,r)$ is a bijection from the motions of the
   model on $J$ onto the pairs (affine curve $X^{\circ}$ with
   $(X^{\circ})''=0$\!, central-force trajectory $r^{\circ}$ for $(\mu,u)$
   with values in $J_0$) on $J$.

Adopt the central-force model of [[post-cm05-central-model]] clause (i) with
masses $m_1,m_2>0$, reduced mass $\mu=m_1m_2/M$, $M=m_1+m_2$, static central
pair potential $u\in C^2(J_0)$, and let $x:J\to Q$ be a motion with relative
coordinate $r$, attached angular momentum $j=\mu\,r\times r'$, and suppose
$j=Je_3$ with $J>0$ for an oriented orthonormal triad $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$
([[pthm-cm05-relative-reduction]], [[lem-cm-oriented-orthonormal-triads]]).
Let $(\rho,\theta)$ be polar data for $r$ in that triad
([[thm-cm-central-force-polar-reduction]]) and put
$$U^{\mathrm{eff}}_J(\rho):=u(\rho)+\frac{J^2}{2\mu\rho^2}\qquad(\rho\in J_0),$$
the **effective potential** of angular momentum $J$, of class $C^2$ on $J_0$
([[def-cm-central-force-trajectory]]). Then:

1. **(Radial problem.)** On $J$: $\rho^2\theta'=J/\mu>0$, the effective
   equation
   $$\mu\,\rho''=-\bigl(U^{\mathrm{eff}}_J\bigr)'(\rho)$$
   holds, and the relative energy
   $E=\tfrac12\mu\lVert r'\rVert_2^2+u(\lvert r\rvert)$ satisfies
   $E=\tfrac12\mu(\rho')^2+U^{\mathrm{eff}}_J(\rho)$ and is constant on $J$;
   equivalently, the radial coordinate solves the one-dimensional mechanical
   initial-value problem of mass $\mu$ on the half-line $\rho>0$ in the
   potential $U^{\mathrm{eff}}_J$.
2. **(Reconstruction.)** Conversely, let $\rho^{\circ}:J\to\mathbb R$ be a
   $C^2$ function with $\rho^{\circ}(t)\in J_0$ and
   $\mu(\rho^{\circ})''=-(U^{\mathrm{eff}}_J)'(\rho^{\circ})$ on $J$, and let
   $\theta^{\circ}:J\to\mathbb R$ be a $C^2$ function with
   $(\theta^{\circ})'=J/\bigl(\mu(\rho^{\circ})^2\bigr)$ on $J$ (for instance
   $\theta^{\circ}(t)=\theta_0+\frac{J}{\mu}\int_{t_0}^{t}\rho^{\circ}(s)^{-2}\mathrm ds$).
   Then
   $$r^{\circ}(t):=\rho^{\circ}(t)\bigl(\cos\theta^{\circ}(t)\,e_1+\sin\theta^{\circ}(t)\,e_2\bigr)\qquad(t\in J)$$
   is a central-force trajectory for $(\mu,u)$ with
   $j^{\circ}=\mu\,r^{\circ}\times(r^{\circ})'=Je_3$ and constant energy
   $\tfrac12\mu\bigl((\rho^{\circ})'\bigr)^2+U^{\mathrm{eff}}_J(\rho^{\circ})$.
3. **(Mutual inversion and model reconstruction.)** The assignments of
   clauses 1 and 2 are mutually inverse: reconstructing from the polar data
   of $r$ returns $r$, and the polar data of the reconstructed $r^{\circ}$
   agree with $(\rho^{\circ},\theta^{\circ})$ up to an additive constant of
   the angular coordinate. Consequently, together with an affine
   centre-of-mass curve $X^{\circ}$ with $(X^{\circ})''=0$ on $J$, the datum
   $(\rho^{\circ},\theta^{\circ})$ reconstructs a motion of the two-label
   model with angular momentum $Je_3$, centre of mass $X^{\circ}$ and relative
   coordinate $r^{\circ}$ ([[pthm-cm05-relative-reduction]] clause 4).

Let $\mu>0$, $\kappa>0$, $U(\rho)=-\kappa/\rho$ on $(0,\infty)$, let
$r:I\to\mathbb R^3$ be a central-force trajectory for $(\mu,U)$ with constant
angular momentum $j=Je_3$, $J>0$ and constant energy $E$
([[def-cm-central-force-trajectory]]), and let
$u:W\to(0,\infty)$, $\theta$ and $\sigma$ be as in
[[thm-cm-kepler-binet-equation]], with $W=\theta(I^\circ)$. Write
$c:=\mu\kappa/J^2>0$ and $p:=1/c=J^2/(\mu\kappa)$. Then:

1. there are $e\ge0$ and $\theta_0\in\mathbb R$ with
   $$u(\varphi)=c\bigl(1+e\cos(\varphi-\theta_0)\bigr)\qquad(\varphi\in W),$$
   and for $t\in I^\circ$ accordingly
   $\rho(t)=p/\bigl(1+e\cos(\theta(t)-\theta_0)\bigr)$;
2. the energy and the eccentricity are related by
   $$E=\frac{\mu\kappa^2}{2J^2}\bigl(e^2-1\bigr);$$ consequently
   $E<0\iff e<1$, $E=0\iff e=1$ and $E>0\iff e>1$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $\mu>0$,
$\kappa>0$, $U(\rho)=-\kappa/\rho$ on $(0,\infty)$, and let $r:I\to\mathbb R^3$
be a central-force trajectory for $(\mu,U)$ with constant angular momentum
$j=Je_3$, $J>0$, and constant energy $E<0$. Let $e\in[0,1)$,
$\theta_0\in\mathbb R$, $p=J^2/(\mu\kappa)$, $a=p/(1-e^2)$,
$b=a\sqrt{1-e^2}$, and $\varrho(\varphi):=p/(1+e\cos(\varphi-\theta_0))$
be the conic data of [[thm-cm-kepler-conic-and-eccentricity]], and let
$(\rho,\theta)$ be polar data as in
[[thm-cm-central-force-polar-reduction]]. Then:

1. **(Completeness.)** $r$ extends uniquely to a central-force trajectory for
   $(\mu,U)$ defined on all of $\mathbb R$; along it
   $\rho(t)\in[p/(1+e),\,p/(1-e)]$ for every $t$, and $\rho$ and $\rho'$ are
   bounded. Consequently every maximal central-force trajectory with these
   data has domain $\mathbb R$.
2. **(Periodicity.)** $\theta:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ is a strictly increasing
   $C^1$ bijection with
   $\dfrac{J}{\mu}\Bigl(\dfrac{1-e}{p}\Bigr)^2\le\theta'\le\dfrac{J}{\mu}\Bigl(\dfrac{1+e}{p}\Bigr)^2$;
   if $t_0\in\mathbb R$ and $T>0$ is determined by
   $\theta(t_0+T)=\theta(t_0)+2\pi$, then $r(t+T)=r(t)$ and
   $r'(t+T)=r'(t)$ for all $t\in\mathbb R$.
3. **(Period value.)** With $r_{\max}:=p/(1-e)$ and $r_{\min}:=p/(1+e)$,
   $$T=\frac{2\pi\mu ab}{J}=2\pi\sqrt{\frac{\mu}{\kappa}}\,a^{3/2}, \qquad T^2=\frac{4\pi^2\mu a^3}{\kappa}.$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Adopt the
two-label gravitational model of [[post-cm05-gravity]] clause (i): inertial
masses $m_1,m_2>0$, $M=m_1+m_2$, reduced mass $\mu=m_1m_2/M$, gravitational
couplings $m_1^{g},m_2^{g}>0$, $\kappa=G_{\mathrm N}m_1^{g}m_2^{g}$, and the
potential $u(\rho)=-\kappa/\rho$ on $(0,\infty)$. Let $x:J\to Q$ be a motion
with relative coordinate $r$, angular momentum $j=Je_3$, $J>0$, and energy
$E<0$, and let $e\in[0,1)$, $\theta_0\in\mathbb R$,
$$p=\frac{J^{2}}{\mu\kappa},\qquad a=\frac{p}{1-e^{2}}=-\frac{\kappa}{2E},\qquad b=a\sqrt{1-e^{2}}$$
be its conic data ([[pthm-cm05-conic]] clauses 1 and 3). Then:

1. **(Period of the relative motion.)** The relative motion extends uniquely
   to a central-force trajectory on all of $\mathbb R$ (as in
   [[pthm-cm05-conic]] clause 3); along that extension (with $\theta$ its
   polar angular coordinate, as supplied by the cited orbit theory), if
   $t_0\in\mathbb R$ and $T>0$ is determined by
   $\theta(t_0+T)=\theta(t_0)+2\pi$, then $r(t+T)=r(t)$ and
   $r'(t+T)=r'(t)$ for all $t\in\mathbb R$, and
   $$T=\frac{2\pi\mu ab}{J}=2\pi\sqrt{\frac{\mu}{\kappa}}\,a^{3/2}, \qquad T^{2}=\frac{4\pi^{2}\mu a^{3}}{\kappa}.$$
2. **(Gravitational parameters.)** With $\mu=m_1m_2/M$ and
   $\kappa=G_{\mathrm N}m_1^{g}m_2^{g}$,
   $$T^{2}=\frac{4\pi^{2}a^{3}m_1m_2}{M\,G_{\mathrm N}\,m_1^{g}m_2^{g}};$$
   if in addition the model adopts the identification
   $m_i^{g}=m_i$ of [[post-cm05-gravity]] clause (ii), this reduces to
   $$T^{2}=\frac{4\pi^{2}a^{3}}{G_{\mathrm N}M}.$$
3. **(Both labels.)** For each $i=1,2$ the position relative to the centre of
   mass is periodic with period $T$,
   $x_i(t+T)-X(t+T)=x_i(t)-X(t)$, while the absolute motions satisfy
   $$x_i(t+T)-x_i(t)=V\,T\qquad(t\in\mathbb R),$$
   with the constant centre-of-mass velocity $V=X'$ of
   [[pthm-cm05-relative-reduction]] clause 2; the absolute motions are
   periodic exactly when $V=0$.
4. **(Area per period.)** The area swept by the relative radius vector in one
   period is $\pi ab$, and it equals $JT/(2\mu)$; equivalently
   $T=2\pi\mu ab/J$ as in clause 1.

Let $\mu>0$, let $J_0\subseteq(0,\infty)$ be an open interval, let
$U:J_0\to\mathbb R$ be of class $C^2$, let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval
with at least two points, and let $r:I\to\mathbb R^3$ be a central-force
trajectory for $(\mu,U)$ whose angular momentum $j=\mu\,r\times r'$ is a nonzero
constant vector ([[thm-cm-central-force-angular-momentum-conservation]]); write
$J:=|j|>0$. Let $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ be an oriented orthonormal triad with
$e_3=j/J$ ([[lem-cm-oriented-orthonormal-triads]]).

Then there are twice differentiable $\rho:I\to(0,\infty)$ and
$\theta:I\to\mathbb R$ with

$$r(t)=\rho(t)\bigl(\cos\theta(t)\,e_1+\sin\theta(t)\,e_2\bigr)\qquad(t\in I),$$

and for **every** such pair $(\rho,\theta)$:

1. $\rho(t)=|r(t)|$ for all $t$;
2. $\rho^2\theta'=J/\mu$ on $I$, so $\theta'>0$;
3. the effective-potential equation $\mu\rho''=-\bigl(U^{\mathrm{eff}}_J\bigr)'(\rho)$
   holds on $I$, with $U^{\mathrm{eff}}_J=U+J^2/(2\mu\rho^2)$
   ([[def-cm-central-force-trajectory]]);
4. $E:=\frac12\mu\lVert r'\rVert_2^2+U(|r|)$ equals
   $\frac12\mu\rho'^2+U^{\mathrm{eff}}_J(\rho)$ and is constant on $I$.

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]), neighbourhoods are those of
[[def-neighbourhood-r]] and limit points those of [[def-limit-point-r]].

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $c \in A$ be a
**limit point of $A$**. The **difference quotient of $f$ at $c$** is the function

$$q_{f,c} : A \setminus \{c\} \to \mathbb{R}, \qquad q_{f,c}(x) := \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c} .$$

The division is legitimate at every point of the domain, since $x \ne c$ gives
$x - c \ne 0$.

**The point $c$ is a limit point of $A \setminus \{c\}$, not merely of $A$.**
For every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the punctured neighbourhood
$N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c)$ omits $c$, so

$$N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c) \cap A \;=\; N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c) \cap (A \setminus \{c\}) ,$$

and the left-hand side is nonempty because $c$ is a limit point of $A$. So
$q_{f,c}$ is a function on a set having $c$ as a limit point, and
$\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x)$ is a notion that [[def-function-limit]] defines.

$f$ is **differentiable at $c$** when that limit exists, and then the
**derivative of $f$ at $c$** is

$$f'(c) \;:=\; \lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x) \;=\; \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c} .$$

**Two obligations are carried by that notation, and both are discharged here.**

1. **Uniqueness.** Writing $f'(c)$ treats the right-hand side as a name for a
   single real number. That is legitimate: $c$ is a limit point of the domain
   $A \setminus \{c\}$ of $q_{f,c}$, so at most one real can satisfy the
   $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ condition, by [[lem-function-limit-unique]] applied to
   $q_{f,c}$. Two reals both meeting the condition are therefore equal, and the
   symbol denotes.
2. **Meaningfulness.** The hypothesis that $c$ is a limit point of $A$ is not
   decoration. At an **isolated** point of $A$ the punctured condition
   $0 < |x - c| < \delta$ is met by no point of the domain at all, so the
   $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ formula is satisfied vacuously by *every* real at
   once; this is why [[def-function-limit]] leaves the limit undefined there,
   and it is why this library defines $f'(c)$ only at a limit point of $A$. At
   an isolated point of its domain a function is neither differentiable nor
   non-differentiable here: the question is not posed.

**The limit sees only $A \setminus \{c\}$, so how the difference quotient is
extended to $c$ is irrelevant.** Let $Q : A \to \mathbb{R}$ agree with
$q_{f,c}$ at every point of $A \setminus \{c\}$, and let $L \in \mathbb{R}$.
Then $\lim_{x \to c} Q(x) = L$ if and only if $\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x) = L$.
Both conditions read: for every real $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a real
$\delta > 0$ such that every point $x$ of the relevant domain with
$0 < |x - c| < \delta$ satisfies $|{\cdot} - L| < \varepsilon$
([[def-function-limit]]). The clause $0 < |x - c|$ removes $x = c$ from both
quantifiers, so in both cases the points quantified over are exactly the
$x \in A \setminus \{c\}$ with $0 < |x - c| < \delta$, at which $Q$ and
$q_{f,c}$ take the same value. The two conditions are the same condition.

**Differentiability on a set.** For $S \subseteq A$, $f$ is **differentiable on
$S$** when it is differentiable at every $c \in S$; implicit in that phrase is
that every point of $S$ is a limit point of $A$. $f$ is **differentiable** when
it is differentiable on the whole of $A$.

**Restriction of the domain.** Let $B \subseteq A$, let $c \in B$ and suppose
$c$ is a limit point of $B$. If $f$ is differentiable at $c$, then so is the
restriction $f|_B : B \to \mathbb{R}$, and

$$(f|_B)'(c) \;=\; f'(c) .$$

Indeed $B \setminus \{c\} \subseteq A \setminus \{c\}$; the displayed identity
of punctured neighbourhoods above, applied to $B$, shows that $c$ is a limit
point of $B \setminus \{c\}$; the difference quotient $q_{f|_B, c}$ is the
restriction of $q_{f,c}$ to $B \setminus \{c\}$, since $f|_B(c) = f(c)$; and
claim 2 of [[lem-limit-is-local]] carries the limit to that restriction.

**Every point of a nondegenerate interval is a limit point of it.** Let
$J \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be order-convex ([[def-interval]]) with at least two
elements and let $p \in J$. Choose $q \in J$ with $q \ne p$, and let a real
$\varepsilon > 0$ be given. If $p < q$, put $y := p + \tfrac{1}{2}\min\{\varepsilon,\ q - p\}$;
then $p < y$, and $y - p \le \tfrac{1}{2}(q-p) < q - p$, so $p < y < q$ and
order-convexity gives $y \in J$, while $0 < |y - p| < \varepsilon$. If $q < p$,
the point $y := p - \tfrac{1}{2}\min\{\varepsilon,\ p - q\}$ serves in the same
way. So $N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(p) \cap J \ne \varnothing$ for every real
$\varepsilon > 0$, that is, $p$ is a limit point of $J$
([[def-limit-point-r]]).

Consequently, for $f$ defined on a nondegenerate interval $I$, the symbol
$f'(c)$ is meaningful at **every** $c \in I$, endpoints included. At an endpoint
the difference quotient is taken over the points of $I$ lying on the one side
that is available, so what other texts call a one-sided derivative is, here,
simply the derivative of $f$ on $I$.

Powers are those of [[def-integer-power]], and $\iota : \mathbb{N} \to
\mathbb{R}$ is the canonical natural of [[def-canonical-natural]], so that
$\iota(0) = 0$ and $\iota(m+1) = \iota(m) + 1$. Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

1. The function $p_0 : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$, $p_0(x) = x^{0}$, is the
   constant function $1$, and it is differentiable at every $c \in \mathbb{R}$
   with $p_0'(c) = 0$ ([[def-derivative]]).
2. For $n \ge 1$ the function $p_n : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$,
   $p_n(x) = x^{n}$, is differentiable at every $c \in \mathbb{R}$, and
   $$p_n'(c) \;=\; \iota(n)\,c^{\,n-1} .$$
3. For $n \ge 1$ put $A_0 := \{\, x \in \mathbb{R} : x \ne 0 \,\}$. The function
   $m_n : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $m_n(x) = x^{-n}$, is differentiable at every
   $c \in A_0$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$m_n'(c) \;=\; -\,\iota(n)\,c^{\,-n-1} .$$
4. Let $a : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ with $a_j = 0$ for $j \ge n$, and let
   $P : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ be the polynomial function
   $P(x) = \sum_{j<n} a_j x^{j}$ ([[def-finite-sum]]). Then $P$ is
   differentiable at every $c \in \mathbb{R}$, and, defining $e : \mathbb{N}
   \to \mathbb{R}$ by $e_0 := 0$ and $e_j := \iota(j)\,a_j\,c^{\,j-1}$ for
   $j \ge 1$,
   $$P'(c) \;=\; \sum_{j<n} e_j .$$

**Claim 2 is stated for $n \ge 1$ and not for $n \ge 0$, and that is not
timidity.** At $n = 0$ its right-hand side reads $\iota(0)\,c^{-1}$, and
$c^{-1}$ is not defined at $c = 0$ ([[def-integer-power]]), so the formula is
not a statement about the whole line. Claim 1 is what covers $n = 0$, and it
says the derivative is $0$ there, which is what the informal reading
"$0 \cdot c^{-1}$" is reaching for. The same shift is why the term $e_0$ of
claim 4 is defined to be $0$ outright rather than by the formula.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) at which $g$ is differentiable
([[def-derivative]]), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a \le b$, let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on the closed bounded interval $[a,b]$ ([[def-interval]],
[[def-continuity-real]]), and let $y \in \mathbb{R}$ satisfy

$$f(a) \le y \le f(b) \qquad \text{or} \qquad f(b) \le y \le f(a) .$$

Then there is $c \in [a,b]$ with $f(c) = y$.

**The construction is canonical, so no choice principle is used.** The bisection
below tests the left half first and takes the right half only when the left one
has been ruled out, so the passage from one interval to the next is a *function*
of that interval, and [[thm-recursion]] applies with nothing selected. This is
the same discipline the library uses wherever a sequence is built one term at a
time.

**Completeness of $\mathbb{R}$ is what does the work.** The bisection produces a
nested sequence of closed bounded intervals whose lengths tend to $0$, and it is
[[thm-nested-interval-property]] — hence the least-upper-bound property — that
supplies the point. Over an ordered field that is not complete the theorem
fails; the witness for that, stated for an arbitrary ordered field and worked
over $\mathbb{Q}$, is
[[cex-evt-and-ivt-fail-over-a-non-complete-field]], which states its own
$\varepsilon$-$\delta$ continuity inline and is not an instance of this page's
definition.

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field with its order and
absolute value ([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[lem-of-abs-value]]), and
neighbourhoods are those of [[def-neighbourhood-r]].

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $c \in A$. Then
$f$ is **continuous at $c$** when

$$(\forall \varepsilon > 0)\ (\exists \delta > 0)\ (\forall x \in A)\ \bigl[\ |x - c| < \delta \ \Longrightarrow\ |f(x) - f(c)| < \varepsilon\ \bigr],$$

with $\varepsilon$ and $\delta$ ranging over the **positive reals**. In the
language of neighbourhoods: for every real $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a real
$\delta > 0$ with

$$f\bigl(A \cap N_{\delta}(c)\bigr) \;\subseteq\; N_{\varepsilon}\bigl(f(c)\bigr).$$

$f$ is **continuous on $A$** when it is continuous at every point of $A$.

**The point $c$ is required to lie in $A$, and the condition is unpunctured.**
Both differ from [[def-function-limit]], and deliberately. There the quantifier
runs over $0 < |x - c| < \delta$, which removes $x = c$; here $x = c$ is allowed,
and at $x = c$ the implication reads $|f(c) - f(c)| = 0 < \varepsilon$, which is
automatic. So allowing $x = c$ costs nothing, and it is what lets the definition
be stated at every point of $A$, including the points where no limit exists.

**Three clauses, and all three are part of the definition.**

1. **At a limit point.** Suppose $c \in A$ is a limit point of $A$
   ([[def-limit-point-r]]). Then $f$ is continuous at $c$ if and only if the
   limit of $f$ at $c$ exists and
   $$\lim_{x \to c} f(x) \;=\; f(c)$$
   ([[def-function-limit]]). Indeed, for a given $\varepsilon > 0$ a $\delta$
   witnessing continuity witnesses the limit condition, because the limit
   condition quantifies over a subset of the points continuity quantifies over;
   and conversely a $\delta$ witnessing $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = f(c)$ witnesses
   continuity, because the one point it omits, $x = c$, satisfies
   $|f(c) - f(c)| < \varepsilon$ anyway.

2. **At an isolated point.** Suppose $c \in A$ is an isolated point of $A$
   ([[def-limit-point-r]]), so that $N_{\eta}(c) \cap A = \{c\}$ for some real
   $\eta > 0$. Then **every** $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is continuous at $c$: take
   $\delta := \eta$, so that the only $x \in A$ with $|x - c| < \delta$ is $c$
   itself, and $|f(c) - f(c)| = 0 < \varepsilon$.

3. **On a set.** Continuity on $A$ is continuity at each point of $A$, and
   nothing more. It is not a condition relating $f$ to points outside $A$.

Every point of $A$ is either a limit point of $A$ or an isolated point of $A$,
and never both ([[def-limit-point-r]]), so clauses 1 and 2 between them describe
continuity at every point of $A$.

**This is not the raw $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ formula of
[[fs-limit-unique-at-every-point-of-the-domain]].** That item records what goes
wrong when the *punctured* formula of [[def-function-limit]] is written down at
an arbitrary point of the domain: at an isolated point it is satisfied
vacuously by every real $L$ at once, so it defines nothing, and this library
therefore leaves $\lim_{x \to c} f(x)$ **undefined** at an isolated point.
Continuity at an isolated point is a different matter: the formula above is not
vacuous — it is a genuine condition on $f(c)$, satisfied because $f(c)$ is the
only value being compared with itself — and it names a single, well-defined
property. The limit is undefined there; the continuity is defined, and is
automatic. Clause 1 is the only place where the two notions meet, and it is
stated only where the limit exists as a notion.

**Where the distinction disappears.** If $A$ is an open subset of $\mathbb{R}$
([[def-open-and-closed-in-r]]), then every $c \in A$ has some
$N_{\eta}(c) \subseteq A$, and a punctured neighbourhood is never empty
([[def-neighbourhood-r]]), so every point of $A$ is a limit point of $A$ and
clause 1 covers the whole of $A$. The same holds when $A$ is a nondegenerate
interval ([[def-interval]]). Isolated points are what force clause 2 to exist at
all, and they occur as soon as $A$ is allowed to be an arbitrary subset of
$\mathbb{R}$, as in $A = \{0\} \cup [1,2]$.

Let $k\in\mathbb N$, let $m,q\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$. A map $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$ is of class $C^k$ when each component is of class $C^k$. Each scalar component uses the word-derivative convention of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]], whose source dimension is positive. The map is **smooth**, or $C^\infty$, when it is $C^k$ for every $k\in\mathbb N$.

Let $n\ge1$ and let $U,V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open. A bijection $f:U\to V$ is a **$C^k$ diffeomorphism** when both $f$ and $f^{-1}$ are $C^k$. For $k\ge1$, a **local $C^k$ diffeomorphism at $a\in U$** is a restriction $f|_P:P\to Q$ between open neighbourhoods of $a$ and $f(a)$ that is a $C^k$ diffeomorphism. At $k=1$ this agrees with [[def-c-one-map-and-local-inverse]]: continuous first partial derivatives give the required total derivative by [[thm-continuous-partial-derivatives-imply-total-differentiability]], while continuity of the total derivative gives continuity of its matrix entries and hence of the first partial derivatives.

Let $I \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be order-convex with at least two elements
([[def-interval]]), let $f : I \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $I$
([[def-continuity-real]]) and injective
([[def-injection-surjection-bijection]]), and let $g : f[I] \to I$ be the
inverse of $f : I \to f[I]$ supplied by [[thm-continuous-inverse]]. Let
$c \in I$ and put $b := f(c)$.

Then $c$ is a limit point of $I$ and $b$ is a limit point of $f[I]$, so that
$f'(c)$ and $g'(b)$ are meaningful symbols ([[def-derivative]]), and, assuming
$f$ is differentiable at $c$:

1. if $f'(c) \ne 0$, then $g$ is differentiable at $b$ and
   $$g'(b) \;=\; \frac{1}{f'(c)} ;$$
2. if $f'(c) = 0$, then $g$ is **not** differentiable at $b$.

**The two claims together say that the inverse inherits differentiability
exactly where the derivative does not vanish.** Nothing is asserted at a point
of $f[I]$ that is not of the form $f(c)$ with $f$ differentiable at $c$, and
nothing is asserted about $g$ being differentiable *on* a set.

**No compactness and no boundedness is assumed.** $I$ may be open, half-open or
unbounded; all that is used of it is order-convexity and the presence of two
distinct points, the latter being exactly what makes every point of $I$ a limit
point of $I$ ([[def-derivative]]).

Let $c < d$ be reals and let $\varphi : [c,d] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable
at every point of $[c,d]$ as a function on $[c,d]$ ([[def-derivative]]), with
$\varphi'$ integrable on $[c,d]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Let
$J \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be order-convex with at least two elements
([[def-interval]]) with $\varphi[\,[c,d]\,] \subseteq J$, and let $f : J \to
\mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $J$ ([[def-continuity-real]]).

Then $(f\circ\varphi)\,\varphi'$ is integrable on $[c,d]$ and

$$\int_{\varphi(c)}^{\varphi(d)} f \;=\; \int_c^d (f\circ\varphi)\,\varphi' ,$$

the left-hand integral being the oriented one of [[def-oriented-integral]].

**Neither injectivity nor monotonicity of $\varphi$ is assumed**, and that is
exactly why the left-hand side is written with oriented limits: $\varphi(d)$ may
lie below $\varphi(c)$, and $\varphi$ may return to the same value many times.
The proof runs through a primitive of $f$ and the chain rule, and no inverse
function is ever formed.

**Continuity of $f$ is a hypothesis and cannot be weakened to integrability.**
With $f$ merely integrable the composite $f \circ \varphi$ need not be
integrable at all, so the right-hand side need not exist; that is
the false statement that weakens it on the companion page.

Let $m \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge 1$ and let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$.

1. **Fundamental theorem, second part, in $\mathbb{R}^{m}$.** Let
   $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ be differentiable at every point of $[a,b]$ as
   a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]), and
   suppose $f' : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ is integrable. Then
   $$\int_a^b f' \;=\; f(b) - f(a).$$
2. **A bounded derivative gives a Lipschitz function.** Let
   $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable at
   every point of $(a,b)$, and let $M \ge 0$ satisfy
   $\lVert f'(t)\rVert_2 \le M$ for every $t \in (a,b)$. Then
   $$\lVert f(t) - f(s)\rVert_2 \;\le\; M\,|t-s| \qquad \text{for all } s,t \in [a,b],$$
   that is, $f$ is Lipschitz with constant $M$ as a map
   $([a,b], d_{\mathbb{R}}) \to (\mathbb{R}^{m}, d_2)$
   ([[def-lipschitz-holder-contraction]], [[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]],
   [[lem-metrics-on-rn]]).

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be bounded
([[def-bounded-set]]). Write $\mathcal{P}$ for the set of all partitions of
$[a,b]$ ([[def-partition-and-refinement]]) and put

$$\mathcal{L} \;:=\; \{\, L(f,P) \ : \ P \in \mathcal{P} \,\}, \qquad \mathcal{U} \;:=\; \{\, U(f,P) \ : \ P \in \mathcal{P} \,\}$$

for the sets of lower and of upper Darboux sums ([[def-darboux-sums]]).

### Both extrema exist

**$\mathcal{P}$ is nonempty**: the pair $(1, t)$ with $t_0 := a$ and $t_k := b$
for $k \ge 1$ is a partition of $[a,b]$, since $a < b$. So $\mathcal{L}$ and
$\mathcal{U}$ are nonempty.

**$\mathcal{L}$ is bounded above and $\mathcal{U}$ is bounded below.** Fix any
$Q \in \mathcal{P}$. By claim 2 of [[lem-refinement-inequalities]],
$L(f,P) \le U(f,Q)$ for every $P \in \mathcal{P}$, so $U(f,Q)$ is an upper bound
of $\mathcal{L}$; and $L(f,Q) \le U(f,P)$ for every $P$, so $L(f,Q)$ is a lower
bound of $\mathcal{U}$.

Hence a nonempty set bounded above has a supremum
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]) and a nonempty set bounded below has an infimum
([[thm-infimum-property]], [[def-infimum]]), each unique ([[lem-sup-unique]]).
The **lower** and **upper Darboux integrals** of $f$ over $[a,b]$ are the real
numbers

$$\underline{\int_a^b} f \;:=\; \sup \mathcal{L} \;=\; \sup_{P} L(f,P), \qquad \overline{\int_a^b} f \;:=\; \inf \mathcal{U} \;=\; \inf_{P} U(f,P) .$$

### The lower integral never exceeds the upper one

$$\underline{\int_a^b} f \;\le\; \overline{\int_a^b} f .$$

Indeed, for each fixed $Q \in \mathcal{P}$ the number $U(f,Q)$ is an upper bound
of $\mathcal{L}$, so the least upper bound satisfies
$\underline{\int_a^b} f \le U(f,Q)$. As $Q$ was arbitrary, $\underline{\int_a^b}f$
is a lower bound of $\mathcal{U}$, and the greatest lower bound satisfies
$\underline{\int_a^b} f \le \overline{\int_a^b} f$ ([[def-infimum]]).

Moreover, for **every** partition $P$,

$$L(f,P) \;\le\; \underline{\int_a^b} f \;\le\; \overline{\int_a^b} f \;\le\; U(f,P) ,$$

the outer inequalities because a member of a set is at most its supremum and at
least its infimum.

### Integrability

$f$ is **Darboux integrable on $[a,b]$**, and on this page simply
**integrable**, when

$$\underline{\int_a^b} f \;=\; \overline{\int_a^b} f ,$$

and then the common value is written

$$\int_a^b f \qquad \text{or} \qquad \int_a^b f(x)\,\mathrm{d}x ,$$

the **integral of $f$ over $[a,b]$**. It is a single well-determined real
number, being the common value of two numbers each of which is unique
([[lem-sup-unique]]). Without the displayed equality the symbol $\int_a^b f$ is
not defined and is never written.

**The inequality above is the whole difficulty.** By the previous paragraph
integrability is *never* a question of one integral exceeding the other, only of
the gap $\overline{\int_a^b} f - \underline{\int_a^b} f \ge 0$ being $0$; and by
[[thm-riemann-criterion]] that gap is $0$ exactly when a single partition can be
found making $U(f,P) - L(f,P)$ small. Whether that is possible is settled
completely, in terms of the discontinuities of $f$, by
[[thm-lebesgue-criterion]].

**"Riemann integrable" means the same thing here.** The definition above is
Darboux's. Riemann's own definition, in terms of tagged partitions of small
mesh, is [[def-tagged-partition-and-riemann-sum]], and the two define the same
class of functions with the same integral by [[thm-darboux-equals-riemann]].
Until that theorem is proved the two phrases are kept apart; after it they are
used interchangeably, as they are throughout the literature.

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-ordered-field]]) with its order
([[def-real-order]]).

A subset $I \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is **order-convex** when

$$x, y \in I \text{ and } x \le z \le y \;\Longrightarrow\; z \in I .$$

The **intervals** of $\mathbb{R}$ are the sets of the following nine forms, where
$a, b \in \mathbb{R}$:

| | bounded forms | | one-sided and full forms |
|---|---|---|---|
| $(a,b)$ | $\{x : a < x < b\}$ | $(a,\infty)$ | $\{x : a < x\}$ |
| $[a,b]$ | $\{x : a \le x \le b\}$ | $[a,\infty)$ | $\{x : a \le x\}$ |
| $[a,b)$ | $\{x : a \le x < b\}$ | $(-\infty,b)$ | $\{x : x < b\}$ |
| $(a,b]$ | $\{x : a < x \le b\}$ | $(-\infty,b]$ | $\{x : x \le b\}$ |
| | | $(-\infty,\infty)$ | $\mathbb{R}$ |

An interval is **open** when both of its written endpoints are excluded, that is
for the forms $(a,b)$, $(a,\infty)$, $(-\infty,b)$ and $(-\infty,\infty)$; it is
**closed** when both written endpoints are included, that is for $[a,b]$,
$[a,\infty)$, $(-\infty,b]$ and $(-\infty,\infty)$. The forms $[a,b)$ and
$(a,b]$ are **half-open**.

**The symbols $\pm\infty$ are notation and not elements of $\mathbb{R}$.** They
mark which side carries no endpoint condition at all; the five forms in the right
column are defined by the displayed conditions on $x$ alone, and no arithmetic is
ever performed with $\infty$. This is the same refusal to extend $\mathbb{R}$
silently that [[rem-sup-conventions]] records for suprema.

**Every one of the nine forms is order-convex.** Each is defined by a conjunction
of at most two conditions, each of the shape $a < x$, $a \le x$, $x < b$ or
$x \le b$, and each such condition is inherited by an intermediate point: if
$a < x$ and $x \le z$ then $a < z$, and if $z \le y$ and $y < b$ then $z < b$,
by transitivity of the order ([[def-ordered-field]]). Applying this to whichever
one or two conditions define the form in question gives $z \in I$ whenever
$x, y \in I$ and $x \le z \le y$.

**Bounded intervals.** An interval is **bounded** ([[def-bounded-set]]) exactly
when it is of one of the four forms in the left column: for those, $a$ is a lower
bound and $b$ an upper bound. The other five forms are unbounded, on the side or
sides written with $\infty$; the verification is in the remarks below.

**Nondegeneracy.** An interval is **degenerate** when it has at most one element,
and **nondegenerate** when it has at least two. For the four bounded forms with
endpoints $a$ and $b$:

- $[a,b]$ is nonempty exactly when $a \le b$, and it is nondegenerate exactly
  when $a < b$. It is the singleton $\{a\}$ when $a = b$.
- $(a,b)$, $[a,b)$ and $(a,b]$ are nonempty exactly when $a < b$, and then each
  is nondegenerate.

The only assertion here that is not immediate from the defining conditions is
that $a < b$ makes $(a,b)$ nonempty with at least two points. It holds because
$a < (a+b)/2 < b$, which follows from $a < b$ by adding $a$, respectively $b$, to
both sides and halving ([[def-ordered-field]]); repeating the halving inside
$(a, (a+b)/2)$ produces a second point.

**Closed bounded intervals.** These are the sets $[a,b]$ with $a \le b$, which is
exactly the condition making them nonempty. They are the intervals the nested
interval property is stated for, and the phrase *closed bounded interval* always
carries the hypothesis $a \le b$ in this library.

**Length.** The **length** of a bounded interval presented by its endpoints
$a \le b$ is

$$\ell = b - a \;\ge\; 0 .$$

Length is attached to the presentation by endpoints and is not recovered from the
set: $(a,b)$, $[a,b)$ and $(a,b]$ are all empty when $a = b$, and so is
$(c,c)$ for any other $c$, while each of these presentations has length $0$, so
nothing inconsistent arises; but the endpoints are named explicitly at every
point where a length is used in this library, and never inferred from the set.
Unbounded intervals are assigned no length.

Let $J_0\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open interval, let $U:J_0\to\mathbb R$ be
continuous ([[def-continuity-real]]), let $m>0$, let $E_0<E_1$ be reals, and
let $a,b:(E_0,E_1)\to J_0$ be functions with

$$a(E)<b(E),\qquad U(a(E))=U(b(E))=E,\qquad U(q)<E\ (a(E)<q<b(E)) \qquad(E_0<E<E_1).$$

The **action variable** of this datum is the function
$J_{\mathrm{a}}:(E_0,E_1)\to\mathbb R$,

$$J_{\mathrm{a}}(E):=\frac{1}{\pi}\int_{a(E)}^{b(E)}\sqrt{2m\bigl(E-U(q)\bigr)}\;dq,$$

the integral being the Riemann integral on the compact interval
$[a(E),b(E)]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). It is defined because
$q\mapsto\sqrt{2m(E-U(q))}$ is continuous on $[a(E),b(E)]$: the radicand is a
continuous nonnegative function there (it vanishes exactly at the two
endpoints), and the nonnegative square root is continuous
([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

**Reading of the notation.** The interval $[a(E),b(E)]$ is the classically
allowed segment between the two turning points of the energy $E$, and the
integral is twice the momentum phase-space area (Tong, Eq. (4.136) with
$I=J_{\mathrm{a}}$); no physical interpretation of $m$, $U$ or $E$ is a
mathematical premise here, and no period is claimed by this definition.

Let $J_0\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open interval, let $U:J_0\to\mathbb R$ be of
class $C^3$ ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]), let $m>0$, let
$E_0<E_1$, and let $a,b:(E_0,E_1)\to J_0$ be functions with
$a(E)<b(E)$, $U(a(E))=U(b(E))=E$, $U(q)<E$ for $a(E)<q<b(E)$, and

$$U'\bigl(a(E)\bigr)<0<U'\bigl(b(E)\bigr)\qquad(E_0<E<E_1)$$

(the energy $E$ has exactly the two simple turning points $a(E)$, $b(E)$ in
$J_0$). Then:

1. $a$ and $b$ are of class $C^1$ on $(E_0,E_1)$;
2. the action variable $J_{\mathrm{a}}$ of
   [[def-cm-one-dimensional-action-variable]] is of class $C^1$ on
   $(E_0,E_1)$, and for every $E\in(E_0,E_1)$
   $$J_{\mathrm{a}}'(E)=\frac{1}{2\pi}T(E),\qquad T(E):=\sqrt{2m}\int_{a(E)}^{b(E)}\frac{\mathrm dq}{\sqrt{E-U(q)}}\in(0,\infty),$$
   where the integral is the improper integral over the open interval
   $(a(E),b(E))$, convergent at both endpoints.

derivations.claim: Derivative and critical point: by [L3], $(U^{\mathrm{eff}})'(\rho)=\frac{\kappa}{\rho^{2}} -\frac{J^{2}}{\mu\rho^{3}} =\frac{\kappa\rho-J^{2}/\mu}{\rho^{3}} =\frac{\kappa(\rho-r_{*})}{\rho^{3}},$ which vanishes exactly at $\rho=r_{*}=J^{2}/(\mu\kappa)$ and has the sign of $\rho-r_{*}$; and $U^{\mathrm{eff}}(r_{*})=-\kappa\mu\kappa/J^{2}+J^{2}\mu^{2}\kappa^{2} /(2\mu J^{4})=-\mu\kappa^{2}/(2J^{2})$. Also $U^{\mathrm{eff}}(r_{*}/2)=-2\mu\kappa^{2}/J^{2}+2\mu\kappa^{2}/J^{2}=0$, and for any $E\in I_{0}$ and $R:=r_{*}+\kappa/|E|$ one has $U^{\mathrm{eff}}(R)>-\kappa/R>-|E|=E$.

Monotonicity and the two simple roots: if $0<\rho_{1}<\rho_{2}\le r_{*}$, then by [L3] the mean-value theorem applied to $U^{\mathrm{eff}}$ on $[\rho_{1},\rho_{2}]$ gives $U^{\mathrm{eff}}(\rho_{2})-U^{\mathrm{eff}}(\rho_{1}) =(U^{\mathrm{eff}})'(\xi)(\rho_{2}-\rho_{1})<0$; hence $U^{\mathrm{eff}}$ is strictly decreasing on $(0,r_{*}]$. Similarly, on $r_{*}\le\rho_{1}<\rho_{2}$, the increment is positive, so $U^{\mathrm{eff}}$ is strictly increasing on $[r_{*},\infty)$. Now fix $E\in I_{0}$. By step 1.1, $U^{\mathrm{eff}}(r_{*})<E<0=U^{\mathrm{eff}}(r_{*}/2)$; since $U^{\mathrm{eff}}$ is continuous, the intermediate-value theorem gives $r_{-}(E)\in(r_{*}/2,r_{*})$ with $U^{\mathrm{eff}}(r_{-}(E))=E$, and strict monotonicity makes it unique on $(0,r_{*}]$. Likewise $U^{\mathrm{eff}}(r_{*})<E<U^{\mathrm{eff}}(R)$ gives a unique $r_{+}(E)\in(r_{*},R)$ with $U^{\mathrm{eff}}(r_{+}(E))=E$, and monotonicity makes the root unique on $[r_{*},\infty)$. The intermediate values on $(r_{-}(E),r_{+}(E))$ lie below $E$ because the only point where $U^{\mathrm{eff}}$ could reach $E$ again would be a third root. The roots are simple: $(U^{\mathrm{eff}})'(r_{-}(E))<0<(U^{\mathrm{eff}})'(r_{+}(E))$ because $r_{-}(E)<r_{*}<r_{+}(E)$ and the sign computation of step 1.1. The assignments $E\mapsto r_{\pm}(E)$ therefore have the properties required in [L4] on the energy interval $I_{0}$.

Applying the action-variable theorem: by step 2.1 the datum $(J_{0},U^{\mathrm{eff}},\mu)$ satisfies the hypotheses of [L4] on $I_{0}=(E_{0},E_{1})$; hence $J_{\mathrm a}$ is $C^{1}$ on $I_{0}$ and $J_{\mathrm a}'(E)=T_{\mathrm{rad}}(E)/(2\pi)$ with the quadrature $T_{\mathrm{rad}}(E)=\sqrt{2\mu}\int_{r_{-}(E)}^{r_{+}(E)} \mathrm d\rho/\sqrt{E-U^{\mathrm{eff}}(\rho)}>0$, which is claim 2.

The quadrature is the radial period: by [L1] the radial coordinate $\rho$ of the motion solves $\mu\rho''=-(U^{\mathrm{eff}})'(\rho)$ with $\tfrac12\mu(\rho')^{2}+U^{\mathrm{eff}}(\rho)=E$, so on every stretch on which $\rho$ is strictly monotone one has $\rho'\neq0$ and $(\rho')^{2}=2(E-U^{\mathrm{eff}}(\rho))/\mu$, i.e. $\rho'=\pm\sqrt{2(E-U^{\mathrm{eff}}(\rho))/\mu}$.
