On the stretch from $r_{-}(E)$ to $r_{+}(E)$ the coordinate $\rho$ is strictly increasing, so its inverse $\rho\mapsto t(\rho)$ is defined; by the one-variable inverse rule of [L3] it satisfies $t'(\rho)=1/\rho'(t(\rho))$, and the time elapsed is $\Delta t=t\bigl(r_{+}(E)\bigr)-t\bigl(r_{-}(E)\bigr) =\int_{r_{-}(E)}^{r_{+}(E)}\frac{\mathrm d\rho}{\rho'(t(\rho))} =\int_{r_{-}(E)}^{r_{+}(E)}\frac{\sqrt{\mu}\,\mathrm d\rho} {\sqrt{2(E-U^{\mathrm{eff}}(\rho))}},$ where the last equality substitutes the positive branch $\rho'=\sqrt{2(E-U^{\mathrm{eff}}(\rho))/\mu}$ along the increasing stretch. The decreasing stretch contributes the same amount by symmetry of the same substitution with the negative branch, and the radial oscillation has two turning points per period; hence its period is $2\Delta t=\sqrt{2\mu}\int_{r_{-}(E)}^{r_{+}(E)} \frac{\mathrm d\rho}{\sqrt{E-U^{\mathrm{eff}}(\rho)}}=T_{\mathrm{rad}}(E).$

Least period and the value of the derivative: by [L2] the radial coordinate satisfies $\rho(t+T)=\rho(t)$ with $T$ the orbital period of the conic data. Since $\theta:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ is a strictly increasing bijection with $\theta(t+T)=\theta(t)+2\pi$ and $\rho(t)=p/(1+e\cos(\theta(t)-\theta_{0}))$ with $0<e<1$, the periastron value $r_{-}(E)=p/(1+e)$ and the apastron value $r_{+}(E)=p/(1-e)$ are attained exactly once in every half-open interval of the form $[t_{0},t_{0}+T)$. Every positive period must carry a periastron time to another periastron time. The strictly increasing polar angle attains successive periastra at increments of $2\pi$, and $\theta(t+T)=\theta(t)+2\pi$ shows their successive times differ by $T$; hence any positive period is at least $T$. Since $T$ is a period, it is the least positive radial period. Therefore $T_{\mathrm{rad}}(E)=T$ by step 3.2, and $J_{\mathrm a}'(E)=\frac{T}{2\pi}=\frac{\mu ab}{J} =\sqrt{\frac{\mu}{\kappa}}\,a^{3/2},$ where the last identity uses $J=\sqrt{\mu\kappa a(1-e^{2})}$ and $b=a\sqrt{1-e^{2}}$: explicitly $\mu ab/J=\mu a^{2}\sqrt{1-e^{2}}/\sqrt{\mu\kappa a(1-e^{2})} =\sqrt{\mu/\kappa}\,a^{3/2}$. Squaring $T=2\pi\sqrt{\mu/\kappa}a^{3/2}$ returns $T^{2}=4\pi^{2}\mu a^{3}/\kappa$. This is claim 3.

Sharpness: if $e=0$ then $r_{-}(E)=r_{+}(E)=a=r_{*}$ and $E=U^{\mathrm{eff}}(r_{*})$, the lower endpoint of $I_{0}$; there is no energy interval on which two distinct simple turning points exist, so the hypothesis of [L4] fails, in agreement with the circular orbit having a constant radial coordinate and no radial oscillation. The case $J=0$ has no term $J^{2}/(2\mu\rho^{2})$ and no critical point with the stated two-sided conservation, so it is outside the example by hypothesis. This is claim 4.
Claims 1-4 are verified by steps 1.1 and 2.1, by step 3.1, by steps 3.2 and 4.1, and by step 5.1 respectively; the example is verified.

boundaries.evidence: The energy window $I_{0}$ is nonempty and for every $E$ in it the two turning points exist (statement, step 2.1).
The radial-collision case $J=0$ is excluded by hypothesis and recorded as claim 4; no division by $J$ occurs in the elementary computations (statement, step 5.1).
One radial degree of freedom is the case of the action-variable theorem applied here (statement, step 3.1).
The circular case $e=0$ makes the two turning points coincide and fails the hypotheses; this is recorded as claim 4 and verified in step 5.1.

The quadrature converges at the two simple turning points and the estimate uses the closed interval; the cited theorem supplies the convergence and the endpoint-rule cancellation (statement, step 3.1).

boundaries.reason: The turning points and the quadrature are explicit; no selection principle is used (steps 2.1 and 3.1).
The chain runs one way only: the two simple turning points give the C1 action derivative, and the conic data give T_rad=T; no converse direction is among claims 1-4.
Claim 4 records the failure at e=0; no reverse assertion is made, e.g. that J_a'(E)=T/(2pi) forces the orbit to be a non-circular ellipse.

citations.quote:
Adopt the force model with potential presentation $(U,d)$ and mechanical
Lagrangian $L=K-U$ of [[def-cm07-action-and-mechanical-lagrangian]], with
the momentum charts and two-form datum of [[def-cm13-two-form]], the
canonical coordinates of [[def-cm13-canonical-form]], the bracket of
[[def-cm13-poisson]], the Hamiltonian fields of [[def-cm13-hamiltonian-field]] and the branch
Hamiltonian $H$ of [[def-cm12-hamiltonian]];
by clause 1 of [[pthm-cm13-two-form-is-symplectic]] each momentum phase
domain is a symplectic manifold for $\omega$, with $\omega$ the standard
two-form in the chart's canonical coordinates
([[def-symplectic-form-and-symplectic-manifold]]). Dimensions are read by
[[def-cm01-units]] and differentiability classes are those of
[[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]].

**(a) The datum.** Let $W_{0}$ be a nonempty open subset of one momentum
phase domain of the presentation, of dimension $2n$, and let

$$F=(F_{1},\dots,F_{n}),\qquad F_{i}:W_{0}\longrightarrow\mathbb R,$$

be phase functions of class $C^{\infty}$ with $F_{1}=H|_{W_{0}}$. The
family $F$ is a **completely integrable datum of the presentation on
$W_{0}$** when

1. $F$ is in involution, $\{F_{i},F_{j}\}=0$ on $W_{0}$ for all $i,j$
   ([[def-cm14-involution]] clause (d)); and
2. the differentials $dF_{1},\dots,dF_{n}$ are linearly independent on a
   dense open subset of $W_{0}$ ([[def-linear-independence]],
   [[def-differential-rank-and-constant-rank]]).

**(b) Reading in the root library.** Since $(W_{0},\omega)$ is a
$2n$-dimensional symplectic manifold and the bracket of
[[def-cm13-poisson]] is the bracket of
[[def-poisson-bracket-on-a-symplectic-manifold]] for $\omega$, a datum
$F$ in the sense of clause (a), with $F_{1}=H$ and the autonomous
Hamiltonian $H$ of the presentation, is exactly a **completely integrable
Hamiltonian system** on $(W_{0},\omega)$ in the sense of
[[def-completely-integrable-hamiltonian-system]], with branches read
through the presentation's Hamiltonians; the root notion of
[[def-first-integral-and-poisson-commuting-functions]] is read through the
bracket criterion of [[pthm-cm13-observable-evolution]] clause 2.

**(c) Integral map, regular locus and fibres.** Attached to a datum $F$
are:

1. the **integral map** $F:W_{0}\to\mathbb R^{n}$;
2. the **regular locus** $W_{\mathrm{reg}}:=\{z\in W_{0}:
   \operatorname{rank}dF(z)=n\}$, which is open by continuity of the partial
   derivatives and dense in $W_{0}$ by clause (a) 2;
3. the **regular values**, namely the values $b\in F(W_{\mathrm{reg}})$;
   for such a value the **regular fibre** $N_{b}:=F^{-1}(b)$ is the
   common level set of $F_{1},\dots,F_{n}$ through $b$;
4. the **Hamiltonian fields** $X_{F_{1}},\dots,X_{F_{n}}$ of the family
   ([[def-cm13-hamiltonian-field]]).

**(d) Status.** The item defines a datum class and its attached objects.
It asserts that no particular model of the force branch is completely
integrable, that no fibre is compact, connected or a torus, that no
action-angle coordinates exist and no measured value is known; the
structural and motion statements are the torus theorem and the
action-angle theorem of this page (items `pthm-cm14-regular-tori` and
`pthm-cm14-action-angle`), conditional on the hypotheses stated there.

Adopt the force model with potential presentation $(U,d)$ and mechanical
Lagrangian $L=K-U$ of [[def-cm07-action-and-mechanical-lagrangian]], with
the momentum charts and two-form datum of [[def-cm13-two-form]], the
Hamiltonian fields of [[def-cm13-hamiltonian-field]], the bracket of
[[def-cm13-poisson]] and the branch Hamiltonian $H$ of
[[def-cm12-hamiltonian]]; the model reading of the Hamiltonian system is
the equivalence of [[pthm-cm13-hamiltonian-field-integrates-the-model-equations]]
(motions of the model are the integral curves of the branch Hamiltonian
field, in each chart with its own Hamiltonian). Dimensions are read by
[[def-cm01-units]] and differentiability classes are those of
[[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]].

**(a) Phase functions and the domain.** Let $W_{0}$ be a nonempty open
subset of one momentum phase domain of the presentation. A **phase
function of the presentation on $W_{0}$ of class $C^{k}$** is a map
$f:W_{0}\to\mathbb R$ of class $C^{k}$, of a declared dimension.

**(b) First integrals.** Let $f:W_{0}\to\mathbb R$ be of class $C^{1}$.
Then $f$ is a **first integral of the branch Hamiltonian $H$ on $W_{0}$**
when for every interval $J\subseteq I_{0}$ with nonempty interior and every
solution $z:J\to W_{0}$ of the Hamiltonian system
$\dot z(t)=X_{H_{t}}(z(t))$
([[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]]) the composite
$t\mapsto f(z(t))$ is constant on $J$. Equivalently, in the reading of
[[pthm-cm13-hamiltonian-field-integrates-the-model-equations]], $f$ is
constant along every motion of the model whose momentum-phase curve lies
in $W_{0}$ (on the potential branch).

**(c) The bracket criterion.** Let $H$ be autonomous on $I_{0}\times W_{0}$
($\partial_{t}U\equiv0$ and $d\equiv0$) and let $f:W_{0}\to\mathbb R$ be
autonomous of class $C^{2}$. Then $f$ is a first integral of $H$ on $W_{0}$
if and only if

$$\{f,H\}=0\qquad\text{everywhere on }W_{0},$$

the bracket being that of [[def-cm13-poisson]]. The equivalence is clause
2 of [[pthm-cm13-observable-evolution]], recorded here as the working
form of the definition; it is not re-proved.

**(d) Involution.** Phase functions $f_{1},\dots,f_{k}:W_{0}\to\mathbb R$
of class $C^{2}$ are **in involution** (or **pairwise Poisson-commuting**)
when

$$\{f_{i},f_{j}\}=0\qquad\text{on }W_{0}\text{ for all }i,j\in\{1,\dots,k\};$$

a **family of first integrals in involution** is a family whose members are
first integrals of $H$ and which is in involution. The notion is the
presentation reading of the root-library notion of
[[def-first-integral-and-poisson-commuting-functions]] under the bracket of
[[def-cm13-poisson]], which is the bracket of
[[def-poisson-bracket-on-a-symplectic-manifold]] for the two-form of
[[def-cm13-two-form]].

**(e) Differential independence.** Phase functions $f_{1},\dots,f_{k}$ of
class $C^{1}$ are **independent at $z\in W_{0}$** when the differentials
$df_{1}(z),\dots,df_{k}(z)$ are linearly independent as elements of the
dual of the tangent space at $z$ ([[def-linear-independence]]); the set
of points at which this holds is the **independence locus** of the family,
$\{z\in W_{0}:\operatorname{rank}(df_{1}(z),\dots,df_{k}(z))=k\}$
([[def-differential-rank-and-constant-rank]],
[[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]). The family is **independent on**
$W_{0}$ when it is independent at every $z\in W_{0}$.

**(f) Status.** The item defines model properties of phase functions and
records one proved equivalence from the evolution theorem of the
companion page. It asserts no existence of a nonconstant first integral
for a given force law, no completeness of any flow, no conservation law
of the model and no measured value; in particular every closure or
constancy statement about brackets is a theorem of this page or of
[[pthm-cm13-observable-evolution]], not part of the definition.

Adopt the force model with potential presentation $(U,d)$ and mechanical
Lagrangian $L=K-U$ of [[def-cm07-action-and-mechanical-lagrangian]], with the
momentum charts and two-form datum of [[def-cm13-two-form]] and the canonical
coordinates of [[def-cm13-canonical-form]]: the Cartesian phase domain
$W=Q\times\mathbb R^{3N}$, its two-form $\omega$, a generalized-coordinate
chart map $\Phi_{X}$ and the form $\omega_{X}$
([[def-cm07-generalized-coordinates-and-forces]]); the presentation is
hyperregular on every chart with the Hamiltonian $H$ of
[[def-cm12-hamiltonian]] and [[pthm-cm12-mechanical-hyperregularity]],

$$H(t,x,p)=\tfrac12\,p\cdot\mathsf M^{-1}p+U(t,x),\qquad \widetilde H(t,q,P)=\tfrac12\,P\cdot G(q)^{-1}P+\widetilde U(t,q).$$

Differentiability classes are those of
[[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]], and gradients those of
[[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]].

**(a) The field of a phase function.** Let $W_{0}\subseteq W$ be nonempty
open and let $f:W_{0}\to\mathbb R$ be of class $C^{2}$. By clause 1 of
[[pthm-cm13-two-form-is-symplectic]] the form $\omega$ is nondegenerate on
$W_{0}$, so there is exactly one $C^{1}$ vector field $X_{f}$ on $W_{0}$ with

$$\iota_{X_{f}}\omega=df$$

(the sign convention of [[def-hamiltonian-vector-field-and-hamiltonian-function]]
and [[prop-cm-hamiltonian-field-and-poisson-bracket-in-a-phase-chart]]); it
is the **Hamiltonian field of $f$ for the presentation**. In the Cartesian
coordinates $(x,p)$, writing $\nabla f=(f_{x^{1}},\dots,f_{x^{3N}},f_{p_{1}},\dots,f_{p_{3N}})$,

$$X_{f}=\bigl(f_{p},\,-f_{x}\bigr)=J\nabla f,\qquad J=\begin{pmatrix}0_{3N}&I_{3N}\\-I_{3N}&0_{3N}\end{pmatrix};$$

in any canonical chart $(\theta^{1},\dots,\theta^{2m})$ of the presentation
the same field reads $X_{f}=\bigl(f_{\theta^{m+1}},\dots,f_{\theta^{2m}},-f_{\theta^{1}},\dots,-f_{\theta^{m}}\bigr)$.
A vector field on $W_{0}$ is called **Hamiltonian for the presentation** when
it is $X_{f}$ for some $C^{2}$ function $f$; in particular
$X_{f}=0$ exactly when $f$ is locally constant on $W_{0}$. Vector fields are
read as tangent-bundle sections of
[[def-smooth-vector-field-as-a-tangent-bundle-section]].

**(b) The field of the branch Hamiltonian.** For each $t\in I_{0}$ the
function $H_{t}:=H(t,\cdot)$ is $C^{2}$ on $W$, and the **Hamiltonian field
of the presentation** at time $t$ is $X_{H_{t}}$:

$$X_{H_{t}}(x,p)=\bigl(\mathsf M^{-1}p,\ -\nabla_{x}U(t,x)\bigr),$$

whose components are a velocity and a force. In the coordinates $X$ the
corresponding field is
$X_{\widetilde H_{t}}(q,P)=\bigl(G(q)^{-1}P,\ -\partial_{q}\widetilde H(t,q,P)\bigr)$,
where the second slot retains the kinetic contribution
$-\tfrac12P\cdot\partial_{q}(G(q)^{-1})P$ when the metric varies. If
$d\not\equiv0$ the model's forced evolution carries the additional momentum
source $d$; the corresponding vector field
$(x,p)\mapsto\bigl(\mathsf M^{-1}p,-\nabla_{x}U(t,x)+d(t,x,\mathsf M^{-1}p)\bigr)$
is generally not a Hamiltonian field for the presentation, and it is one
exactly when the residual force has a potential independent of the velocity
slot (the criterion is proved in clause 4 of the corresponding theorem of this
page).

**(c) Time dependence and status.** For a time-dependent $H$ the assignment
$t\mapsto X_{H_{t}}$ is a time-dependent field on the phase domain; each
$X_{H_{t}}$ is $C^{1}$, hence locally Lipschitz in the state variable, and no
completeness of its integral curves is asserted here. The item defines the
field datum and its chart expressions; the identification of the model's
motions with the integral curves, and all conservation or invariance
properties, are the subject of the other items of this page. The field is
defined by the intrinsic equation $\iota_{X}\omega=dH$ and therefore does not
depend on the canonical chart used to compute it.

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]).

A subset $U \subseteq X$ is **open in $(X,d)$** if for every $x \in U$ there is a
real $r > 0$ with $B(x,r) \subseteq U$ ([[def-metric-ball]]). A subset
$F \subseteq X$ is **closed in $(X,d)$** if its complement $X \setminus F$ is
open.

The collection

$$\mathcal{T}_d := \{\, U \subseteq X : U \text{ is open in } (X,d) \,\}$$

of all open subsets is the **metric topology** of $d$ on $X$. A subset of $X$
that is both open and closed is called **clopen**.

**Two sets are open for trivial reasons.** $\emptyset$ is open, because the
defining condition quantifies over no points; and $X$ is open, because
$B(x,r) \subseteq X$ for every $x$ and every $r > 0$. Consequently $X$ and
$\emptyset$ are also closed, and both are clopen.

**A neighbourhood of a point $x$** is any set containing an open set that
contains $x$; an **open neighbourhood** is an open set containing $x$. In a
metric space, a set is a neighbourhood of $x$ exactly when it contains some
ball $B(x,r)$ with $r>0$. Thus $U$ is open exactly when it is a neighbourhood of
each of its points, and metric balls suffice to test this condition.

**The metric, not the set, determines $\mathcal{T}_d$.** Two metrics on the same
set may have different metric topologies, and two different metrics may have the
same one; the systematic comparison is [[def-equivalent-metrics]].

Let $k\in\mathbb N$, let $m,q\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$. A map $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$ is of class $C^k$ when each component is of class $C^k$. Each scalar component uses the word-derivative convention of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]], whose source dimension is positive. The map is **smooth**, or $C^\infty$, when it is $C^k$ for every $k\in\mathbb N$.

Let $n\ge1$ and let $U,V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open. A bijection $f:U\to V$ is a **$C^k$ diffeomorphism** when both $f$ and $f^{-1}$ are $C^k$. For $k\ge1$, a **local $C^k$ diffeomorphism at $a\in U$** is a restriction $f|_P:P\to Q$ between open neighbourhoods of $a$ and $f(a)$ that is a $C^k$ diffeomorphism. At $k=1$ this agrees with [[def-c-one-map-and-local-inverse]]: continuous first partial derivatives give the required total derivative by [[thm-continuous-partial-derivatives-imply-total-differentiability]], while continuity of the total derivative gives continuity of its matrix entries and hence of the first partial derivatives.

Let $A$ and $B$ be sets and let $f : A \to B$ be a function ([[def-function]]).

- $f$ is **injective** (one-to-one) if $f(x) = f(y)$ implies $x = y$, for all
  $x, y \in A$.
- $f$ is **surjective** (onto) if for every $b \in B$ there is some $x \in A$
  with $f(x) = b$; equivalently, the image $f[A] := \{ f(x) : x \in A \}$ equals
  $B$.
- $f$ is **bijective** if it is both injective and surjective.

For $S \subseteq A$ we write $f[S] = \{ f(x) : x \in S \}$ for the image of $S$,
and for $T \subseteq B$ we write $f^{-1}[T] = \{ x \in A : f(x) \in T \}$ for the
preimage of $T$; these are the image and preimage of a set under $f$ read as a
relation ([[def-image-and-preimage-under-a-relation]]).

Let $V$ be a vector space over a field $F$ ([[def-vector-space]]). As in
[[def-linear-combination-and-span]], a **finite list** of vectors is a function
$v : n \to V$ on a von Neumann natural $n = \{0, \dots, n-1\}$
([[def-natural-numbers]], [[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), written
$v_i := v(i)$, and

$$\sum_{i<n} \lambda_i v_i$$

is the finite sum of [[def-monoid-finite-product]] read additively in the abelian
group $(V,+,0_V)$, applied to the list $i \mapsto \lambda_i v_i$. No second notion
of finite sum is introduced here.

### Independence of a list

A finite list $v : n \to V$ is **linearly independent** when, for every list of
scalars $\lambda : n \to F$,

$$\sum_{i<n} \lambda_i v_i = 0_V \quad \Longrightarrow \quad \lambda_i = 0_F \text{ for every } i < n,$$

and **linearly dependent** otherwise, that is, when some $\lambda : n \to F$ has
$\sum_{i<n}\lambda_i v_i = 0_V$ while $\lambda_j \ne 0_F$ for at least one
$j < n$. Such a $\lambda$ is called a **witness** to the dependence of $v$.

### Independence of a subset

A subset $S \subseteq V$ is **linearly independent** when **every injective**
finite list $v : n \to S$ ([[def-injection-surjection-bijection]]) is linearly
independent, and **linearly dependent** otherwise, that is, when some injective
finite list into $S$ is linearly dependent.

**The injectivity clause is not decoration.** A linear combination in
[[def-linear-combination-and-span]] is indexed by an arbitrary list $v : n \to S$,
which is **not** required to be injective. If the definition above quantified
over all such lists, then for any $w \in S$ the list $v : 2 \to S$ with
$v_0 = v_1 = w$ and the scalars $\lambda_0 = 1_F$, $\lambda_1 = -1_F$ would give

$$\sum_{i<2}\lambda_i v_i = (0_V + 1_F w) + (-1_F)w = w + (-w) = 0_V$$

with $\lambda_0 = 1_F \ne 0_F$ ([[def-field]],
[[lem-vector-space-elementary-consequences]]), so **every** nonempty subset of
$V$ would be dependent and the notion would be empty. Quantifying over injective
lists is what makes the subset notion the intended one. It costs nothing for
lists: [[lem-independent-list-is-injective]] shows that the vanishing condition
above already forces a list to be injective, so no injectivity hypothesis has to
be carried alongside independence of a list.

### The boundary cases are genuine cases

$\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$ ([[def-natural-numbers]]), so both of the following are
instances of the definitions and neither is a convention.

- **The empty list is independent.** For $n = 0$ the only list of scalars is the
  empty one, and the condition "$\lambda_i = 0_F$ for every $i < 0$" holds
  vacuously.
- **$\varnothing \subseteq V$ is independent.** The only function $v : n \to
  \varnothing$ is the empty one, with $n = 0$, and it is independent by the
  previous point.
- **$\{0_V\}$ is dependent.** The list $v : 1 \to \{0_V\}$ with $v_0 = 0_V$ is
  injective, and taking $\lambda_0 = 1_F$ gives
  $\sum_{i<1}\lambda_i v_i = 0_V + 1_F 0_V = 0_V$ by the recursion of
  [[def-monoid-finite-product]] and $\lambda 0_V = 0_V$
  ([[lem-vector-space-elementary-consequences]]), while $1_F \ne 0_F$ in a field
  ([[def-field]]). So $\{0_V\}$, and hence every subset of $V$ containing $0_V$,
  is linearly dependent.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_{\omega}$
([[def-countable-choice]]). Adopt the force model with potential
presentation $(U,d)$ and mechanical Lagrangian $L=K-U$ of
[[def-cm07-action-and-mechanical-lagrangian]], with the momentum charts and
two-form datum of [[def-cm13-two-form]], the Hamiltonian fields of
[[def-cm13-hamiltonian-field]] and the branch Hamiltonian $H$ of
[[def-cm12-hamiltonian]]; by clause 1 of
[[pthm-cm13-two-form-is-symplectic]] each momentum phase domain is a
symplectic manifold for the presentation's two-form $\omega$
([[def-symplectic-form-and-symplectic-manifold]]). Let $W_{0}\subseteq W$
be a nonempty open phase domain of dimension $2n$ and let
$F=(F_{1}=H|_{W_{0}},\dots,F_{n})$ be a completely integrable datum of the
presentation on $W_{0}$ ([[def-cm14-complete-integrability]]). Let $b_{0}$
be a regular value of the integral map whose regular fibre
$N:=F^{-1}(b_{0})\subseteq W_{0}$ is nonempty, compact and connected, and
assume there are a saturated open neighbourhood $U\subseteq W_{0}$ of $N$
and a ball $B\subseteq\mathbb R^{n}$ of regular values with $F(U)=B$ such
that $\pi:=F|_{U}:U\to B$ is a proper submersion with connected fibres.
Then:

1. **(Lagrangian fibre)** $N$ is a compact connected embedded
   $n$-dimensional Lagrangian submanifold of $(W_{0},\omega)$, and for
   every $z\in N$
   $$T_{z}N=\operatorname{span}\{X_{F_{1}}(z),\dots,X_{F_{n}}(z)\},$$
   the fields being those of [[def-cm13-hamiltonian-field]].
2. **(commuting flows and period lattice)** The fields
   $X_{F_{1}},\dots,X_{F_{n}}$ have pairwise commuting flows; these flows
   combine into a local $\mathbb R^{n}$ action on $W_{\mathrm{reg}}$, and
   on the compact invariant fibre $N$ their restrictions are complete and
   generate a transitive action of $\mathbb R^{n}$ whose stabilizer at
   every point is one and the same full lattice $\Gamma\subseteq
   \mathbb R^{n}$, with $N\cong\mathbb R^{n}/\Gamma$.
3. **(torus)** $N$ is diffeomorphic to the torus
   $T^{n}=\mathbb R^{n}/\mathbb Z^{n}$.

The statement is conditional on the adopted force branch, the declared
presentation, the smooth completely integrable datum and the listed
hypotheses on the fibre; it asserts no global product structure of $U$, no
action-angle coordinates, no completeness of any flow outside the compact
fibre and no empirical content.

derivations.claim: By [L1] the datum $F=(H)$ is completely integrable on $W_{0}$ and $H^{-1}(0)=\{(0,0)\}$: indeed $H(x,p)=0$ forces $p=0$ and $x=0$ because $H$ is a sum of two squares divided by the positive number $2m$. The set $H^{-1}(0)$ is therefore nonempty, compact (a single point) and connected.

The point $(0,0)$ is a critical point of $H$ by [L1], so $0$ is a critical value and the fibre $H^{-1}(0)$ is a critical (not regular) fibre; the hypothesis of [L3] fails, and the torus conclusion is not available. This already shows that the regular-value hypothesis is needed, but the point of the counterexample is stronger.

The fibre is not diffeomorphic to $T^{1}$: it has exactly one point, while $T^{1}$ is infinite, and a diffeomorphism is a bijection by [L2]; no bijection exists between a one-point set and an infinite set. Hence the refuted statement fails at the declared model datum.

The failure is confined to the critical level: for every $E>0$ the level $H^{-1}(E)$ is the ellipse $\{(x,p):p^{2}/(2m)+kx^{2}/2=E\}$, a one-dimensional compact connected manifold, the phase curve of a nonconstant harmonic motion; in the period-one chart of the companion example it is exactly the circle $I=\mathrm{const}$ of the action-angle coordinates, in agreement with the torus theorem at regular values. Thus the datum exhibits both a critical fibre that is a point and regular fibres that are circles, and the unqualified compactness/connectedness version of the torus claim is false exactly at the critical value.

Collecting: the common level set $H^{-1}(0)$ of the completely integrable datum $(H)$ is nonempty, compact and connected but not diffeomorphic to a torus, so the refuted statement is false; the regular values of the same datum do satisfy the torus conclusion, so no claim of [[pthm-cm14-regular-tori]] is affected.

boundaries.evidence: The refuted universal claim is refuted by a nonempty fibre: $H^{-1}(0)=\{(0,0)\}$ (step 1.1).
The zero-energy level is the counterexample itself, and $0$ is its critical value (steps 1.1 and 2.1).
The one-degree-of-freedom datum $(H)$ and the comparison torus $T^{1}$ are the objects of the refutation (steps 1.1 and 2.1).
The critical (degenerate) level is exactly the exhibited failure of the regularity hypothesis (step 2.1).

boundaries.reason: No boundary or endpoint claim is made.
The fibre is a single explicit point; no selection principle is used.
The universal torus claim is refuted by the single critical level H=0; an existential counterexample needs no forward implication chain.
After the refutation nothing is asserted about which level values are tori, so no reverse implication is used or claimed.

Adopt the force model with potential presentation $(U,d)$ and mechanical
Lagrangian $L=K-U$ of [[def-cm07-action-and-mechanical-lagrangian]], with
the momentum charts and two-form datum of [[def-cm13-two-form]], the
canonical coordinates of [[def-cm13-canonical-form]], the bracket of
[[def-cm13-poisson]], the Hamiltonian fields of [[def-cm13-hamiltonian-field]] and the branch
Hamiltonian $H$ of [[def-cm12-hamiltonian]];
by clause 1 of [[pthm-cm13-two-form-is-symplectic]] each momentum phase
domain is a symplectic manifold for $\omega$, with $\omega$ the standard
two-form in the chart's canonical coordinates
([[def-symplectic-form-and-symplectic-manifold]]). Dimensions are read by
[[def-cm01-units]] and differentiability classes are those of
[[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]].

**(a) The datum.** Let $W_{0}$ be a nonempty open subset of one momentum
phase domain of the presentation, of dimension $2n$, and let

$$F=(F_{1},\dots,F_{n}),\qquad F_{i}:W_{0}\longrightarrow\mathbb R,$$

be phase functions of class $C^{\infty}$ with $F_{1}=H|_{W_{0}}$. The
family $F$ is a **completely integrable datum of the presentation on
$W_{0}$** when

1. $F$ is in involution, $\{F_{i},F_{j}\}=0$ on $W_{0}$ for all $i,j$
   ([[def-cm14-involution]] clause (d)); and
2. the differentials $dF_{1},\dots,dF_{n}$ are linearly independent on a
   dense open subset of $W_{0}$ ([[def-linear-independence]],
   [[def-differential-rank-and-constant-rank]]).

**(b) Reading in the root library.** Since $(W_{0},\omega)$ is a
$2n$-dimensional symplectic manifold and the bracket of
[[def-cm13-poisson]] is the bracket of
[[def-poisson-bracket-on-a-symplectic-manifold]] for $\omega$, a datum
$F$ in the sense of clause (a), with $F_{1}=H$ and the autonomous
Hamiltonian $H$ of the presentation, is exactly a **completely integrable
Hamiltonian system** on $(W_{0},\omega)$ in the sense of
[[def-completely-integrable-hamiltonian-system]], with branches read
through the presentation's Hamiltonians; the root notion of
[[def-first-integral-and-poisson-commuting-functions]] is read through the
bracket criterion of [[pthm-cm13-observable-evolution]] clause 2.

**(c) Integral map, regular locus and fibres.** Attached to a datum $F$
are:

1. the **integral map** $F:W_{0}\to\mathbb R^{n}$;
2. the **regular locus** $W_{\mathrm{reg}}:=\{z\in W_{0}:
   \operatorname{rank}dF(z)=n\}$, which is open by continuity of the partial
   derivatives and dense in $W_{0}$ by clause (a) 2;
3. the **regular values**, namely the values $b\in F(W_{\mathrm{reg}})$;
   for such a value the **regular fibre** $N_{b}:=F^{-1}(b)$ is the
   common level set of $F_{1},\dots,F_{n}$ through $b$;
4. the **Hamiltonian fields** $X_{F_{1}},\dots,X_{F_{n}}$ of the family
   ([[def-cm13-hamiltonian-field]]).

**(d) Status.** The item defines a datum class and its attached objects.
It asserts that no particular model of the force branch is completely
integrable, that no fibre is compact, connected or a torus, that no
action-angle coordinates exist and no measured value is known; the
structural and motion statements are the torus theorem and the
action-angle theorem of this page (items `pthm-cm14-regular-tori` and
`pthm-cm14-action-angle`), conditional on the hypotheses stated there.

Adopt the force model with potential presentation $(U,d)$ and mechanical
Lagrangian $L=K-U$ of [[def-cm07-action-and-mechanical-lagrangian]], with
the momentum charts and two-form datum of [[def-cm13-two-form]], the
Hamiltonian fields of [[def-cm13-hamiltonian-field]], the bracket of
[[def-cm13-poisson]] and the branch Hamiltonian $H$ of
[[def-cm12-hamiltonian]]; the model reading of the Hamiltonian system is
the equivalence of [[pthm-cm13-hamiltonian-field-integrates-the-model-equations]]
(motions of the model are the integral curves of the branch Hamiltonian
field, in each chart with its own Hamiltonian). Dimensions are read by
[[def-cm01-units]] and differentiability classes are those of
[[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]].

**(a) Phase functions and the domain.** Let $W_{0}$ be a nonempty open
subset of one momentum phase domain of the presentation. A **phase
function of the presentation on $W_{0}$ of class $C^{k}$** is a map
$f:W_{0}\to\mathbb R$ of class $C^{k}$, of a declared dimension.

**(b) First integrals.** Let $f:W_{0}\to\mathbb R$ be of class $C^{1}$.
Then $f$ is a **first integral of the branch Hamiltonian $H$ on $W_{0}$**
when for every interval $J\subseteq I_{0}$ with nonempty interior and every
solution $z:J\to W_{0}$ of the Hamiltonian system
$\dot z(t)=X_{H_{t}}(z(t))$
([[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]]) the composite
$t\mapsto f(z(t))$ is constant on $J$. Equivalently, in the reading of
[[pthm-cm13-hamiltonian-field-integrates-the-model-equations]], $f$ is
constant along every motion of the model whose momentum-phase curve lies
in $W_{0}$ (on the potential branch).

**(c) The bracket criterion.** Let $H$ be autonomous on $I_{0}\times W_{0}$
($\partial_{t}U\equiv0$ and $d\equiv0$) and let $f:W_{0}\to\mathbb R$ be
autonomous of class $C^{2}$. Then $f$ is a first integral of $H$ on $W_{0}$
if and only if

$$\{f,H\}=0\qquad\text{everywhere on }W_{0},$$

the bracket being that of [[def-cm13-poisson]]. The equivalence is clause
2 of [[pthm-cm13-observable-evolution]], recorded here as the working
form of the definition; it is not re-proved.

**(d) Involution.** Phase functions $f_{1},\dots,f_{k}:W_{0}\to\mathbb R$
of class $C^{2}$ are **in involution** (or **pairwise Poisson-commuting**)
when

$$\{f_{i},f_{j}\}=0\qquad\text{on }W_{0}\text{ for all }i,j\in\{1,\dots,k\};$$

a **family of first integrals in involution** is a family whose members are
first integrals of $H$ and which is in involution. The notion is the
presentation reading of the root-library notion of
[[def-first-integral-and-poisson-commuting-functions]] under the bracket of
[[def-cm13-poisson]], which is the bracket of
[[def-poisson-bracket-on-a-symplectic-manifold]] for the two-form of
[[def-cm13-two-form]].

**(e) Differential independence.** Phase functions $f_{1},\dots,f_{k}$ of
class $C^{1}$ are **independent at $z\in W_{0}$** when the differentials
$df_{1}(z),\dots,df_{k}(z)$ are linearly independent as elements of the
dual of the tangent space at $z$ ([[def-linear-independence]]); the set
of points at which this holds is the **independence locus** of the family,
$\{z\in W_{0}:\operatorname{rank}(df_{1}(z),\dots,df_{k}(z))=k\}$
([[def-differential-rank-and-constant-rank]],
[[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]). The family is **independent on**
$W_{0}$ when it is independent at every $z\in W_{0}$.

**(f) Status.** The item defines model properties of phase functions and
records one proved equivalence from the evolution theorem of the
companion page. It asserts no existence of a nonconstant first integral
for a given force law, no completeness of any flow, no conservation law
of the model and no measured value; in particular every closure or
constancy statement about brackets is a theorem of this page or of
[[pthm-cm13-observable-evolution]], not part of the definition.

Adopt the force model with potential presentation $(U,d)$ and mechanical
Lagrangian $L=K-U$ of [[def-cm07-action-and-mechanical-lagrangian]], with the
momentum charts and two-form datum of [[def-cm13-two-form]] and the canonical
coordinates of [[def-cm13-canonical-form]]: the Cartesian phase domain
$W=Q\times\mathbb R^{3N}$, its two-form $\omega$, a generalized-coordinate
chart map $\Phi_{X}$ and the form $\omega_{X}$
([[def-cm07-generalized-coordinates-and-forces]]); the presentation is
hyperregular on every chart with the Hamiltonian $H$ of
[[def-cm12-hamiltonian]] and [[pthm-cm12-mechanical-hyperregularity]],

$$H(t,x,p)=\tfrac12\,p\cdot\mathsf M^{-1}p+U(t,x),\qquad \widetilde H(t,q,P)=\tfrac12\,P\cdot G(q)^{-1}P+\widetilde U(t,q).$$

Differentiability classes are those of
[[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]], and gradients those of
[[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]].

**(a) The field of a phase function.** Let $W_{0}\subseteq W$ be nonempty
open and let $f:W_{0}\to\mathbb R$ be of class $C^{2}$. By clause 1 of
[[pthm-cm13-two-form-is-symplectic]] the form $\omega$ is nondegenerate on
$W_{0}$, so there is exactly one $C^{1}$ vector field $X_{f}$ on $W_{0}$ with

$$\iota_{X_{f}}\omega=df$$

(the sign convention of [[def-hamiltonian-vector-field-and-hamiltonian-function]]
and [[prop-cm-hamiltonian-field-and-poisson-bracket-in-a-phase-chart]]); it
is the **Hamiltonian field of $f$ for the presentation**. In the Cartesian
coordinates $(x,p)$, writing $\nabla f=(f_{x^{1}},\dots,f_{x^{3N}},f_{p_{1}},\dots,f_{p_{3N}})$,

$$X_{f}=\bigl(f_{p},\,-f_{x}\bigr)=J\nabla f,\qquad J=\begin{pmatrix}0_{3N}&I_{3N}\\-I_{3N}&0_{3N}\end{pmatrix};$$

in any canonical chart $(\theta^{1},\dots,\theta^{2m})$ of the presentation
the same field reads $X_{f}=\bigl(f_{\theta^{m+1}},\dots,f_{\theta^{2m}},-f_{\theta^{1}},\dots,-f_{\theta^{m}}\bigr)$.
A vector field on $W_{0}$ is called **Hamiltonian for the presentation** when
it is $X_{f}$ for some $C^{2}$ function $f$; in particular
$X_{f}=0$ exactly when $f$ is locally constant on $W_{0}$. Vector fields are
read as tangent-bundle sections of
[[def-smooth-vector-field-as-a-tangent-bundle-section]].

**(b) The field of the branch Hamiltonian.** For each $t\in I_{0}$ the
function $H_{t}:=H(t,\cdot)$ is $C^{2}$ on $W$, and the **Hamiltonian field
of the presentation** at time $t$ is $X_{H_{t}}$:

$$X_{H_{t}}(x,p)=\bigl(\mathsf M^{-1}p,\ -\nabla_{x}U(t,x)\bigr),$$

whose components are a velocity and a force. In the coordinates $X$ the
corresponding field is
$X_{\widetilde H_{t}}(q,P)=\bigl(G(q)^{-1}P,\ -\partial_{q}\widetilde H(t,q,P)\bigr)$,
where the second slot retains the kinetic contribution
$-\tfrac12P\cdot\partial_{q}(G(q)^{-1})P$ when the metric varies. If
$d\not\equiv0$ the model's forced evolution carries the additional momentum
source $d$; the corresponding vector field
$(x,p)\mapsto\bigl(\mathsf M^{-1}p,-\nabla_{x}U(t,x)+d(t,x,\mathsf M^{-1}p)\bigr)$
is generally not a Hamiltonian field for the presentation, and it is one
exactly when the residual force has a potential independent of the velocity
slot (the criterion is proved in clause 4 of the corresponding theorem of this
page).

**(c) Time dependence and status.** For a time-dependent $H$ the assignment
$t\mapsto X_{H_{t}}$ is a time-dependent field on the phase domain; each
$X_{H_{t}}$ is $C^{1}$, hence locally Lipschitz in the state variable, and no
completeness of its integral curves is asserted here. The item defines the
field datum and its chart expressions; the identification of the model's
motions with the integral curves, and all conservation or invariance
properties, are the subject of the other items of this page. The field is
defined by the intrinsic equation $\iota_{X}\omega=dH$ and therefore does not
depend on the canonical chart used to compute it.

Adopt the force model with potential presentation $(U,d)$ and mechanical
Lagrangian $L=K-U$ of [[def-cm07-action-and-mechanical-lagrangian]] with the
data, charts and Hamiltonian field of [[def-cm13-two-form]],
[[def-cm13-hamiltonian-field]]: masses $m_{1},\dots,m_{N}>0$ and open
configuration domain $Q\subseteq\mathbb R^{3N}$ with mass operator
$\mathsf M$ ([[def-cm01-configuration]]), time window $I_{0}$, $C^{2}$
potential $U$ and residual forces $d$ of the standing regularity
([[def-cm03-potential-and-mechanical-energy]],
[[post-cm02-force-superposition]], [[def-cm01-units]]), the Cartesian
Hamiltonian $H(t,x,p)=\tfrac12p\cdot\mathsf M^{-1}p+U(t,x)$ and, for a
generalized-coordinate map $X:\Omega\to Q$ with kinetic metric
$G=DX^{\mathsf T}\mathsf M\,DX$, the chart Hamiltonian
$\widetilde H(t,q,P)=\tfrac12P\cdot G(q)^{-1}P+\widetilde U(t,q)$
([[def-cm12-hamiltonian]], [[pthm-cm12-mechanical-hyperregularity]],
[[def-cm07-generalized-coordinates-and-forces]],
[[def-cm12-cotangent-momentum]]). Let $J\subseteq I_{0}$ be a nonempty open
interval. Then:

1. **(potential branch, Cartesian chart)** Assume $d\equiv0$ on the state
   domain. For a $C^{2}$ curve $x:J\to Q$ with $p(t):=\mathsf Mx'(t)$ the
   following are equivalent: (a) $x$ is a motion of the model
   ([[def-cm02-newtonian-flow]]); (b) $\dot x(t)=H_{p}(t,x(t),p(t))$ and
   $\dot p(t)=-H_{x}(t,x(t),p(t))$ for every $t\in J$; (c) the curve
   $t\mapsto(x(t),p(t))$ is an integral curve of the time-dependent field
   $t\mapsto X_{H_{t}}$, i.e. satisfies
   $\dot z(t)=X_{H_{t}}(z(t))$ with $z=(x,p)$
   ([[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]]).
2. **(generalized-coordinate chart)** Let $X:\Omega\to Q$ be a
   generalized-coordinate map and let $q:J\to\Omega$ be a $C^{2}$ curve with
   $x:=X\circ q$ and $P(t):=G(q(t))q'(t)$. Then the declared Lagrange
   equations with residual generalized force,
   $\Lambda(\widetilde L)(q)(t)=Q^{\mathrm{res}}(t,q(t),q'(t))$, are
   equivalent to
   $q'(t)=\widetilde H_{P}(t,q(t),P(t))$ and
   $P'(t)=-\widetilde H_{q}(t,q(t),P(t))+Q^{\mathrm{res}}(t,q(t),q'(t))$;
   in particular, when $d\equiv0$, they are equivalent to
   $(q,P)$ being an integral curve of $X_{\widetilde H_{t}}$.
3. **(residual forces, Cartesian chart)** For a $C^{2}$ curve $x:J\to Q$
   with $p=\mathsf Mx'$, the model's forced equation
   $\mathsf Mx''=-\nabla_{x}U(t,x)+d(t,x,x')$ holds on $J$ if and only if
   $\dot x=H_{p}$ and $\dot p=-H_{x}+d(t,x,\mathsf M^{-1}p)$ on $J$.
4. **(when is the forced field Hamiltonian?)** The forced field
   $(x,p)\mapsto\bigl(\mathsf M^{-1}p,-\nabla_{x}U(t,x)+d(t,x,\mathsf M^{-1}p)\bigr)$
   is the Hamiltonian field of a $C^{2}$ phase function on its domain if and
   only if there is a $C^{2}$ function $V:I_{0}\times Q\to\mathbb R$ with
   $d(t,x,v)=-\nabla_{x}V(t,x)$ for every $(t,x,v)$ of the state domain; in
   that case the phase function is $H+V$ up to an independently chosen
   additive $C^2$ function of $t$ on each connected component of $Q$, and the model's forced motions are the motions of the potential
   presentation $(U+V,0)$.

The statement is conditional on the adopted force branch, the declared
presentation and the declared chart; it asserts no existence or uniqueness of
solutions, no completeness, no conservation law and no empirical content.
