Let $m,n\ge 1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be $C^1$ ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]). The **rank of $f$ at $a\in U$** is
$$\operatorname{rank}_a f:=\operatorname{rank}Df(a),$$
where rank is the dimension of the image ([[def-rank-and-nullity]]). In the standard bases, this is also the rank of the Jacobian matrix $Jf(a)$ ([[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]).

For $S\subseteq U$ and $0\le r\le\min\{m,n\}$, the map $f$ has **constant rank $r$ on $S$** when $\operatorname{rank}Df(x)=r$ for every $x\in S$. On the empty set this condition is vacuous, so it may hold for more than one $r$; every assertion that needs a determined rank will assume $S$ is nonempty or specify $r$.

Let $(X, \mathcal{T})$ be a topological space ([[def-topological-space]]).

- An **open cover** of $(X,\mathcal{T})$ is a family
  $\mathcal{U} \subseteq \mathcal{T}$ of open sets with $X = \bigcup \mathcal{U}$,
  where $\bigcup \mathcal{U} = \{\, x \in X : x \in U \text{ for some } U \in \mathcal{U} \,\}$.
- A **subcover** of $\mathcal{U}$ is a subfamily $\mathcal{V} \subseteq \mathcal{U}$
  that is itself an open cover.
- A family $\mathcal{V}$ of sets is **finite** when $\mathcal{V} = \varnothing$ or
  there are $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and sets $V_0, \dots, V_n$ with
  $\mathcal{V} = \{V_0, \dots, V_n\}$; repetitions in the list are allowed and
  harmless.
- $(X,\mathcal{T})$ is **compact** when every open cover of it has a finite
  subcover: for every open cover $\mathcal{U}$, either $X = \varnothing$ and the
  empty subfamily covers it, or there are $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and
  $U_0, \dots, U_n \in \mathcal{U}$ with
  $$X = U_0 \cup \dots \cup U_n .$$
- A subset $A \subseteq X$ is a **compact subset** of $X$ when the subspace
  $(A, \mathcal{T}_A)$ is a compact topological space, $\mathcal{T}_A$ being the
  subspace topology ([[def-subspace-topology-top]]).

**Compactness of a subset is defined intrinsically, and only intrinsically.**
The last clause speaks about the subspace $(A, \mathcal{T}_A)$ and its own open
sets, not about families of open subsets of the ambient $X$. The two readings do
agree, but that is a theorem and not a convention: it is
[[lem-compactness-of-a-subspace-is-ambient]], and no item of this library may use
the ambient reading without citing it. Taking the intrinsic reading makes
compactness a property of the topological space $(A, \mathcal{T}_A)$ alone.
Hence it is preserved when $A$ is embedded homeomorphically as a subspace, or
when another ambient space induces the same topology on $A$; it need not be
preserved if the induced topology changes. This is exactly the convention already fixed for
metric spaces by [[def-metric-compactness]], and the agreement of that
definition with this one is [[thm-compactness-agrees-with-metric-compactness]].

**The empty space is compact**, since the empty subfamily of any family covers
it; this is the reason the clause above is written with the two cases. Every
space listed as $\{x_0, \dots, x_n\}$ is compact too: given a cover, each $x_i$
lies in some member, and finitely many members named in this way already cover.
So every finite space is compact, whatever its topology, and in particular the
discrete topology on a finite set is compact while the discrete topology on an
infinite set is not ([[def-standard-topologies]]).

**The finiteness convention.** "Finite" above is the listing form. It agrees with
the definition of finiteness by equinumerosity with a natural number
([[def-countable]]), in both directions, and the agreement is the one already
discharged in [[def-metric-compactness]]: a nonempty set equinumerous with
$m \ge 1$ is listable, and a set listed as $\{a_0, \dots, a_n\}$ injects into
$\sigma(n)$ by sending $x$ to the least $i \le n$ with $a_i = x$. Neither
direction uses a choice principle; the second selects nothing, taking a least
index instead.

**Quasicompact is not used here.** Some authors, following Bourbaki, reserve
*compact* for a space that is both compact in the above sense and Hausdorff, and
call the open-cover condition alone *quasicompact*. This library follows the more
widely adopted convention: **compact** means the open-cover condition and nothing
more, and a Hausdorff hypothesis is always written out. The fork is recorded in
[[rem-compactness-conventions-and-choice-ledger]].

Let $(X,d)$ be a nonempty compact metric space ([[def-metric-compactness]],
[[def-metric-space]]) and let $f : X \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous
([[def-metric-continuity]]), $\mathbb{R}$ carrying its usual metric
$d_{\mathbb{R}}(s,t) = |s-t|$ ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]). Then the
image $f[X]$ is bounded above and below ([[def-bounded-set]]), and it has a
maximum and a minimum ([[def-max-min]]): there are points
$x_{\max}, x_{\min} \in X$ with

$$f(x_{\min}) \;\le\; f(x) \;\le\; f(x_{\max}) \qquad \text{for every } x \in X,$$

and then $f(x_{\max}) = \sup f[X]$ and $f(x_{\min}) = \inf f[X]$
([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-infimum]]).

Nonemptiness of $X$ is a hypothesis and not an oversight: for $X = \emptyset$ the
image is empty and has neither a supremum nor a maximum. No choice principle is
used.

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field with its order and
absolute value ([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[lem-of-abs-value]]), and
neighbourhoods are those of [[def-neighbourhood-r]].

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $c \in A$. Then
$f$ is **continuous at $c$** when

$$(\forall \varepsilon > 0)\ (\exists \delta > 0)\ (\forall x \in A)\ \bigl[\ |x - c| < \delta \ \Longrightarrow\ |f(x) - f(c)| < \varepsilon\ \bigr],$$

with $\varepsilon$ and $\delta$ ranging over the **positive reals**. In the
language of neighbourhoods: for every real $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a real
$\delta > 0$ with

$$f\bigl(A \cap N_{\delta}(c)\bigr) \;\subseteq\; N_{\varepsilon}\bigl(f(c)\bigr).$$

$f$ is **continuous on $A$** when it is continuous at every point of $A$.

**The point $c$ is required to lie in $A$, and the condition is unpunctured.**
Both differ from [[def-function-limit]], and deliberately. There the quantifier
runs over $0 < |x - c| < \delta$, which removes $x = c$; here $x = c$ is allowed,
and at $x = c$ the implication reads $|f(c) - f(c)| = 0 < \varepsilon$, which is
automatic. So allowing $x = c$ costs nothing, and it is what lets the definition
be stated at every point of $A$, including the points where no limit exists.

**Three clauses, and all three are part of the definition.**

1. **At a limit point.** Suppose $c \in A$ is a limit point of $A$
   ([[def-limit-point-r]]). Then $f$ is continuous at $c$ if and only if the
   limit of $f$ at $c$ exists and
   $$\lim_{x \to c} f(x) \;=\; f(c)$$
   ([[def-function-limit]]). Indeed, for a given $\varepsilon > 0$ a $\delta$
   witnessing continuity witnesses the limit condition, because the limit
   condition quantifies over a subset of the points continuity quantifies over;
   and conversely a $\delta$ witnessing $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = f(c)$ witnesses
   continuity, because the one point it omits, $x = c$, satisfies
   $|f(c) - f(c)| < \varepsilon$ anyway.

2. **At an isolated point.** Suppose $c \in A$ is an isolated point of $A$
   ([[def-limit-point-r]]), so that $N_{\eta}(c) \cap A = \{c\}$ for some real
   $\eta > 0$. Then **every** $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is continuous at $c$: take
   $\delta := \eta$, so that the only $x \in A$ with $|x - c| < \delta$ is $c$
   itself, and $|f(c) - f(c)| = 0 < \varepsilon$.

3. **On a set.** Continuity on $A$ is continuity at each point of $A$, and
   nothing more. It is not a condition relating $f$ to points outside $A$.

Every point of $A$ is either a limit point of $A$ or an isolated point of $A$,
and never both ([[def-limit-point-r]]), so clauses 1 and 2 between them describe
continuity at every point of $A$.

**This is not the raw $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ formula of
[[fs-limit-unique-at-every-point-of-the-domain]].** That item records what goes
wrong when the *punctured* formula of [[def-function-limit]] is written down at
an arbitrary point of the domain: at an isolated point it is satisfied
vacuously by every real $L$ at once, so it defines nothing, and this library
therefore leaves $\lim_{x \to c} f(x)$ **undefined** at an isolated point.
Continuity at an isolated point is a different matter: the formula above is not
vacuous — it is a genuine condition on $f(c)$, satisfied because $f(c)$ is the
only value being compared with itself — and it names a single, well-defined
property. The limit is undefined there; the continuity is defined, and is
automatic. Clause 1 is the only place where the two notions meet, and it is
stated only where the limit exists as a notion.

**Where the distinction disappears.** If $A$ is an open subset of $\mathbb{R}$
([[def-open-and-closed-in-r]]), then every $c \in A$ has some
$N_{\eta}(c) \subseteq A$, and a punctured neighbourhood is never empty
([[def-neighbourhood-r]]), so every point of $A$ is a limit point of $A$ and
clause 1 covers the whole of $A$. The same holds when $A$ is a nondegenerate
interval ([[def-interval]]). Isolated points are what force clause 2 to exist at
all, and they occur as soon as $A$ is allowed to be an arbitrary subset of
$\mathbb{R}$, as in $A = \{0\} \cup [1,2]$.

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]).

A subset $U \subseteq X$ is **open in $(X,d)$** if for every $x \in U$ there is a
real $r > 0$ with $B(x,r) \subseteq U$ ([[def-metric-ball]]). A subset
$F \subseteq X$ is **closed in $(X,d)$** if its complement $X \setminus F$ is
open.

The collection

$$\mathcal{T}_d := \{\, U \subseteq X : U \text{ is open in } (X,d) \,\}$$

of all open subsets is the **metric topology** of $d$ on $X$. A subset of $X$
that is both open and closed is called **clopen**.

**Two sets are open for trivial reasons.** $\emptyset$ is open, because the
defining condition quantifies over no points; and $X$ is open, because
$B(x,r) \subseteq X$ for every $x$ and every $r > 0$. Consequently $X$ and
$\emptyset$ are also closed, and both are clopen.

**A neighbourhood of a point $x$** is any set containing an open set that
contains $x$; an **open neighbourhood** is an open set containing $x$. In a
metric space, a set is a neighbourhood of $x$ exactly when it contains some
ball $B(x,r)$ with $r>0$. Thus $U$ is open exactly when it is a neighbourhood of
each of its points, and metric balls suffice to test this condition.

**The metric, not the set, determines $\mathcal{T}_d$.** Two metrics on the same
set may have different metric topologies, and two different metrics may have the
same one; the systematic comparison is [[def-equivalent-metrics]].

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_{\omega}$
([[def-countable-choice]]). Adopt the force model with potential
presentation $(U,d)$ and mechanical Lagrangian $L=K-U$ of
[[def-cm07-action-and-mechanical-lagrangian]], with the momentum charts and
two-form datum of [[def-cm13-two-form]], the Hamiltonian fields of
[[def-cm13-hamiltonian-field]] and the branch Hamiltonian $H$ of
[[def-cm12-hamiltonian]]; by clause 1 of
[[pthm-cm13-two-form-is-symplectic]] each momentum phase domain is a
symplectic manifold for the presentation's two-form $\omega$
([[def-symplectic-form-and-symplectic-manifold]]). Let $W_{0}\subseteq W$
be a nonempty open phase domain of dimension $2n$ and let
$F=(F_{1}=H|_{W_{0}},\dots,F_{n})$ be a completely integrable datum of the
presentation on $W_{0}$ ([[def-cm14-complete-integrability]]). Let $b_{0}$
be a regular value of the integral map whose regular fibre
$N:=F^{-1}(b_{0})\subseteq W_{0}$ is nonempty, compact and connected, and
assume there are a saturated open neighbourhood $U\subseteq W_{0}$ of $N$
and a ball $B\subseteq\mathbb R^{n}$ of regular values with $F(U)=B$ such
that $\pi:=F|_{U}:U\to B$ is a proper submersion with connected fibres.
Then:

1. **(Lagrangian fibre)** $N$ is a compact connected embedded
   $n$-dimensional Lagrangian submanifold of $(W_{0},\omega)$, and for
   every $z\in N$
   $$T_{z}N=\operatorname{span}\{X_{F_{1}}(z),\dots,X_{F_{n}}(z)\},$$
   the fields being those of [[def-cm13-hamiltonian-field]].
2. **(commuting flows and period lattice)** The fields
   $X_{F_{1}},\dots,X_{F_{n}}$ have pairwise commuting flows; these flows
   combine into a local $\mathbb R^{n}$ action on $W_{\mathrm{reg}}$, and
   on the compact invariant fibre $N$ their restrictions are complete and
   generate a transitive action of $\mathbb R^{n}$ whose stabilizer at
   every point is one and the same full lattice $\Gamma\subseteq
   \mathbb R^{n}$, with $N\cong\mathbb R^{n}/\Gamma$.
3. **(torus)** $N$ is diffeomorphic to the torus
   $T^{n}=\mathbb R^{n}/\mathbb Z^{n}$.

The statement is conditional on the adopted force branch, the declared
presentation, the smooth completely integrable datum and the listed
hypotheses on the fibre; it asserts no global product structure of $U$, no
action-angle coordinates, no completeness of any flow outside the compact
fibre and no empirical content.

derivations.claim: By [L1] and [L2], for every regular value $E>0$ the level set $N:=H^{-1}(E)=\{(x,p):\lvert p\rvert=\rho\}=\mathbb R^{3}\times S^{2}_{\rho}$ is a nonempty regular common level set of a completely integrable datum of the presentation.

Noncompactness: the continuous function $f(x,p):=x_{1}$ restricted to $N$ takes the value $c$ at $\bigl((c,0,0),(\rho,0,0)\bigr)\in N$ for every $c\in\mathbb R$, so it is unbounded on $N$. If $N$ were compact, then by [L3] the continuous function $f|_{N}$ would attain a maximum and in particular be bounded; it is not. Hence $N$ is not compact, and the compactness clause of the refuted statement fails at a regular level set of a completely integrable datum.

No periods and no lattice: by [L1] the field is $X_{H}(x,p)=(p/m,0)$, so its flow is $\Phi^{t}(x,p)= igl(x+(p/m)t,\,p igr)$; along $N$ one has $p
eq0$, hence $(p/m)t
eq0$ for every $t
eq0$ and $\Phi^{t}(x,p)
eq(x,p)$. The flow therefore has no nonzero period on $N$, its stabilizer is trivial at every point, and $N$ carries no nonzero period lattice, let alone a full one; the periodicity clause of the refuted statement fails.

Consistency with the qualified theorem: [L4] requires a compact connected regular fibre; $N$ is regular but noncompact, so the theorem's hypotheses fail and no contradiction arises. The example exhibits exactly the compactness hypothesis as the indispensable one: the free label's motion is uniform translation, its action $\lvert p\rvert^{2}/(2m)$ is conserved but does not quantize the motion into circles.

Collecting: $N$ is a nonempty regular common level set of a completely integrable datum that is noncompact and carries no period, so the refuted statement is false; the qualified conclusions of [[pthm-cm14-regular-tori]] and [[pthm-cm14-action-angle]] are unaffected because their compactness hypothesis fails here.

boundaries.evidence: The regular level $N=\{|p|=\rho\}$ is nonempty for $E>0$ (step 1.1).
The fibre excludes $p=0$ by $|p|=\rho>0$, which is why the flow has no period (steps 1.1 and 2.1).
The datum has one integral $F_{1}=H$; the label lives in $\mathbb R^{3}$ and the level is five-dimensional (statement, step 1.1).
Regularity at $p\neq0$ is verified, so the counterexample is not a degeneracy of the datum but of the unqualified claim (step 1.1).

boundaries.reason: No boundary-value or endpoint claim is made.
All objects are explicit and the unboundedness is exhibited by a formula (steps 1.1 and 2.1).
One regular level H^{-1}(E) with E>0 that is noncompact and carries no full period lattice refutes the universal compactness-and-periodicity claim; no equivalence is asserted.
No converse is claimed, for instance that compact regular fibres or periodic flow are automatic outside the torus theorem's hypotheses.

citations.quote:
**(i) Setting.** Work in the one-dimensional model class of
[[def-cm04-one-dimensional-models-and-equilibria]] with time window
$I_{0}=\mathbb R$, configuration domain $Q=\mathbb R$, a fixed mass $m>0$
and a **spring constant** $k>0$ of dimension $\mu\tau^{-2}$, read in newtons
per metre ([[def-cm01-units]]). The **harmonic model** is the model whose
force law is the **linear restoring force**
$$F(x,v):=-k\,x .$$
Its equation of motion is $m\,x''=-k\,x$, equivalently $m\,x''+k\,x=0$; the
model is autonomous and velocity-independent, and its potential is
$$U(x):=\tfrac12 k\,x^{2},$$
of dimension $\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-2}$ (joules), which presents the force law in
the sense of clause (d) of [[def-cm04-one-dimensional-models-and-equilibria]]:
$U$ is of class $C^{2}$ and $-U'(x)=-k\,x=F(x)$ ([[lem-derivative-of-a-power]],
[[def-derivative]]). The harmonic model is therefore a **conservative**
model of the class, with the potential representative $U$ declared above and
no residual force.

**(ii) Regularity and framework status.** The force law is affine in the
state; it is continuous, and $\lvert F(x)-F(x')\rvert=k\lvert x-x'\rvert\le
k\,\lVert(x,v)-(x',v')\rVert_{2}$, so it is locally Lipschitz in the state
variable with the global constant $k$, uniformly in time
([[def-locally-lipschitz-in-the-state-variable]]). The harmonic model is
thus an admissible model of the class of clause (a) of
[[def-cm04-one-dimensional-models-and-equilibria]], and the existence,
uniqueness and conservation statements of this page apply to it. It is
adopted as a restricted model class of the framework, at the same primitive
level as the force maps of [[post-cm02-force-superposition]]: the force law
is model input.

**(iii) Physical reading and regime.** The model idealizes a **restoring
force linear in the displacement**: an ideal spring, or the quadratic
approximation of a potential $U$ near a strict local minimum $x_{*}$ with $U''(x_*)>0$, where
the Taylor expansion of the effective potential begins with the quadratic
term $\tfrac12 U''(x_{*})(x-x_{*})^{2}$ and the linearized equation carries
the **effective spring constant** $U''(x_{*})$ (the sources' linearization
procedure). The model is adopted for a stated regime — displacements so
small that the neglected remainder of the potential is adequate for the
purpose at hand — and it is **not** claimed to describe large-amplitude
oscillations, nonlinear springs, plasticity, or any given real system. The
coefficient $k$ is a model parameter, not a constant of the framework; when
its value is taken from a calibration experiment, that value is an empirical
premise carrying the apparatus conditions and the measurement uncertainty,
and the framework asserts none of it here. The linear form is the simplest
restoring law satisfying the standing regularity; that is a modelling
convenience, not a derivation.

**(iv) Status.** Adopted assumption of the framework when a model invokes
it; it selects no law of nature on its own. Every consequence below is a
conditional statement about the declared equation of motion.

Adopt the harmonic model of [[post-cm04-harmonic-model]]: the
one-dimensional model of [[def-cm04-one-dimensional-models-and-equilibria]]
with $m>0$, $k>0$, force law $F(x)=-kx$ and potential $U(x)=\tfrac12kx^{2}$.
Write
$$\omega:=\sqrt{\frac{k}{m}}>0$$
for its **undamped frequency** in the sense of
[[def-cm-oscillator-model-and-phase-system]]. Then:

1. **Motions.** Let $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval with nonempty
   interior and let $t_{0}\in J$. A curve $x:J\to\mathbb R$ is a motion of the
   model on $J$ if and only if there are reals $A,B$ with
   $$x(t)=A\cos\bigl(\omega(t-t_{0})\bigr)+B\sin\bigl(\omega(t-t_{0})\bigr) \qquad(t\in J).$$
   For every datum $(t_{0},x_{0},v_{0})$ there is exactly one maximal motion,
   it is defined on all of $\mathbb R$, and its coefficients are
   $A=x_{0}$, $B=v_{0}/\omega$; every motion with that datum is its
   restriction.
All claims involving every real time, periods or the whole phase ellipse below refer to the unique maximal extension of clause 1; on a local motion interval the same formulas hold by restriction.

2. **Amplitude and phase.** With $A,B$ as in clause 1 put
   $R:=\sqrt{A^{2}+B^{2}}$. Then $\lvert x(t)\rvert\le R$ for every $t$; if
   $R>0$ there is a real $\varphi$ with $\cos\varphi=A/R$ and
   $\sin\varphi=B/R$, and then
   $$x(t)=R\cos\bigl(\omega(t-t_{0})-\varphi\bigr)\qquad(t\in\mathbb R).$$
   If $R=0$ the motion is the rest motion $x\equiv0$.
3. **Period and frequency.** For every motion $x(t+T)=x(t)$ holds for all
   $t$ whenever $\omega T\in2\pi\mathbb Z$. If $R>0$, conversely every
   period $T>0$ of $x$ satisfies $\omega T\in2\pi\mathbb Z$, so the **least
   positive period** of the motion is $T_{\mathrm{per}}=2\pi/\omega$, and the
   **frequency** in cycles per second is $f=1/T_{\mathrm{per}}=\omega/(2\pi)$.
   If $R=0$ every $T$ is a period.
4. **Energy and phase curves.** Along every motion with coefficients $A,B$
   the mechanical energy is
   $$E\bigl(x(t),x'(t)\bigr)=\tfrac12k\bigl(A^{2}+B^{2}\bigr)=\tfrac12kR^{2}$$
   for every $t$, the phase curve is contained in the ellipse
   $$\Sigma_{R}:=\Bigl\{(x,v)\in\mathbb R^{2}:\frac{x^{2}}{R^{2}}+\frac{v^{2}}{\omega^{2}R^{2}}=1\Bigr\}$$
   when $R>0$, and it is exactly that ellipse: every point of $\Sigma_{R}$
   lies on the phase curve of the motion and is attained at exactly the times
   $t=t_{0}+\bigl(\theta_{1}+\varphi+2\pi n\bigr)/\omega$, $n\in\mathbb Z$,
   for the appropriate $\theta_{1}$. For $R=0$ the phase curve is the single
   point $(0,0)$, which is also the level set of energy $0$.
5. **Rest point.** The origin $(0,0)$ is the only rest point of the model,
   and it is Lyapunov stable, by
   [[pthm-cm04-equilibrium-stability-at-a-strict-minimum]]; no asymptotic
   stability is asserted.

The statement uses the declared data $m,k$ only through $\omega$ and the
energy; no value of $m$ or $k$ is asserted, and no real oscillator is claimed
to obey the model.

Adopt the force model with potential presentation $(U,d)$ and mechanical
Lagrangian $L=K-U$ of [[def-cm07-action-and-mechanical-lagrangian]] with the
data and conventions of [[def-cm12-cotangent-momentum]]: masses
$m_{1},\dots,m_{N}>0$, open configuration domain $Q\subseteq\mathbb R^{3N}$,
time window $I_{0}$, mass operator $\mathsf M$
([[def-cm01-configuration]]), $C^{2}$ potential
$U:I_{0}\times Q\to\mathbb R$ and residual forces $d$ of the standing
regularity ([[def-cm03-potential-and-mechanical-energy]],
[[post-cm02-force-superposition]]). Let $X:\Omega\to Q$ be a
generalized-coordinate map with substituted Lagrangian $\widetilde L$,
kinetic metric $G(q)=DX(q)^{\mathsf T}\mathsf M\,DX(q)$ and substituted
potential $\widetilde U(t,q)=U(t,X(q))$
([[def-cm07-generalized-coordinates-and-forces]]), and let $H$ and
$\widetilde H$ be the Hamiltonians of [[def-cm12-hamiltonian]]. Then:

1. **(Cartesian chart)** The fibre momentum map
   $\mathbb F_{t,x}(v)=\mathsf Mv$ is a bijection of $\mathbb R^{3N}$ onto
   $\mathbb R^{3N}$ for every $(t,x)\in I_{0}\times Q$, and the inverse
   Legendre branch is the $C^{2}$ map
   $v(t,x,p)=\mathsf M^{-1}p$ on the whole phase chart
   $I_{0}\times Q\times\mathbb R^{3N}$. Hence the presentation is
   hyperregular on the Cartesian chart in the sense of
   [[def-cm12-hyperregularity]], and the Hamiltonian of the branch is

$$H(t,x,p)=\tfrac12\,p\cdot\mathsf M^{-1}p+U(t,x),$$

with the dot product of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]],

   a $C^{2}$ function of dimension $\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-2}$.

2. **(generalized-coordinate chart)** The fibre map
   $v\mapsto G(q)v$ is a bijection of $\mathbb R^{r}$ onto $\mathbb R^{r}$
   for every $(t,q)\in I_{0}\times\Omega$, and the inverse Legendre branch is
   the $C^{2}$ map $v(t,q,p)=G(q)^{-1}p$ on
   $I_{0}\times\Omega\times\mathbb R^{r}$. Hence the presentation is
   hyperregular on the chart of $X$, and the Hamiltonian in the coordinates
   $X$ is

$$\widetilde H(t,q,p)=\tfrac12\,p\cdot G(q)^{-1}p+\widetilde U(t,q),$$

   a $C^{2}$ function of dimension $\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-2}$.

The statement is conditional on the adopted force branch and the declared
presentation; it asserts no equation of motion, no conservation law and no
empirical content.

Adopt the force model with potential presentation $(U,d)$ and mechanical
Lagrangian $L=K-U$ of [[def-cm07-action-and-mechanical-lagrangian]] with the
data and conventions of [[def-cm12-cotangent-momentum]]: masses
$m_{1},\dots,m_{N}>0$, open configuration domain $Q\subseteq\mathbb R^{3N}$,
time window $I_{0}$, mass operator $\mathsf M$
([[def-cm01-configuration]]), $C^{2}$ potential $U$ and residual forces $d$ of
the standing regularity ([[def-cm03-potential-and-mechanical-energy]],
[[post-cm02-force-superposition]]); dimensions are read by
[[def-cm01-units]] and the Euclidean pairing is
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]].

**(a) Cartesian Hamiltonian.** Assume the presentation is hyperregular on the
Cartesian chart, with inverse Legendre branch
$v:I_{0}\times Q\times\mathbb R^{3N}\to\mathbb R^{3N}$
([[def-cm12-hyperregularity]], [[def-cm-legendre-map-in-a-time-dependent-chart]]).
The **Hamiltonian of the presentation on the Cartesian chart** is the function

$$H:I_{0}\times Q\times\mathbb R^{3N}\longrightarrow\mathbb R,\qquad H(t,x,p):=p\cdot v(t,x,p)-L\bigl(t,x,v(t,x,p)\bigr),$$

where $p\cdot v(t,x,p)$ is the Euclidean pairing of the momentum covector
with the inverse-branch velocity ([[def-cm12-cotangent-momentum]],
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]]). The momentum phase chart
$I_{0}\times Q\times\mathbb R^{3N}$ with coordinates $(t,x,p)$ is the
**Hamiltonian phase chart** of the presentation on the Cartesian chart.

**(b) Generalized-coordinate Hamiltonian.** Let $X:\Omega\to Q$ be a
generalized-coordinate map with substituted Lagrangian $\widetilde L$, kinetic
metric $G$ and inverse Legendre branch $v$ on
$I_{0}\times\Omega\times\mathbb R^{r}$ ([[def-cm07-generalized-coordinates-and-forces]],
[[def-cm12-hyperregularity]]). The **Hamiltonian of the presentation in the
coordinates $X$** is

$$\widetilde H:I_{0}\times\Omega\times\mathbb R^{r}\longrightarrow\mathbb R,\qquad \widetilde H(t,q,p):=p\cdot v(t,q,p)-\widetilde L\bigl(t,q,v(t,q,p)\bigr).$$

For the Cartesian chart, $X=\mathrm{id}$ and $\widetilde H=H$; the general
definition is the same formula applied to the substituted fibre-full chart.

**(c) Dimensions and conventions.** Each term of the defining difference has
dimension $\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-2}$ (energy): the pairing $p\cdot v$ multiplies
$\mu\ell\tau^{-1}$ by $\ell\tau^{-1}$ in Cartesian data
([[def-cm12-cotangent-momentum]]), and $L$ has energy dimension
([[def-cm07-action-and-mechanical-lagrangian]]). In the coordinates $X$ the
pairing is dimensionally consistent for every declared coordinate dimension
$\gamma_{a}$ and the dimension is unchanged. The Hamiltonian is $C^{1}$ on
its domain, being a sum of products of $C^{1}$ maps
([[thm-ck-euclidean-maps-closed-under-algebra-and-composition]],
[[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]). The pairing is the coordinate
Euclidean product; no metric on momentum space and no symplectic form is
introduced by this definition.

**(d) Dependence and status.** The Hamiltonian depends on the declared chart,
on the declared inverse Legendre branch (when more than one branch exists it
is part of the data, as in [[def-cm12-hyperregularity]]) and on the potential
representative: replacing $U$ by $U+c(t)$ leaves the branch unchanged and
replaces $L$ by $L-c(t)$, hence replaces $H$ by $H+c(t)$
([[def-cm03-potential-and-mechanical-energy]] clause (c),
[[def-cm07-action-and-mechanical-lagrangian]] clause (b)). It asserts no
equation of motion, no conservation property and no measured value; the
explicit kinetic-plus-potential form of $H$ for the mechanical branch, the
equivalence of its equations with the model's equation of motion and its
relation to the mechanical energy are the theorems of this page. Matrix
identities used by those theorems are read through
[[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]].

Let a force model of [[post-cm02-force-superposition]] be given: time window
$I_{0}\subseteq\mathbb R$ nondegenerate and open, configuration domain
$Q\subseteq\mathbb R^{3N}$ open ([[def-cm01-configuration]] clause (a)),
fixed masses $m_{1},\dots,m_{N}>0$ ([[post-cm01-worldlines]] clause (v)), and a
force map $F$ with the standing continuity and state-local-Lipschitz
hypotheses of clause (iii) of that postulate.

**(a) State domain and inverse-mass operator.** The **state domain** of the
model is

$$D:=I_{0}\times Q\times(\mathbb R^{3})^{N}\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^{3N}\times\mathbb R^{3N},$$

an open subset of $\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^{6N}$; a point $(t,x,v)\in D$ is a
time together with the **state** $z=(x,v)$ of positions $x\in Q$ and coordinate
velocities $v\in(\mathbb R^{3})^{N}$ of the labels ([[def-cm01-velocity-acceleration]],
[[def-cm01-units]]). The **inverse-mass operator** is the linear map

$$\mathsf M^{-1}:\mathbb R^{3N}\to\mathbb R^{3N},\qquad \mathsf M^{-1}(u_{1},\dots,u_{N}):=\Bigl(\frac{u_{1}}{m_{1}},\dots,\frac{u_{N}}{m_{N}}\Bigr),$$

the inverse of the mass operator $\mathsf M$ of clause (d) of
[[def-cm01-configuration]].

**(b) Associated first-order system.** The **associated first-order field** of
the model is

$$\mathcal F:D\longrightarrow\mathbb R^{3N}\times\mathbb R^{3N},\qquad \mathcal F(t,x,v):=\Bigl(v,\ \mathsf M^{-1}F(t,x,v)\Bigr),$$

and the **associated first-order system** is $z'=\mathcal F(t,z)$ on the open
domain $D$, in the sense of
[[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]]; here
$z=(x,v)\in\mathbb R^{6N}$. The map $\mathcal F$ satisfies the
Picard–Lindelöf hypotheses of
[[thm-picard-lindelof-local-existence-and-uniqueness]]: it is continuous on
$D$, and it is locally Lipschitz in the state variable $z$ locally uniformly
in time, because its first component $z\mapsto v$ is linear and its second is
the composition of the force map $F$ — which is locally Lipschitz in $(x,v)$
locally uniformly in time by [[post-cm02-force-superposition]] clause (iii) —
with the linear map $\mathsf M^{-1}$.

**(c) Motions.** Let $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval with nonempty
interior, endpoints read with one-sided derivatives as in
[[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]]. A **motion** of
the model on $J$ is a curve $x:J\to Q$ of class $C^{2}$ such that
$t\in I_{0}$ for every $t\in J$ and

$$m_{i}\,\ddot x_{i}(t)=F_{i}\bigl(t,x(t),\dot x(t)\bigr)\qquad(i=1,\dots,N,\ t\in J).$$

Equivalently: the state curve $z=(x,\dot x):J\to D$ is a solution of the
associated first-order system on $J$. Indeed, if $x$ is a motion then
$z=(x,x')$ is $C^{1}$ with
$z'=(x',x'')=(x',\mathsf M^{-1}F(t,x,x'))=\mathcal F(t,z)$ and $z(t)\in D$;
conversely, if $z=(x,v)$ is a solution with $z(t)\in D$ for all $t$, then
$x'=v$ and $v'=\mathsf M^{-1}F(t,x,v)$, so $v$ is $C^{1}$, $x$ is $C^{2}$, and
multiplying the second equation by the masses returns the displayed
second-order equation. Motions of the labels of the model are exactly these
curves by [[post-cm02-force-superposition]] clause (iv).

**(d) Initial data and maximal motion.** An **initial datum** of the model is
a triple $(t_{0},x_{0},v_{0})$ with $t_{0}\in I_{0}$, $x_{0}\in Q$ and
$v_{0}\in(\mathbb R^{3})^{N}$; write $z_{0}:=(x_{0},v_{0})$. A **maximal
motion** with this datum is a motion $x:J_{\max}\to Q$ with $x(t_{0})=x_{0}$
and $\dot x(t_{0})=v_{0}$ that has no extension to a motion of the model on a
strictly larger interval. By the Picard–Lindelöf hypotheses verified in (b)
and the maximal-solution theorem
[[thm-existence-and-uniqueness-of-a-maximal-ode-solution]] (with
[[def-maximal-ode-solution]]): every initial datum has exactly one maximal
motion, its **maximal interval** $J_{\max}$ is an open interval containing
$t_{0}$ and contained in $I_{0}$, and every motion with the same datum is the
restriction of the maximal one. The restriction statement transfers from the
associated first-order system to motions through the equivalence in (c).

**(e) Newtonian flow.** The **Newtonian flow** of the model is the map

$$\Phi:\Omega\longrightarrow Q\times\mathbb R^{3N},\qquad \Omega:=\bigl\{(t,t_{0},z_{0}):t_{0}\in I_{0},\ z_{0}\in Q\times\mathbb R^{3N},\ t\in J_{\max}(t_{0},z_{0})\bigr\},$$

defined by $\Phi(t;t_{0},z_{0}):=z(t)$, where $t\mapsto z(t)=(x(t),\dot x(t))$
is the state curve of the maximal motion with datum $(t_{0},z_{0})$. By (d) the
assignment is well defined: the maximal motion is unique, so $\Phi$ is a
function on $\Omega$ and not merely a relation. For fixed $t_{0}$ and $z_{0}$
the curve $t\mapsto\Phi(t;t_{0},z_{0})$ is defined exactly on the maximal
interval $J_{\max}(t_{0},z_{0})$.

Let $k\in\mathbb N$, let $m,q\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$. A map $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$ is of class $C^k$ when each component is of class $C^k$. Each scalar component uses the word-derivative convention of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]], whose source dimension is positive. The map is **smooth**, or $C^\infty$, when it is $C^k$ for every $k\in\mathbb N$.

Let $n\ge1$ and let $U,V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open. A bijection $f:U\to V$ is a **$C^k$ diffeomorphism** when both $f$ and $f^{-1}$ are $C^k$. For $k\ge1$, a **local $C^k$ diffeomorphism at $a\in U$** is a restriction $f|_P:P\to Q$ between open neighbourhoods of $a$ and $f(a)$ that is a $C^k$ diffeomorphism. At $k=1$ this agrees with [[def-c-one-map-and-local-inverse]]: continuous first partial derivatives give the required total derivative by [[thm-continuous-partial-derivatives-imply-total-differentiability]], while continuity of the total derivative gives continuity of its matrix entries and hence of the first partial derivatives.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, $a\in U$, $v\in\mathbb R^m$, and $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$. If the line map $t\mapsto f(a+tv)$ is defined near $0$, its derivative at $0$ is the **directional derivative**

$$D_vf(a):=\lim_{t\to0}\frac{f(a+tv)-f(a)}{t}.$$

For a standard basis vector $e_j$ ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]), $D_{e_j}f(a)$ is the **$j$th partial derivative**, written $\partial_jf(a)$. These are ordinary vector-valued one-variable derivatives in the sense of [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]].

If every partial derivative $\partial_jf_i(a)$ of $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ exists, the **Jacobian matrix** is $Jf(a)=(\partial_jf_i(a))_{i<n,j<m}$. For scalar-valued $f$, its **gradient** is

$$\nabla f(a):=(\partial_0f(a),\ldots,\partial_{m-1}f(a))\in\mathbb R^m,$$

with coordinates understood in the standard basis ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]). The partial derivatives are those of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]].

The functions $\sin$ and $\cos$ are differentiable on $\mathbb R$, with
$$(\sin x)'=\cos x,\qquad(\cos x)'=-\sin x.$$
Also $\sin0=0$ and $\cos0=1$.

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) at which $g$ is differentiable
([[def-derivative]]), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

For every real $x$,
$$\sin x=0\Longleftrightarrow x=m\pi\text{ for some }m\in\mathbb Z,\qquad \cos x=0\Longleftrightarrow x=(m+1/2)\pi\text{ for some }m\in\mathbb Z.$$
Both sine and cosine have period $2\pi$, and no smaller positive number is a common period.

For every real $x$,
$$\sin(-x)=-\sin x,\qquad\cos(-x)=\cos x,\qquad\sin^2x+\cos^2x=1.$$
Consequently $|\sin x|\le1$ and $|\cos x|\le1$.

Let $I \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be order-convex with at least two elements
([[def-interval]]), let $f : I \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $I$
([[def-continuity-real]]) and injective
([[def-injection-surjection-bijection]]), and let $g : f[I] \to I$ be the
inverse of $f : I \to f[I]$ supplied by [[thm-continuous-inverse]]. Let
$c \in I$ and put $b := f(c)$.

Then $c$ is a limit point of $I$ and $b$ is a limit point of $f[I]$, so that
$f'(c)$ and $g'(b)$ are meaningful symbols ([[def-derivative]]), and, assuming
$f$ is differentiable at $c$:

1. if $f'(c) \ne 0$, then $g$ is differentiable at $b$ and
   $$g'(b) \;=\; \frac{1}{f'(c)} ;$$
2. if $f'(c) = 0$, then $g$ is **not** differentiable at $b$.

**The two claims together say that the inverse inherits differentiability
exactly where the derivative does not vanish.** Nothing is asserted at a point
of $f[I]$ that is not of the form $f(c)$ with $f$ differentiable at $c$, and
nothing is asserted about $g$ being differentiable *on* a set.

**No compactness and no boundedness is assumed.** $I$ may be open, half-open or
unbounded; all that is used of it is order-convexity and the presence of two
distinct points, the latter being exactly what makes every point of $I$ a limit
point of $I$ ([[def-derivative]]).

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]), neighbourhoods are those of
[[def-neighbourhood-r]] and limit points those of [[def-limit-point-r]].

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $c \in A$ be a
**limit point of $A$**. The **difference quotient of $f$ at $c$** is the function

$$q_{f,c} : A \setminus \{c\} \to \mathbb{R}, \qquad q_{f,c}(x) := \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c} .$$

The division is legitimate at every point of the domain, since $x \ne c$ gives
$x - c \ne 0$.

**The point $c$ is a limit point of $A \setminus \{c\}$, not merely of $A$.**
For every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the punctured neighbourhood
$N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c)$ omits $c$, so

$$N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c) \cap A \;=\; N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c) \cap (A \setminus \{c\}) ,$$

and the left-hand side is nonempty because $c$ is a limit point of $A$. So
$q_{f,c}$ is a function on a set having $c$ as a limit point, and
$\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x)$ is a notion that [[def-function-limit]] defines.

$f$ is **differentiable at $c$** when that limit exists, and then the
**derivative of $f$ at $c$** is

$$f'(c) \;:=\; \lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x) \;=\; \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c} .$$

**Two obligations are carried by that notation, and both are discharged here.**

1. **Uniqueness.** Writing $f'(c)$ treats the right-hand side as a name for a
   single real number. That is legitimate: $c$ is a limit point of the domain
   $A \setminus \{c\}$ of $q_{f,c}$, so at most one real can satisfy the
   $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ condition, by [[lem-function-limit-unique]] applied to
   $q_{f,c}$. Two reals both meeting the condition are therefore equal, and the
   symbol denotes.
2. **Meaningfulness.** The hypothesis that $c$ is a limit point of $A$ is not
   decoration. At an **isolated** point of $A$ the punctured condition
   $0 < |x - c| < \delta$ is met by no point of the domain at all, so the
   $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ formula is satisfied vacuously by *every* real at
   once; this is why [[def-function-limit]] leaves the limit undefined there,
   and it is why this library defines $f'(c)$ only at a limit point of $A$. At
   an isolated point of its domain a function is neither differentiable nor
   non-differentiable here: the question is not posed.

**The limit sees only $A \setminus \{c\}$, so how the difference quotient is
extended to $c$ is irrelevant.** Let $Q : A \to \mathbb{R}$ agree with
$q_{f,c}$ at every point of $A \setminus \{c\}$, and let $L \in \mathbb{R}$.
Then $\lim_{x \to c} Q(x) = L$ if and only if $\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x) = L$.
Both conditions read: for every real $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a real
$\delta > 0$ such that every point $x$ of the relevant domain with
$0 < |x - c| < \delta$ satisfies $|{\cdot} - L| < \varepsilon$
([[def-function-limit]]). The clause $0 < |x - c|$ removes $x = c$ from both
quantifiers, so in both cases the points quantified over are exactly the
$x \in A \setminus \{c\}$ with $0 < |x - c| < \delta$, at which $Q$ and
$q_{f,c}$ take the same value. The two conditions are the same condition.

**Differentiability on a set.** For $S \subseteq A$, $f$ is **differentiable on
$S$** when it is differentiable at every $c \in S$; implicit in that phrase is
that every point of $S$ is a limit point of $A$. $f$ is **differentiable** when
it is differentiable on the whole of $A$.

**Restriction of the domain.** Let $B \subseteq A$, let $c \in B$ and suppose
$c$ is a limit point of $B$. If $f$ is differentiable at $c$, then so is the
restriction $f|_B : B \to \mathbb{R}$, and

$$(f|_B)'(c) \;=\; f'(c) .$$

Indeed $B \setminus \{c\} \subseteq A \setminus \{c\}$; the displayed identity
of punctured neighbourhoods above, applied to $B$, shows that $c$ is a limit
point of $B \setminus \{c\}$; the difference quotient $q_{f|_B, c}$ is the
restriction of $q_{f,c}$ to $B \setminus \{c\}$, since $f|_B(c) = f(c)$; and
claim 2 of [[lem-limit-is-local]] carries the limit to that restriction.

**Every point of a nondegenerate interval is a limit point of it.** Let
$J \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be order-convex ([[def-interval]]) with at least two
elements and let $p \in J$. Choose $q \in J$ with $q \ne p$, and let a real
$\varepsilon > 0$ be given. If $p < q$, put $y := p + \tfrac{1}{2}\min\{\varepsilon,\ q - p\}$;
then $p < y$, and $y - p \le \tfrac{1}{2}(q-p) < q - p$, so $p < y < q$ and
order-convexity gives $y \in J$, while $0 < |y - p| < \varepsilon$. If $q < p$,
the point $y := p - \tfrac{1}{2}\min\{\varepsilon,\ p - q\}$ serves in the same
way. So $N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(p) \cap J \ne \varnothing$ for every real
$\varepsilon > 0$, that is, $p$ is a limit point of $J$
([[def-limit-point-r]]).

Consequently, for $f$ defined on a nondegenerate interval $I$, the symbol
$f'(c)$ is meaningful at **every** $c \in I$, endpoints included. At an endpoint
the difference quotient is taken over the points of $I$ lying on the one side
that is available, so what other texts call a one-sided derivative is, here,
simply the derivative of $f$ on $I$.

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-ordered-field]]) with its order
([[def-real-order]]).

A subset $I \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is **order-convex** when

$$x, y \in I \text{ and } x \le z \le y \;\Longrightarrow\; z \in I .$$

The **intervals** of $\mathbb{R}$ are the sets of the following nine forms, where
$a, b \in \mathbb{R}$:

| | bounded forms | | one-sided and full forms |
|---|---|---|---|
| $(a,b)$ | $\{x : a < x < b\}$ | $(a,\infty)$ | $\{x : a < x\}$ |
| $[a,b]$ | $\{x : a \le x \le b\}$ | $[a,\infty)$ | $\{x : a \le x\}$ |
| $[a,b)$ | $\{x : a \le x < b\}$ | $(-\infty,b)$ | $\{x : x < b\}$ |
| $(a,b]$ | $\{x : a < x \le b\}$ | $(-\infty,b]$ | $\{x : x \le b\}$ |
| | | $(-\infty,\infty)$ | $\mathbb{R}$ |

An interval is **open** when both of its written endpoints are excluded, that is
for the forms $(a,b)$, $(a,\infty)$, $(-\infty,b)$ and $(-\infty,\infty)$; it is
**closed** when both written endpoints are included, that is for $[a,b]$,
$[a,\infty)$, $(-\infty,b]$ and $(-\infty,\infty)$. The forms $[a,b)$ and
$(a,b]$ are **half-open**.

**The symbols $\pm\infty$ are notation and not elements of $\mathbb{R}$.** They
mark which side carries no endpoint condition at all; the five forms in the right
column are defined by the displayed conditions on $x$ alone, and no arithmetic is
ever performed with $\infty$. This is the same refusal to extend $\mathbb{R}$
silently that [[rem-sup-conventions]] records for suprema.

**Every one of the nine forms is order-convex.** Each is defined by a conjunction
of at most two conditions, each of the shape $a < x$, $a \le x$, $x < b$ or
$x \le b$, and each such condition is inherited by an intermediate point: if
$a < x$ and $x \le z$ then $a < z$, and if $z \le y$ and $y < b$ then $z < b$,
by transitivity of the order ([[def-ordered-field]]). Applying this to whichever
one or two conditions define the form in question gives $z \in I$ whenever
$x, y \in I$ and $x \le z \le y$.

**Bounded intervals.** An interval is **bounded** ([[def-bounded-set]]) exactly
when it is of one of the four forms in the left column: for those, $a$ is a lower
bound and $b$ an upper bound. The other five forms are unbounded, on the side or
sides written with $\infty$; the verification is in the remarks below.

**Nondegeneracy.** An interval is **degenerate** when it has at most one element,
and **nondegenerate** when it has at least two. For the four bounded forms with
endpoints $a$ and $b$:

- $[a,b]$ is nonempty exactly when $a \le b$, and it is nondegenerate exactly
  when $a < b$. It is the singleton $\{a\}$ when $a = b$.
- $(a,b)$, $[a,b)$ and $(a,b]$ are nonempty exactly when $a < b$, and then each
  is nondegenerate.

The only assertion here that is not immediate from the defining conditions is
that $a < b$ makes $(a,b)$ nonempty with at least two points. It holds because
$a < (a+b)/2 < b$, which follows from $a < b$ by adding $a$, respectively $b$, to
both sides and halving ([[def-ordered-field]]); repeating the halving inside
$(a, (a+b)/2)$ produces a second point.

**Closed bounded intervals.** These are the sets $[a,b]$ with $a \le b$, which is
exactly the condition making them nonempty. They are the intervals the nested
interval property is stated for, and the phrase *closed bounded interval* always
carries the hypothesis $a \le b$ in this library.

**Length.** The **length** of a bounded interval presented by its endpoints
$a \le b$ is

$$\ell = b - a \;\ge\; 0 .$$

Length is attached to the presentation by endpoints and is not recovered from the
set: $(a,b)$, $[a,b)$ and $(a,b]$ are all empty when $a = b$, and so is
$(c,c)$ for any other $c$, while each of these presentations has length $0$, so
nothing inconsistent arises; but the endpoints are named explicitly at every
point where a length is used in this library, and never inferred from the set.
Unbounded intervals are assigned no length.

Adopt the force model with potential presentation $(U,d)$ and mechanical
Lagrangian $L=K-U$ of [[def-cm07-action-and-mechanical-lagrangian]] with the
data and conventions of [[def-cm12-cotangent-momentum]]: masses
$m_{1},\dots,m_{N}>0$, open configuration domain $Q\subseteq\mathbb R^{3N}$,
time window $I_{0}$, mass operator $\mathsf M$
([[def-cm01-configuration]]), $C^{2}$ potential $U$ and residual forces $d$
of the standing regularity ([[def-cm03-potential-and-mechanical-energy]],
[[post-cm02-force-superposition]]). Assume the presentation is hyperregular
on its charts, with the Hamiltonians $H$ and $\widetilde H$ and inverse
Legendre branches of [[def-cm12-hamiltonian]],
[[def-cm12-hyperregularity]],
[[pthm-cm12-mechanical-hyperregularity]]. The momentum charts, their forms
and their canonical coordinates are those of [[def-cm13-two-form]] and
[[def-cm13-canonical-form]]; dimensions are read by [[def-cm01-units]] and
differentiability classes are those of
[[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]].

**(a) The chart datum.** Fix one momentum chart of the presentation: either
the Cartesian chart with the coordinates $(t,x,p)$ on
$I_{0}\times Q\times\mathbb R^{3N}$ and the Hamiltonian $H$ of
[[def-cm12-hamiltonian]] clause (a), or the chart of a
generalized-coordinate map $X:\Omega\to Q$ with $r$ coordinates, the
coordinates $(t,q,p)$ on $I_{0}\times\Omega\times\mathbb R^{r}$ and the
Hamiltonian $\widetilde H$ of clause (b). Write $m\in\{3N,r\}$ for the
number of momentum pairs, let $V\subseteq\mathbb R^{m}$ denote the
configuration-coordinate domain of the chart ($Q$ in the Cartesian case,
$\Omega$ in the other), and write $H$ for the corresponding Hamiltonian,

$$H:I_{0}\times V\times\mathbb R^{m}\longrightarrow\mathbb R,\qquad (t,q,p)\longmapsto H(t,q,p),$$

a function of class $C^{2}$ and dimension $\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-2}$ (energy) by
[[pthm-cm12-mechanical-hyperregularity]]. Let $J'\subseteq I_{0}$,
$U'\subseteq V$ and $A'\subseteq\mathbb R^{m}$ be nonempty open sets
([[def-metric-topology]], [[def-interval]]).

**(b) Solutions of the equation.** A map

$$S:J'\times U'\times A'\longrightarrow\mathbb R,\qquad (t,q,\alpha)\longmapsto S(t,q,\alpha),$$

of class $C^{3}$ **solves the Hamilton-Jacobi equation associated with $H$
on $J'\times U'\times A'$** when

$$S_{t}(t,q,\alpha)+H\bigl(t,\,q,\,S_{q}(t,q,\alpha)\bigr)=0\qquad\bigl((t,q,\alpha)\in J'\times U'\times A'\bigr),$$
where $S_{t}$ is the partial derivative in $t$ and
$S_{q}=(S_{q^{1}},\dots,S_{q^{m}})$ is the gradient in $q$
([[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]],
[[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]); the momentum slot of $H$ is
substituted by $p=S_{q}(t,q,\alpha)$. This is exactly the mathematical
Hamilton-Jacobi equation of
[[def-cm-hamilton-jacobi-equation-and-complete-integral]] associated with
the function $H$ on the open set $J'\times U'\times\mathbb R^{m}$, read in
the chart coordinates $(t,q,p)$; the two definitions determine the same
class of functions.

**(c) Dimensions and chart consistency.** The equation forces
$[S]=\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-1}$ (action): $S_{t}$ has dimension $[S]\tau^{-1}$
and $H$ has dimension $\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-2}$, while each $S_{q^{a}}$ has
dimension $[S]/\gamma_{a}$ with $\gamma_{a}$ the declared dimension of the
coordinate $q^{a}$ in this chart; the substitution is dimensionally
consistent in every chart because the chart momenta of
[[def-cm12-cotangent-momentum]] have dimension
$\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-1}\gamma_{a}^{-1}$. In the Cartesian chart all
$\gamma_{a}=\ell$ and $[S]/\ell=\mu\ell\tau^{-1}$, the momentum dimension.

**(d) Status.** The equation is attached to the declared datum: replacing
the chart, the inverse Legendre branch or the potential representative
changes $H$ by the rules recorded in clause (d) of
[[def-cm12-hamiltonian]] and hence changes the equation, and a solution
family $S$ is a solution for that datum only. The item defines a class of
functions; whether a given datum admits solutions, and how solutions
produce curves of the model, is not asserted here. In particular no
existence theorem, no global solution, no equation of motion for the model,
no conservation law and no measured value is claimed.

Adopt the datum of [[def-cm14-hamilton-jacobi-equation]]: one momentum chart
of a hyperregular potential presentation, its $C^{2}$ Hamiltonian $H$ of
dimension $\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-2}$ on $I_{0}\times V\times\mathbb R^{m}$, open
sets $J'\subseteq I_{0}$, $U'\subseteq V$ and $A'\subseteq\mathbb R^{m}$,
and a $C^{3}$ map $S:J'\times U'\times A'\to\mathbb R$ that solves the
Hamilton-Jacobi equation associated with $H$ on $J'\times U'\times A'$.
Dimensions are read by [[def-cm01-units]] and differentiability classes are
those of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]].

**(a) Complete integral.** Let $(t_{0},q_{0},\alpha_{0})\in
J'\times U'\times A'$. The solution $S$ is a **complete integral of the
model's Hamilton-Jacobi equation at $(t_{0},q_{0},\alpha_{0})$** when the
mixed derivative

$$S_{q\alpha}(t,q,\alpha):=\Bigl(\frac{\partial^{2}S}{\partial q^{a}\partial\alpha_{j}}(t,q,\alpha)\Bigr)_{a,j=1}^{m}\in\mathbb R^{m\times m}$$
is invertible at the base point, $\det S_{q\alpha}(t_{0},q_{0},\alpha_{0})
\ne0$ ([[def-determinant-of-a-square-matrix]],
[[def-invertible-euclidean-linear-map]], mixed partials being those of
[[def-total-derivative-in-euclidean-space]]). This is exactly the
mathematical notion of a complete integral of
[[def-cm-hamilton-jacobi-equation-and-complete-integral]] applied to the
function $H$ on the chart domain $J'\times U'\times\mathbb R^{m}$.

**(b) Parameters and their dimensions.** The third variable
$\alpha=(\alpha_{1},\dots,\alpha_{m})$ is read with the declared coordinate
dimensions $\gamma_{a}$ of $q$ in the fixed chart,
$[\alpha_{j}]=\gamma_{j}$. With this reading the entries of
$S_{q\alpha}$ are dimensionless, so the nondegeneracy condition is
dimensionally meaningful and chart-consistent, and the momentum map below
carries the momentum dimension.

**(c) Momentum map and Jacobi constants.** For a complete integral $S$ the
**momentum map** and the **Jacobi constants** of $S$ are the maps

$$p(t,q,\alpha):=S_{q}(t,q,\alpha),\qquad\beta(t,q,\alpha):=S_{\alpha}(t,q,\alpha),$$
so that $p$ has the chart-momentum dimensions of
[[def-cm12-cotangent-momentum]], $[p_{a}]=\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-1}
\gamma_{a}^{-1}$, and $\beta$ has the same dimensions as $p$,
$[\beta_{j}]=\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-1}\gamma_{j}^{-1}$: the product
$\beta_{j}\,\alpha_{j}$ has the action dimension $\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-1}$ of
$S$. The pair $(\beta,\alpha)$ is the **Jacobi data** of the complete
integral at the base point.

**(d) Status.** The item defines data attached to the presentation and to
the chosen solution. It asserts neither that a complete integral exists
for a given presentation, nor that its characteristic curves are motions
of the model, nor that $\beta$ is constant along such curves; those are
the claims of the page's characteristics theorem. It also
asserts no global statement: $\det S_{q\alpha}\ne0$ is required at the
base point only, and the theorem below records its local consequences.

Adopt the force model with potential presentation $(U,d)$ and mechanical
Lagrangian $L=K-U$ of [[def-cm07-action-and-mechanical-lagrangian]] with the
data and conventions of [[def-cm12-cotangent-momentum]]: masses
$m_{1},\dots,m_{N}>0$, open configuration domain $Q\subseteq\mathbb R^{3N}$,
time window $I_{0}$, mass operator $\mathsf M$
([[def-cm01-configuration]]), $C^{2}$ potential $U$ and residual forces $d$
of the standing regularity ([[def-cm03-potential-and-mechanical-energy]],
[[post-cm02-force-superposition]]), the presentation being hyperregular on
its charts ([[pthm-cm12-mechanical-hyperregularity]],
[[def-cm12-hamiltonian]]). Fix one momentum chart of the presentation
(Cartesian coordinates $(t,x,p)$, or the chart $(t,q,p)$ of a
generalized-coordinate map $X:\Omega\to Q$
([[def-cm07-generalized-coordinates-and-forces]])), with $m$ pairs of
coordinates and Hamiltonian $H$ of class $C^{2}$ on
$J_{0}\times V\times\mathbb R^{m}$; let $S:J\times U\times A\to\mathbb R$
be a $C^{3}$ complete integral of the model's Hamilton-Jacobi equation at
$(t_{0},q_{0},\alpha_{0})\in J\times U\times A$ in the sense of
[[def-cm14-hamilton-jacobi-equation]] and [[def-cm14-complete-integral]]
($J\subseteq J_{0}$, $U\subseteq V$, $A\subseteq\mathbb R^{m}$ open), and
put

$$\beta_{0}:=S_{\alpha}(t_{0},q_{0},\alpha_{0}).$$

Then:

1. **(characteristic curves)** For every $\alpha$ sufficiently close to
   $\alpha_{0}$ there is an open interval $I_{\alpha}\ni t_{0}$ and a
   $C^{1}$ curve $q:I_{\alpha}\to U$ with $q(t_{0})=q_{0}$ solving
   $q'(t)=H_{p}\bigl(t,q(t),S_{q}(t,q(t),\alpha)\bigr)$, and with
   $p(t):=S_{q}(t,q(t),\alpha)$ the pair $(q,p)$ satisfies Hamilton's
   equations $q'=H_{p}$, $p'=-H_{q}$ on $I_{\alpha}$. If the chart is the
   Cartesian chart and $d\equiv0$ on the state domain, then $x:=q$ is a
   motion of the model on $I_{\alpha}$ and $p(t)=\mathsf Mx'(t)$
   ([[def-cm02-newtonian-flow]], [[def-cm12-cotangent-momentum]]); if the
   chart is the chart of a generalized-coordinate map and $d\equiv0$, then
   $q$ solves the declared Lagrange equations of the substituted
   Lagrangian and $p(t)=G(q(t))q'(t)$
   ([[def-cm07-generalized-coordinates-and-forces]],
   [[pthm-cm12-hamilton-equivalence]]).
2. **(Jacobi constants)** With $(q,p)$ as in clause 1,
   $\beta(t):=S_{\alpha}(t,q(t),\alpha)$ is constant on $I_{\alpha}$ and
   equal to $S_{\alpha}(t_{0},q_{0},\alpha)$.
3. **(local converse)** For $(\alpha,\beta)$ sufficiently close to
   $(\alpha_{0},\beta_{0})$ the equation $\beta=S_{\alpha}(t,q,\alpha)$
   can be solved locally for $q=Q(t,\alpha,\beta)$, and with
   $p:=S_{q}\bigl(t,Q(t,\alpha,\beta),\alpha\bigr)$ the curve
   $t\mapsto(Q,p)$ solves Hamilton's equations; in the Cartesian chart on
   the potential branch it is the momentum-phase curve of a motion of the
   model.
4. **(canonical labels)** On the domain of the local diffeomorphism
   $(q,p)\mapsto(\beta,\alpha)$ obtained by composing
   $(q,p)\mapsto(q,\alpha)$ (solving $p=S_{q}$) with
   $(q,\alpha)\mapsto(\beta,\alpha)$, one has
   $\omega=d\beta\wedge d\alpha$ at every fixed $t$, where $\omega$ is the
   two-form of the presentation in this chart
   ([[def-cm13-two-form]]); equivalently, $(\beta,\alpha)$ are canonical
   coordinates of the presentation in the sense of clause (a) of
   [[def-cm13-canonical-form]].

Adopt the force model with potential presentation $(U,d)$ and mechanical
Lagrangian $L=K-U$ of [[def-cm07-action-and-mechanical-lagrangian]], with the
momentum charts and two-form datum of [[def-cm13-two-form]] and the canonical
coordinates of [[def-cm13-canonical-form]]: the Cartesian phase domain
$W=Q\times\mathbb R^{3N}$, its two-form $\omega$, a generalized-coordinate
chart map $\Phi_{X}$ and the form $\omega_{X}$
([[def-cm07-generalized-coordinates-and-forces]]); the presentation is
hyperregular on every chart with the Hamiltonian $H$ of
[[def-cm12-hamiltonian]] and [[pthm-cm12-mechanical-hyperregularity]],

$$H(t,x,p)=\tfrac12\,p\cdot\mathsf M^{-1}p+U(t,x),\qquad \widetilde H(t,q,P)=\tfrac12\,P\cdot G(q)^{-1}P+\widetilde U(t,q).$$

Differentiability classes are those of
[[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]], and gradients those of
[[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]].

**(a) The field of a phase function.** Let $W_{0}\subseteq W$ be nonempty
open and let $f:W_{0}\to\mathbb R$ be of class $C^{2}$. By clause 1 of
[[pthm-cm13-two-form-is-symplectic]] the form $\omega$ is nondegenerate on
$W_{0}$, so there is exactly one $C^{1}$ vector field $X_{f}$ on $W_{0}$ with

$$\iota_{X_{f}}\omega=df$$

(the sign convention of [[def-hamiltonian-vector-field-and-hamiltonian-function]]
and [[prop-cm-hamiltonian-field-and-poisson-bracket-in-a-phase-chart]]); it
is the **Hamiltonian field of $f$ for the presentation**. In the Cartesian
coordinates $(x,p)$, writing $\nabla f=(f_{x^{1}},\dots,f_{x^{3N}},f_{p_{1}},\dots,f_{p_{3N}})$,

$$X_{f}=\bigl(f_{p},\,-f_{x}\bigr)=J\nabla f,\qquad J=\begin{pmatrix}0_{3N}&I_{3N}\\-I_{3N}&0_{3N}\end{pmatrix};$$

in any canonical chart $(\theta^{1},\dots,\theta^{2m})$ of the presentation
the same field reads $X_{f}=\bigl(f_{\theta^{m+1}},\dots,f_{\theta^{2m}},-f_{\theta^{1}},\dots,-f_{\theta^{m}}\bigr)$.
A vector field on $W_{0}$ is called **Hamiltonian for the presentation** when
it is $X_{f}$ for some $C^{2}$ function $f$; in particular
$X_{f}=0$ exactly when $f$ is locally constant on $W_{0}$. Vector fields are
read as tangent-bundle sections of
[[def-smooth-vector-field-as-a-tangent-bundle-section]].

**(b) The field of the branch Hamiltonian.** For each $t\in I_{0}$ the
function $H_{t}:=H(t,\cdot)$ is $C^{2}$ on $W$, and the **Hamiltonian field
of the presentation** at time $t$ is $X_{H_{t}}$:

$$X_{H_{t}}(x,p)=\bigl(\mathsf M^{-1}p,\ -\nabla_{x}U(t,x)\bigr),$$

whose components are a velocity and a force. In the coordinates $X$ the
corresponding field is
$X_{\widetilde H_{t}}(q,P)=\bigl(G(q)^{-1}P,\ -\partial_{q}\widetilde H(t,q,P)\bigr)$,
where the second slot retains the kinetic contribution
$-\tfrac12P\cdot\partial_{q}(G(q)^{-1})P$ when the metric varies. If
$d\not\equiv0$ the model's forced evolution carries the additional momentum
source $d$; the corresponding vector field
$(x,p)\mapsto\bigl(\mathsf M^{-1}p,-\nabla_{x}U(t,x)+d(t,x,\mathsf M^{-1}p)\bigr)$
is generally not a Hamiltonian field for the presentation, and it is one
exactly when the residual force has a potential independent of the velocity
slot (the criterion is proved in clause 4 of the corresponding theorem of this
page).

**(c) Time dependence and status.** For a time-dependent $H$ the assignment
$t\mapsto X_{H_{t}}$ is a time-dependent field on the phase domain; each
$X_{H_{t}}$ is $C^{1}$, hence locally Lipschitz in the state variable, and no
completeness of its integral curves is asserted here. The item defines the
field datum and its chart expressions; the identification of the model's
motions with the integral curves, and all conservation or invariance
properties, are the subject of the other items of this page. The field is
defined by the intrinsic equation $\iota_{X}\omega=dH$ and therefore does not
depend on the canonical chart used to compute it.

derivations.claim: Mixed derivative: by [L2], differentiating the displayed $S$ gives $S_{x}=m\omega(x\cot(\omega t)-\alpha\csc(\omega t))$ and hence $S_{x\alpha}=-m\omega\csc(\omega t)=-m\omega/\sin(\omega t)$; this is finite and nonzero exactly when $\sin(\omega t)\neq0$, and $|S_{x\alpha}|\to+\infty$ as $\omega t\to k\pi$, $k\in\mathbb Z$, because $\sin(k\pi)=0$. By [L3] and the companion computation that $S$ solves $S_{t}+H(x,S_{x})=0$ on the strips, $S$ is a complete integral at every point of the strips and has no finite nondegenerate extension across the conjugate times. This is claim 1.

Characteristic curves: by [L3], solving $\beta=S_{\alpha}(t,x,\alpha) =m\omega(\alpha\cot(\omega t)-x\csc(\omega t))$ for $x$ gives $x(t)=\alpha\cos(\omega t)-\frac{\beta}{m\omega}\sin(\omega t),$ and with $p=S_{x}$ the pair solves $x'=p/m$, $p'=-m\omega^{2}x$; explicitly $x'(t)=-\alpha\omega\sin(\omega t)-\beta m^{-1}\cos(\omega t)$ and $\partial_{\beta}x(t)=-\sin(\omega t)/(m\omega)$, which vanishes exactly at $\omega t\in\pi\mathbb Z$; moreover $(\partial_{\beta}x)(t)=1/S_{x\alpha}(t)$ by step 1.1. At those times the label $\beta$ has no first-order effect on the position, so the map from the Jacobi label to the position degenerates while the mixed derivative is unbounded: this is the conjugate time of the family. This is claim 2.

Refocusing: by [L1] the curve $x(t;q)=x_{0}\cos(\omega(t-t_{0}))+qm^{-1}\omega^{-1} \sin(\omega(t-t_{0}))$ is the motion of the model with $x(t_{0})=x_{0}$ and $x'(t_{0})=q/m$. At $t_{1}=t_{0}+\pi/\omega$, [L2] gives $\cos\pi=-1$ and $\sin\pi=0$, so $x(t_{1};q)=-x_{0}$ for every $q$, and $\partial x(t;q)/\partial q=(m\omega)^{-1}\sin(\omega(t-t_{0}))=0$ at $t=t_{1}$. Hence every member of the family of model solutions through $(t_{0},x_{0})$ passes through the single point $(t_{1},-x_{0})$, and the initial-momentum label cannot be recovered from the position at $t_{1}$; by the inverse-function rule of [L2] this is the same degeneration as in step 2.1. This is claim 3.
Claims 1-3 are steps 1.1, 2.1 and 3.1 respectively; the example is verified.

boundaries.reason: No possibly empty family occurs: the time strips and the label sets are nonempty (example).

boundaries.evidence: The labels $\alpha=0$, $\beta=0$ are included in the computations; the degeneration is in $\sin(\omega t)$, not in the labels (steps 1.1 and 2.1).
One degree of freedom is the case of the example (example).
The conjugate time $\omega t\in\pi\mathbb Z$ is exactly the degenerate case displayed: unbounded mixed derivative and refocusing (steps 1.1, 2.1 and 3.1).
The conjugate time is approached as the endpoint of each strip and is not attained; the limit of $|S_{x\alpha}|$ is computed in step 1.1.

boundaries.reason: All computations are explicit; no selection principle is used.
The pole of S_xa, the vanishing of dx/dbeta and the refocusing are computed for the single displayed family; no general equivalence between caustics and label degeneration is asserted.
The identity dx/dbeta=1/S_xa makes the two degenerations simultaneous for this family only; no converse is claimed for other families, energies or potentials.
